1572.name: The fundamentals of effective discussion
1572.description: In this unit, pupils solidify and build thier spoken language skills. They start by learning what an effective discussion is and how they can use listening skills effectively. They then look at how questions and evidence can improve discussions before practising have conversations.
1572.why: This unit starts our secondary English curriculum because it is essential pupils see the importance of building effective spoken language skills. This unit builds on the extensive spoken language practice pupils have in our primary English curriculum. In particular, it builds on their understanding of speaking and listening by showing them how they can contribute to conversations effectively to keep them going. This unit's spoken language content underpins all future units, but in particular it prepares pupils for the unit 'participating in effective debates'.

1939.name: Step into the unknown: fiction reading and creative writing
1939.description: In this unit, pupils develop their fiction reading and creative writing by reading extracts from famous fiction and then emulating key techniques in their own writing. They start by securing and extending their knowledge of key sentence grammar, before reading and emulating the extracts.
1939.why: This units uses and builds on pupils' knowledge of fiction and descriptive writing from their primary school curriculum. This unit introduces them to many of the key components of secondary English study, and gives them a strong grounding in both analytical reading and creative writing. This sets them up for the rest of the secondary English curriculum. This unit particularly prepares pupils for the 'Dystopian settings' unit where they will build on their understanding of sentence structure and variation from this unit and start to utilise it to create atmospheric settings.

234.name: 'The Tempest'
234.description: In this unit, pupils learn about the plot and characters of Shakespeare's 'The Tempest', and read sections of the play. They explore how Prospero treats Ariel, Caliban and Miranda, and write monlogues from their perspectives. Finally, they write and perform their own monologues inspired by the play.
234.why: Pupils will already have encountered some aspects of Shakespeare's plays at primary school. This unit is a bridge between primary and secondary study of Shakespeare. Rather than read the whole play, pupils explore key sections to deepen their understanding. Similarly, pupils complete creative and spoken responses to the play rather than academic critical essays. This helps to ease their transition between primary and secondary studies of Shakespeare. This unit also starts pupils' exploration of outsiders within Shakespeare's play, which is developed across all of our Shakespeare units.

238.name: Poetry about place and home
238.description: In this unit, pupils read and respond to poems that explore the links between place and identity. They start by exploring a selection of poems including Grace Nichol's 'Island Man' and Lemn Sissay's 'Anthem of the North'. They then write and perform their own poems about place and home.
238.why: Pupils explored a wide range of poetry in our primary curriculum, with a focus on how poets, including Joseph Coelho and Matt Goodfellow, responded to place in their poems. Pupils now read more complex secondary poets, and start to use analytical skills to explore the methods writers use to respond to place. They also start to emulate those more complex techniques so that their poetry writing and appreciation becomes more accomplished. Later in the curriculum, pupils look at Maya Angelou's poetry in depth to explore how context shapes a writer's voice, and then find their own poetic voice.

247.name: Sherlock Holmes: short stories
247.description: In this unit, pupils read and explore two famous Sherlock Holmes stories. They start by reading and analysing 'The Speckled Band' before using it as inspiration to write a newspaper article. They then read and analyse 'The Boscombe Valley Murder' before writing a comparison of the two stories.
247.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' reading and initial exploration of Sherlock Holmes in the primary curriculum. In primary, pupils explored retellings of Sherlock stories, but they now read Arthur Conan Doyle's original language in full and complete more analysis of his stories. They also start to learn about the Victorian context in which he was writing, which prepares them for later study of Victorian literature. This unit particulary prepares pupils for the unit 'A Monster Within', where they will read increasingly challenging nineteenth century literature and learn about the Gothic.

256.name: 'The Twisted Tree': fiction reading
256.description: In this unit, pupils read, explore and respond to the modern fairytale novel 'The Twisted Tree'. They start by reading the novel before practising writing analytically about the novel's key characters and themes. They finally respond creatively to the novel by writing an article and short script.
256.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of authorial choices from the Sherlock Holmes unit. In this unit, pupils start to develop their analytical writing more comprehensively so that they can start to write coherently and succinctly in response to a text. This unit is also the pupils' first introduction to the Gothic, which then sets up their understanding for the full 'exploring the gothic' thread. This unit prepares pupils for 'The Monster Within', where they will look at gothic fiction more deeply through some classic gothic texts.

262.name: Dystopian settings: descriptive writing
262.description: In this unit, pupils learn to write atmospheric dystopian settings. They first review and deepen their understanding of sentence types, before looking at how to use figurative language and sophisticated punctuation to enhance their descriptions. They finally plan and write a dystopian setting.
262.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of sentence structure, deliberate language choices and descriptive writing from 'A step into the unknown'. It gives pupils a deeper and more focused opportunity to extend and apply their understanding of descriptive writing to new contexts. This content prepares them for the writing elements of the Year 8 unit 'A monster within', where they continue to refine their language choices in descriptive writing by applying it to a different context with new semantic fields.

224.name: Myths, legends and stories that inspire
224.description: In this unit, pupils read and explore a range of text types in connection to classical myths and legends. They first look at poetry before doing some descriptive writing inspired by poetry and paintings. They then explore Chaucer and modern retellings of myths to inspire their narrative writing.
224.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of fiction and creative writing from the Year 7 unit 'Step into the unknown'. In this unit, they build on their understanding of how writers create vivid descriptions by looking at how they utilise powerful imagery and symbolism to make their writing more impactful. This unit prepares pupils for a number of units, including their first reading of 'Animal Farm' in Key Stage 4. In 'Animal Farm', pupils will learn more about how symbolism and allegory can be used to carry powerful messages.

228.name: 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'
228.description: In this unit, pupils read and explore Shakespeare's comedy 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'. They focus on the character Puck and the theme of the supernatural, and analyse their role and importance at different points in the play. Finally, they plan and write an essay about Puck and the supernatural.
228.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of Shakespeare, outsiders and genre from 'The Tempest'. They begin to analyse more of Shakepseare's form and techniques, as well as reading more of Shakespeare's language. They also move from creative responses to Shakespeare towards analytical reponses. This unit prepares pupils for their study of 'Othello' and 'Macbeth' by deepening their understanding of genre, form and the role of outsiders and the supernatural in Shakespeare.

1575.name: Participating in effective debates
1575.description: In this unit, pupils learn about debate and practise having debates. They first learn what a debate is, before presenting arguments for a debate and then learning how you create rebuttals in debates. Pupils then finish the unit by having a debate.
1575.why: This unit builds on the primary English units where pupils started to have simple structured debates. It also builds on the secondary English unit, 'the fundamentals of effective discussion', where pupils learnt about how to form opinions and listen carefully to others. In this unit, pupils learn how they can use their active listening skills to understand and counter other people's arguements. This unit builds towards the unit 'creating and performing slam poetry', where pupils will continue to build their confidence in articulating themselves in public speaking.

181.name: Taking a stand
181.description: In this unit, pupils learn about the different ways that writers have expressed their points of view across history. They look at some key techniques that writers use, such as motif and triad, before reading a speech, article, poem and song. They finally write and deliver their own presentation.
181.why: This is the first time in the curriculum that pupils have developed non-fiction writing and written presentations for performance. In this unit, pupils gain a strong foundation in their understanding of non-fiction conventions, and start to learn how to craft and deliver spoken language presentations. This unit prepares pupils for the 'Victorian childhood' unit, where they will practise giving presentations in a parliamentary debate, as well as answering questions about their topic.

230.name: Single poet study: Maya Angelou
230.description: In this unit, pupils read and discover the work of Maya Angelou. They explore some of Angelou's most famous poems, such as 'Caged Bird' and 'Still I Rise', and practise writing and performing poems inspired by her work. As the unit develops, pupils find their own distinctive poetic voice.
230.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of poetry, voice and performance from 'Poetry about Place and Home'. Pupils are now emulating more complex poetry, and starting to think about more complex themes of identity and belonging in their poetry. Pupils are now starting to think more about their own distinctive voice. This prepares pupils for later study of poetry, such as in their GCSE poetry anthology, and for other texts that reflect on themes of identity and belonging, such as 'Small Island' and 'Leave Taking'.

183.name: Victorian childhood: non-fiction reading and writing
183.description: In this unit, pupils read a mixture of contemporary and nineteenth-century non-fiction texts that explore a common theme of childhood. They first read and compare the texts, before then writing and delivering a speech as part of a debate on Victorian working class children.
183.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of non-fiction writing and presentation delivery from 'Taking a stand'. In this unit, they learn to create more sophisticated presentations by first learning more about a topic through wide reading. They also learn to develop a speech as part of a debate, which develops the dynamism of their spoken language. This unit preapres pupils for 'Women's rights across the ages', where they will develop and refine their spoken language capabities by learning more about tone and language choices.

189.name: A monster within: reading and writing Gothic fiction
189.description: In this unit, pupils explore the Gothic. They start by learning what the Gothic is, before reading extracts from 'Frankenstein' and 'Jane Eyre', practising descriptive writing and reading 'The Tell-Tale Heart'. They finally learn how to write opinion articles and then write their own.
189.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils first introduction to gothic ideas and themes in 'The Twisted Tree'. Pupils now read extracts from some of the most famous gothic texts in history, and analyse more deeply how they have been constructed. They also extend their understanding of fiction and non-fiction writing by deepening their understanding of gothic conventions. This unit prepares pupils for the 'gothic poetry' unit where they will look in more detail at how the Gothic is expressed in different formats.

192.name: Gothic poetry
192.description: In this unit, pupils read and explore two nineteenth-century gothic poems by Edgar Allen Poe. They first read and analyse 'The Raven' and 'The Haunted Palace' in isolation, before comparing them to each other and developing a personal response. Finally, they practise performing one of the poems.
192.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' new understanding of the Gothic from 'A Monster Within'. Having learnt about gothic fiction in 'A Monster Within', pupils now see how gothic themes can be expressed in poetry. This prepares pupils for the 'Malevolent characters' unit, where they will use their understanding of gothic fiction to write gothic stories.

193.name: A history of language
193.description: In this unit, pupils explore the history of the English Language. They first learn about the development of the English Language, before using a single word and the Lord's Prayer to explore how language changes. They then plan, write and deliver a persuasive speech about a new word.
193.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of speech writing from the earlier units 'Victorian childhood' and 'Taking a stand'. Pupils are now devloping their presentation abilities by writing them from scratch on their own concept and idea rather than relying on research and models from other lessons. This prepares pupils for later units in the curriculum, such as 'Women's rights across the ages', where they will develop increasing confidence and flair in their spoken language presentations.

204.name: 'Lord of the Flies'
204.description: In this unit, pupils read and explore 'The Lord of the Flies' by considering Golding's message about human nature. They first read the novel, before analysing the characters Ralph, Simon, Jack and Piggy. They then look at setting and symbolism before planning and writing an essay on human nature.
204.why: This unit builds on pupils' exploration of human nature and negative societal influences in 'A Monster Within'. In this unit, pupils look at a different societal context, and think more about how human nature interacts with circumstances. This prepares pupils for their first 'Modern text' study in Year 10. In particular, it prepares pupils for the 'Animal Farm' option and Orwell's exploration of the corrupting nature of power.

205.name: Women's rights across the ages: non-fiction reading and writing
205.description: In this unit, pupils read a wide range of non-fiction texts from across history that are centered around the topic of women's rights. They first read a range of texts and identify key themes and techniques within them, before then planning, writing, re-drafting and delivering their own speech.
205.why: This unit builds on pupils' understanding of non-fiction texts and speech writing from the 'Victorian childhood' unit. In this unit, they read a greater range of non-fiction texts and start to look at more sophisticated techniques to help them deliver complex ideas. They also explore how language and structure can help them to communicate their ideas. Similarly, they start looking at how re-drafting can improve their writing. This unit prepares pupils for 'non-fiction: crime and punishment', where they will start comparing non-fiction texts across time.

206.name: Malevolent characters: fiction writing
206.description: In this unit, pupils create and write malevolent characters. They first look at the conventions of malevolent characters, before learning about the techniques they can use to present their malevolent characters. They finally plan and write their fiction with a malevolent character in it.
206.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of narrative and descriptive writing from 'Myths, legends and stories that inspire'. Pupils now start to look beyond just narrative and description, and learn the importance of creating characters with distinct identities. In the process, they further develop their skills as a writer by utilising the power of dialogue and juxtaposition. This unit prepares pupils for the unit 'Fiction: read around the world' where they start emulating classic texts by practising how to write key specific parts of a narrative or description.

177.name: Literary perspectives from the First World War
177.description: In this unit, pupils explore and compare texts written about the First World War. They first read Beck's 'Propping up the line', Mansfield's 'The Fly' and Wilfred Owen's 1917 letter home to his mum. They finally read Brittain's 'Testament of Youth', and then plan and write a comparative response.
177.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of power and coflict from previous units, including 'Lord of the Flies'. In 'Lord of the Flies' pupils explored how Golding presented natural and animalistic power. In this unit, pupils see how various writers have responded to the horrors of war, and they start to compare how they present power and conflict.This deepens pupils' conceptual understanding of power and conflict, and prepares them for 'Comparing Poetry from the First World War' and Key Stage 4 poetry units, where they will see how poets respond to other conflicts.

180.name: Comparing poetry from the First World War
180.description: In this unit, pupils explore how poets responded to the horrors of the First World War. They first explore Brooke's 'The Soldier', before looking at McCrae's 'In Flanders Fields' and Naidu's 'The Gift of India'. They finally write a comparative response on perspectives of war and sacrifice.
180.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of First World War writing from the companion unit, 'Literary perspectives from the First World War'. Having looked at prose responses to the First World War, they now look at poetry responses. They also start to be more detailed and precise in their comparitve writing, which prepares them for their GCSE comparative poetry writing. In particular, this unit prepares pupils for the AQA Power and Conflict and Edexcel Conflict poetry anthologies, where pupils will critically analyse and compare poetic responses to a range of conflicts.

1580.name: Creating and performing slam poetry
1580.description: In this unit, pupils learn about slam poetry and practise performing it. They first learn what slam poetry is, before analysing and emulating the sounds used in slam poetry. They then plan and create a slam poem, before then developing their performance of it.
1580.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' previous poetry units, such as 'Single Poet Focus: Maya Angelou', and the spoken language units, such as 'Participating in effective debates'. Whilst pupils have previously performed poems and participated in debates, they now see how they can bring those skills together to create engaging poetry performances. This helps them develop their confidence in public speaking so they can engage audiences effectively. This unit builds towards the unit 'spoken language: the language of change', where pupils plan how to write impactful and engaging presentations.

211.name: 'Small Island'
211.description: In this unit, pupils explore the playtext adaptation of Andrea Levy's novel 'Small Island'. They first explore the transition from novel to stage, before reading the playtext in full and exploring key scenes in detail. They then plan and write an essay on the theme of 'hope' in the text.
211.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of drama and stagecraft from 'The Tempest', developing their understanding of identity and belonging from the characters Ariel and Caliban. The unit also builds on pupils' understanding of belonging and identity from the 'Single Poet Study: Maya Angelou' unit. Pupils are prepared for the four 'Leave Taking' units in Years 10 and 11 by being given a grounding in modern theatre stagecraft and how Black female British writers have explored modern British identity and belonging, which is further developed in 'Leave Taking'.

218.name: 'Othello'
218.description: In this unit, pupils explore Shakespeare's 'Othello'. They start by learning about Aristotelian tragedy and how Shakespeare adapted it. They read long extracts from across the play, and consider the presentation of Othello, Iago and Desdemona. Finally, they look at key themes, such as jealousy.
218.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of Shakespearean form and language from the 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' and 'The Tempest' units. It also deepens their understanding of outsiders within Shakespeare, which was started in their exploration of Puck, Caliban and Ariel in previous units. This unit prepares pupils for their deep study of 'Macbeth' at GCSE where they will continue to learn about Shakespearean tragedy and the role of outsiders within his plays.

1737.name: Simon Armitage: writing your world
1737.description: In this unit, pupils learn more about how to read and write poetry by listening to words of wisdom from the Poet Laureate, Simon Armitage. They read a range of his poems about his life and the wider world, and start to write increasingly poetically in response to them.
1737.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils understanding of poetry from the unit 'Singe poet study: Maya Angelou'. In that unit, pupils started to think more deeply about how and why poets write about their worlds. In this unit, pupils gain a richer understanding of poetry by hearing directly from one of the most prominent poets in the world, Simon Armitage. They start to recognise where poems come from, and how they have been crafted for effect. This prepares pupils for the first GCSE Poetry Anthology units, where pupils start to develop personal interpretations about a wider range of poetry.

339.name: Leave Taking: a sense of belonging
339.description: In this unit, pupils start their exploration of Winsome Pinnock's play, 'Leave Taking'. They first learn about the play's context of 1980s Britain and the Windrush generation before then reading and exploring the full play. They finally explore themes and characters before working on essay writing.
339.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of identity, belongiing, the Windrush generation and stagecraft from 'Small Island'. Pupils start to learn more about how context influences a text, and how a writer uses form to respond to the world they inhabit. They also deepen their analytical skills so they can write with more complexity and nuance about the themes of identity and belonging. This unit gives them a strong grounding in the play's plot, themes and characters, which prepares them for their three 'Leave Taking' deep dive units on education, intersectionality and stagecraft.

1605.name: An Inspector Calls: power and responsibility

1586.description: In this unit, pupils read and analyse 'Romeo and Juliet' by focusing on the role of fate. They start by understanding the play's tragedy and the concept of fate, before exploring key characters and themes in detail. They finally prepare and write an essay about the role of fate in the play.
1586.why: This unit uses and builds on pupil's understanding of Shakespearean tragedy from 'Othello'. It also develops their understanding of a Shakespearean tragic hero, and enables them to see different conceptions of tragic heroes. This unit gives pupils a firm grounding in the play's key themes, characters and scenes, which sets them up for the deep dive units in year 11. In particular, this unit builds towards the first deep dive, which focuses on the relationship between masculinity and honour and violence.

195.name: Jekyll & Hyde: duality and evil
195.description: In this unit, pupils read and explore 'A Christmas Carol'. They start by reading the novella in full, pausing during each stave to analyse key scenes, characters, themes and methods. After reading the novella, pupils chart Scrooge's redemptive journey and craft an essay on the presentation of fear.
195.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of Victorian literature from 'Sherlock Holmes: short stories', 'Victorian childhood' and 'A monster within'. In those earlier units, pupils read short Victorian stories and extracts from longer texts, but in this unit they read and analyse a full Victorian novella. Pupils now gain a deeper understanding of how Victorian writers used and debated key tropes and ideas in literature. This unit prepares pupils for the first 'A Christmas Carol' deep dive, 'A ghost story', where they start to think more conceptually and critically about the novella.

162.name: Non-fiction: crime and punishment
162.description: In this unit, pupils develop their non-fiction reading and writing skills by reading and responding to a selection of nineteenth century and modern non-fiction texts on the theme of crime and punishment. They practise summarising and comparing texts before writing an article and information text.
162.why: This unit builds on pupils' knowledge of non-fiction conventions and comparison from the the unit 'Women's rights across the ages'. Here, pupils start to explore increasingly complex texts and also develop more sophisticated and nuanced comparisons between texts. They also develop their summarising skills to show that they have comprehended what they have read, and develop their ability to emulate sophisticated skills from other non-fiction writers. This unit builds towards the unit 'Changing views', where pupils develop additional techniques to express themselves in non-fiction writing.

165.name: Fiction: read around the world
165.description: In this unit, pupils read extracts from four novels from around the world, and use them to develop their narrative writing. In particular, pupils explore writers' use of structure. At the end of the unit, pupils consider their own use of paragraphs for effect and write an engaging narrative.
165.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of structure from the unit 'Literary perspectives from the First World War'. In that unit, pupils started to notice and comment on writers' structural choices. In this unit, pupils become more conscious of structure, and start to make more complex observations about how writers use structure to manipulate readers. They start to use structure purposefully in their own writing for effect. This prepares them for the unit 'Science fiction writing', where they develop their literary analysis to focus on writers' language choices and their impact.

338.description: In this unit, pupils look at powerful speeches and emulate them by writing their own speeches. They first read, analyse and compare powerful speeches. They then hone their craft by understanding the features that contribute towards creating a powerful speech. They finally plan and write a speech.
338.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of speeches and speech writing from the unit 'Women's rights across the ages'. Pupils build on this understanding by reading more complex speeches and using them to drive and inspire their own writing. Pupils also learn more about how to deliver their speeches, and become more expert in how to present themselves. This prepares pupils for their final spoken language unit, 'Spoken language masters', where pupils focus intensely on finding their voice and delivering their speeches confidently and compellingly.

1579.why: This unit builds on pupils' knowledge of non-fiction writing from 'changing views' and 'crime and punishment'. In this unit, pupils develop increasingly sophisticated and nuanced non-fiction writing skills, such as the use of passive voice, and also develop their strong original voice. This unit builds towards the unit 'teenage kicks', where pupils will continue to develop nuance in their letter and article writing.

175.description: In this unit, pupls read extracts from three science fiction texts and analyse how writers use language for effect. They first look at how writers use sentences and punctuation, before looking at semantic fields, noun phrases and sensory language. Pupils use this to write thier own descriptions.
175.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of writers' impactful choices from the unit 'Read around the world'. This unit expands and develops their thinking by focusing more intently on writers' language choices and their impact. They use this to now focus on descriptive writing instead of narrative writing, which further enhances their repetoire of creative writing skills. This unit prepares pupils for the unit 'Ending stories', where they will focus on how they can make impactful language and structural choices in narrative writing to create powerful story endings.

176.description: In this unit, pupils develop their non-fiction reading and writing skills. They look at a range of nineteenth century and modern texts in tandem, and practise comparing viewpoints. They then practise emulating different techniques from the texts in order to develop their speech and opinion writing.
176.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' knowledge of non-fiction reading and writing from the unit 'Crime and Punishment'. In this unit, pupils focus more closely on how writers express their viewpoints, and practise comparing those viewpoints. They develop thier non-fiction writing skills by looking at how more complex techniques, such as anaphora, can be used thoughtfully to improve their speech and opinion writing. They also start to move from emulating to crafting original voices. This unit builds towards the unit 'letter writing', where pupils will further develop their original voice.

This unit builds towards the unit 'Books that changed my world', where pupis will look at some of the more subtle methods writers use to manipulate readers and create impact.

This is a culmination of all the knowledge developed on Shakespearean tragedy from their earlier readings of 'Macbeth' and 'Othello'. 1717.name: Romeo and Juliet: the tragedy of societal expectations
1717.description: In this unit, pupils explore the tragedy of societal expectations in 'Romeo and Juliet'. They look at the problem through a range of different prisms, including the tension between individualism and the status quo. They plan and write an essay on Shakespeare's presentation of societal expectations.
1717.why: This unit uses and builds on all of the previous 'Romeo and Juliet' units. It enables pupils to develop deeper and more nuanced responses, and write in a more tentative and considered way. This ensures that they have a more fully rounded understanding of the play and Shakespeare's intentions, and can write from a range of different perspectives.

1534.name: 'Jekyll & Hyde': the dark side of the Industrial Revolution
1534.description: In this unit, pupils explore how Dickens presents 'A Christmas Carol' as a critique of dominant Victorian values. They first look at how he presents Victorian London, before looking at how he depicts poverty, suffering, wealth and status. They then look at what Dickens is critiquing in the novella.
1534.why: This unit uses and builds on pupils' understanding of 'A Christmas Carol ' from the second deep dive, 'a Christian parable'. In that unit, pupils saw how Dickens used religion as a way to present his social message in the novella. In this unit, pupils extend that thinking by focusing on Dickens' wider social and political ideas, as well as how he uses a variety of different methods to express those ideas. This helps them to develop deeper, richer and more nuanced ideas about the novella and Dickens' ideas.

6712.name: Working together: productive discussions and active listening skills
6712.outcome: I can explain what makes a productive discussion and understand what makes an effective active listener
points: A productive discussion means thinking, listening and speaking clearly to develop it in a meaningful way.
Listening is an important discussion skill - it helps to create a supportive and respectful environment.
Active listening means you are completely engaged and focused on what is being delivered to you.
Using positive body language can help demonstrate active listening and keep you focused on the content being delivered.
keywords: paying full attention to what someone else is saying, so you can understand them and respond thoughtfully
how we use our posture and gestures to communicate meaning, confidence and feelings
to accomplish something in an efficient and effective way
showing consideration and kindness for others' feelings and opinions; treating people politely
in speaking and discussions this means saying things without prior planning or preparation

starter.q: Which skills are you most likely to be using when in a discussion?
Which of these would not be considered appropriate in a discussion?
What does it mean to be a good listener in a discussion?

options.text: giving full attention to the speaker and not interrupting
thinking about what you're going to say next

starter.q: Which of the following shows you are being respectful during a discussion?

options.text: rolling your eyes when someone speaks
nodding and waiting your turn to speak

starter.q: Why might it be a good idea to ask questions during a discussion?

options.text: to show that you are paying attention and to clarify understanding
to prove that you are right

starter.q: When giving your opinion in a discussion, what is the best way to communicate?

options.text: shouting to make sure you're heard
refusing to listen to others' opinions
speaking without thinking about what you're saying
speaking clearly and calmly, using reasons to explain your opinion

exit.q: What does active listening involve?
Which of these is **not** a key spoken language skill for a productive discussion?
When referring to speaking and discussions, which word beginning with 's' can be described as: 'saying things without prior planning or preparation'?
Which positive body language gesture demonstrates active listening?
How can active listening improve discussions?

options.text: It ensures the listener is always quiet.
It helps the listener respond thoughtfully and develop ideas.
It allows the speaker to finish quickly.

exit.q: Which of the following words are synonyms for the word 'respectful'?

6713.name: Moving discussions forward by responding and asking questions
6713.outcome: I can develop a discussion by responding appropriately and asking effective questions.
points: Discussion can be more spontaneous than other forms of spoken language.
Using the ABC strategy can help you to respond in a discussion and develop comments.
Using active listening skills can help you to ask relevant questions.
Open questions allow the speaker to respond in a developed way and move the discussion forward.
keywords: paying full attention to what someone else is saying, so you can understand them and respond thoughtfully
question starting with a wh- word that has more information in the answer than yes/no
in speaking and discussions this means saying things without prior planning or preparation

starter.q: Which of the following would **not** be considered a spoken language skill?
Which **three** spoken language skills would be useful to demonstrate your listening skills?
Which answer would **not** be considered part of active listening?
Which of the below are good practice when part of a discussion?
Which word beginning with 'r' can be described as: 'showing consideration and kindness for others' feelings and opinions; treating people politely.'?
Which definition best describes the word 'spontaneous'?

options.text: fully concentrating, understanding and responding thoughtfully to someone
showing consideration and kindness for others' feelings and opinions
achieving a lot or producing good results in an efficient way
saying or doing things without prior planning or preparation

exit.q: Match the words to their definitions.
pairs: a plan or method used to help achieve something
in discussions this means saying things without prior planning
fully concentrating, understanding and responding thoughtfully to what
non-verbal cues or gestures such as facial expressions and posture

exit.q: What does the 'ABC' strategy stand for when responding to a speaker?
Which of the following statements is an example of agreeing with a comment?

options.text: Another aspect to consider would be …

exit.q: Which of these actions would **not** demonstrate active listening?

options.text: fully concentrating on what the speaker is saying
interrupting the speaker to clarify points
waiting for your turn to respond

exit.q: Which of the following is an example of an open question?

options.text: Is cricket a good a sport?
How do you feel about the main character in the story?

exit.q: Why are open questions better for discussions than closed questions?

options.text: They only require a 'yes' or 'no' answer.
They allow for more detailed responses and encourage further discussion.
They make it harder for others to respond.

6714.name: Using evidence to elevate discussions
6714.outcome: I can effectively choose and use evidence to develop my comments in a discussion.
points: Discussions can be elevated with the inclusion of evidence.
Written responses, textual evidence can also be used in discussions.
Different types of evidence can be used, depending on the question, for example: anecdotal evidence or speculation.
It is a good idea to use tentative phrases when evidence is not verified or anecdotal.
keywords: based on personal stories or experiences rather than on hard facts or scientific evidence
the information from a text that can support or justify our reasoning
based on guesses or ideas rather than solid evidence or facts
something that has been checked and confirmed to be true, accurate or valid

starter.q: Which of these do you **not** need to consider when practicing your discussion skills?
What should you do if you don't understand something during a discussion?

options.text: ask for clarification or more details
pretend you understand and move on

4255.belief: As long as I am being quiet, I am listening.
4255.statement: As long as I am being quiet, I am listening.

844.belief: You can't prepare in advance for a discussion.
844.statement: You can't prepare in advance for a discussion.
844.correction: Developing an effective strategy and learning some phrases, will enable you to take part in discussions successfully and confidently. These can help you feel more prepared in discussion scenarios.

845.belief: You can't prepare for discussions, so it's not really something you can practise.
845.statement: You can't prepare for discussions, so it's not really something you can practise.
845.correction: Just like writing, you can learn phrases and strategies that can help you to respond and develop comments in a discussion, especially when offering evidence. These can help you feel more prepared in discussion scenarios.

2776.belief: Evaluating is about simply identifying whether something is good or bad.
2776.statement: Evaluating is about simply identifying whether something is good or bad.
2776.correction: The best evaluation will involve looking closely at something, thinking about its strengths and weaknesses, and explaining why it works well or not. It’s about making a thoughtful judgement based on evidence, not just a simple 'good' or 'bad' label.

10009.belief: The subject of a sentence is always the person in the sentence.
10009.statement: That the subject of a sentence is always the person in the sentence.
10009.correction: A subject is the person, place, or thing that is performing the action of the sentence.

3628.belief: You should immediately start trying to spot language devices when reading an unseen extract.
3628.statement: That you should immediately start trying to spot language devices when reading an unseen extract.
3628.correction: It's better to take the time to understand what is happening before starting to think about how the writer creates meaning.

10604.belief: You should always use the most impressive sounding words in your description.
10604.statement: You should always use the most impressive sounding words in your description.
10604.correction: While you should reach for ambitious words, you want to ensure that all the words you use are creating a consistent atmosphere.

1637.belief: The choice of sentence type isn't important as long as the grammar and punctuation is correct.
1637.statement: That the choice of sentence type isn't important as long as the grammar and punctuation is correct.
1637.correction: The choice of sentence type can impact the way that a reader responds to your writing.

4295.belief: Looking at punctuation is very dry and has no impact on the way you see a text or a character.
4295.statement: That looking at punctuation is very dry and has no impact on the way you see a text or a character.
4295.correction: The way that writers use and play with punctuation can have a profound impact on the way we view a text or character's emotions.

2105.belief: Creating an effective piece of descriptive writing is all about using linguistic devices.
2105.statement: Creating an effective piece of descriptive writing is all about using linguistic devices.
2105.correction: Varying your sentences can also be a very effective way of conveying emotion and detail to help the reader visualise the scene.

9220.belief: There is a set formula to follow when it comes to choosing what to focus on in an image.
9220.statement: That there is a set formula to follow when it comes to choosing what to focus on in an image.
9220.correction: When looking at an image for descriptive writing, you should think about what catches your eye and then focus on those elements.

5518.belief: A piece of writing is completely finished once you have written it.
5518.statement: That a piece of writing is completely finished once you have written it.
5518.correction: The first time you complete a piece of writing is it in its draft form. You want to go back and continually revise it.

9269.belief: You shouldn't judge a book by its cover.
9269.statement: That you shouldn't judge a book by its cover.
9269.correction: If we consider a literal book cover, it has been chosen to introduce the reader to the tone of the text.

8677.belief: You should put literary analysis in every part of your analytical writing.
8677.statement: That you should put literary analysis in every part of your analytical writing.
8677.correction: You shouldn't put literary analysis in your topic sentence - it should just explain the main idea of the paragraph concisely.

8917.belief: We will all respond to a description in the same way.
8917.statement: That we will all respond to a description in the same way.
8917.correction: The way we respond to a description and the language devices will always be unique because we all have different experiences.

2272.belief: Descriptive writing is all about telling the reader what's in the image.
2272.statement: That descriptive writing is all about telling the reader what's in the image.
2272.correction: Descriptive writing is about showing the reader what's in the image through sensory and figurative language.

5531.belief: You always have to plan before a piece of creative writing.
5531.statement: That you always have to plan before a piece of creative writing.
5531.correction: While a plan is very useful, and should be used in most cases, sometimes free writing can be a way of unleashing creativity that can then be revised.

2823.belief: Everyone will respond to an image in the same way.
2823.statement: Everyone will respond to an image in the same way.
2823.correction: How you respond to an image, and what you choose to zoom in on, will be different for each person since we're all unique with different memories and experiences.

5366.belief: Pathetic fallacy can only be used to give emotion to the weather.
5366.statement: That pathetic fallacy can only be used to give emotion to the weather.
5366.correction: Pathetic fallacy is where human emotions are given to any non-human object or thing.

10548.statement: That the unknown is always scary.
10548.correction: While we typically think of the unknown as something scary and overwhelming, it can also be something exciting and refreshing.

4543.belief: Meeting someone unknown in a strange place will always be scary.
4543.statement: That meeting someone unknown in a strange place will always be scary.
4543.correction: Instead of feeling scared, you might also feel excited or intrigued and you can use language to have this effect on the reader.

9624.belief: Stories are purely intended to entertain us.
9624.statement: That stories are purely intended to entertain us.
9624.correction: While stories are entertaining, often there is also a message or a purpose behind the story that is designed to teach us something.

9075.belief: We will all have the same response to certain words.
9075.statement: That we will all have the same response to certain words.
9075.correction: Our response to words depends on our own individual experiences and memories and therefore we are likely to all get different connotations from words.

4338.belief: Magic in stories always happens in a make-believe, faraway world.
4338.statement: That magic in stories always happens in a make-believe, faraway world.
4338.correction: Magical-realist stories are set in the real world but magic and fantastical events happen.

2253.belief: You can only describe light in a two-dimensional way.
2253.statement: You can only describe light in a two-dimensional way.
2253.correction: There are many ways to describe light to have an effect. You can talk about the dawn, the twilight or the way the light gleams or flickers in order to influence the reader's perception.

9068.belief: We will all have the same answer to a question about how a writer presents a particular character or theme.
9068.statement: That we will all have the same answer to a question about how a writer presents a particular character or theme.
9068.correction: The way we respond to how a writer presents a particular character or theme will be very individual since our responses depend on our own experiences or memories.

10593.belief: You should use definitive, authoritative language in your analytical writing to prove to the reader that you are right.
10593.statement: That you should use definitive, authoritative language in your analytical writing to prove to the reader that you are right.
10593.correction: You should use tentative language because we can never be truly sure of the writer's intentions - you should use evidence and clear explanations to prove your idea to the reader.

10216.belief: Textures aren't an important detail in descriptive writing.
10216.statement: That textures aren't an important detail in descriptive writing.
10216.correction: The textures that writers choose to use can help us to make inferences about the nature of the object or place.

5769.belief: Prepositions aren't an important focal point for descriptive writing.
5769.statement: That prepositions aren't an important focal point for descriptive writing.
5769.correction: Not only do prepositions indicate the relationship between words, but they also influence our perception of people based on their body language and positioning in a scene.

3896.belief: It's impossible to guess what will happen in a text.
3896.statement: That it's impossible to guess what will happen in a text.
3896.correction: While we can't know for certain, we can pick up on clues that the writer gives us to make predictions about what will happen in a text.

5370.belief: A pattern within a text is random and just happened by chance.
5370.statement: That a pattern within a text is random and just happened by chance.
5370.correction: Patterns are a way for writers to emphasise certain information or convey importance onto a concept because our brains are wired to recognise and remember patterns.

1640.belief: You should choose the quotation with the most techniques as your evidence.
1640.statement: That you should choose the quotation with the most techniques as your evidence.
1640.correction: You need to select a quotation that matches the point of your topic sentence rather than simply being the one with the most techniques.

8770.belief: The reader will automatically be able to follow your train of thought.
8770.statement: That the reader will automatically be able to follow your train of thought.
8770.correction: We all have different connotations from words; you need to clearly explain how you have reached your idea in order for the reader to be able to understand your argument.

2109.belief: Creative writing is more effective when it focuses on something extraordinary.
2109.statement: Creative writing is more effective when it focuses on something extraordinary.
2109.correction: Describing something very well known to you can be more effective as you're able to spend the time focusing on the little details.

10737.belief: Using similes is in itself effective descriptive writing.
10737.statement: That using similes is in itself effective descriptive writing.
10737.correction: You should aim to have a simile that creates a specific emotion and avoids clichés.

10600.belief: You should use generic sensory language to create an effective description.
10600.statement: That you should use generic sensory language to create an effective description.
10600.correction: You need to use sensory language tailored to the atmosphere that you want to create in order for it to be effective.

4700.belief: The modern experience of going to the theatre is the same as in Shakespearean times.
4700.statement: That the modern experience of going to the theatre is the same as in Shakespearean times.
4700.correction: The experience was very different - the modern theatre experience is quiet and respectful while the Shakespearean experience was riotous.

9237.belief: Shakespearean theatre didn't have special effects.
9237.statement: That Shakespearean theatre didn't have special effects.
9237.correction: Although they didn't have access to modern technology, the theatre used many special effects to help make the production more realistic.

2217.belief: The defining feature of a comedy play is that they are funny.
2217.statement: The defining feature of a comedy play is that they are funny.
2217.correction: While Shakespeare's comedies do employ humour, the defining feature is that everything is resolved at the end of the play.

5395.belief: People didn't believe in magic in Shakespeare's time.
5395.statement: That people didn't believe in magic in Shakespeare's time.
5395.correction: In Shakespeare's time, most people believed in magic and thought it could bring ill luck and misfortune.

5271.belief: Our feelings towards characters must be consistent.
5271.statement: That our feelings towards characters must be consistent.
5271.correction: Our feelings towards characters can change depending on what is happening during the plot.

377.statement: That Ariel is a female character.
377.correction: There is no gender assigned to Ariel.

263.belief: An analysis of a play only consists of the word the characters say.
263.statement: That an analysis of a play only consists of the word the characters say.
263.correction: The amount of lines a character has as well as stage directions are also important aspects of analysing a play.

8731.belief: You should quote entire sentences of text in order to prove your point.
8731.statement: That you should quote entire sentences of text in order to prove your point.
8731.correction: Often, individual words and short quotes are more effective in analytical writing.

10218.belief: A theatre performance is all about actors interacting with each other on the stage.
10218.statement: That a theatre performance is all about actors interacting with each other on the stage.
10218.correction: Often the most memorable moments from a performance are the actors' monologues where they express their character's inner thoughts.

5546.statement: That planning is a pointless endeavour.
5546.correction: Planning is a really important aspect of any writing task as it makes the process easier and allows you to organise your thoughts.

808.belief: Caliban and Prospero always have a negative relationship.
808.statement: That Caliban and Prospero always have a negative relationship.
808.correction: When Prospero first arrived, Caliban showed Prospero how to survive on the island so it began as a positive relationship.

3897.belief: It's obvious how a character should be interpreted by the audience.
3897.statement: That it's obvious how a character should be interpreted by the audience.
3897.correction: The staging of a performance from body language to costuming can make a huge difference in how different audiences interpret a character.

950.belief: Characters are only meant to be read as themselves.
950.statement: That characters are only meant to be read as themselves.
950.correction: Often in literature, the characters are the writer's way of commenting on something happening in the world.

375.belief: An argument only means a heated, angry exchange.
375.statement: That an argument only means a heated, angry exchange.
375.correction: An argument about a text means presenting your idea and your points to prove that your idea is correct.

2472.belief: You don't need to use quotes in your essay.
2472.statement: That you don't need to use quotes in your essay.
2472.correction: Quotes act as textual evidence and are needed to write a successful analytical essay.

5876.belief: Proofreading is a waste of time.
5876.statement: That proofreading is a waste of time.
5876.correction: Proofreading helps you to spot errors that might hinder the readers' understanding of your work.

3963.belief: We know for certain how Shakespeare intended his characters to be seen.
3963.statement: That we know for certain how Shakespeare intended his characters to be seen.
3963.correction: We don't know how Shakespeare intended the audience to perceive his characters - we can just look at the language and decide from that.

811.belief: Calling someone a 'monster' means that you find them terrifying.
811.statement: That calling someone a 'monster' means that you find them terrifying.
811.correction: While calling someone a 'monster' can mean you find them terrifying, it can also be a way of ridiculing someone and showing your dislike.

376.belief: An argument needs to present a balanced viewpoint for both sides of the argument.
376.statement: That an argument needs to present a balanced viewpoint for both sides of the argument.
376.correction: An argument needs to give your reasons behind your answer to the question.

3623.belief: Images and sentences always need to be varied in writing.
3623.statement: That images and sentences always need to be varied in writing.
3623.correction: Repeated images and sentences can be an effective way of crafting a convincing character voice.

949.belief: Characters in literature are just there to create a good story.
949.statement: Characters in literature are just there to create a good story.
949.correction: Characters in literature often represent things bigger than themselves such as colonialism or gender inequality.

9967.belief: Women were completely powerless in Shakespeare's time.
9967.statement: Students sometimes think that women were completely powerless in Shakespeare's time.
9967.correction: While there were legal restrictions and social pressures on women in Shakespeare's time, there were some women who had power and influence.

9968.belief: Women in Shakespeare's time always obeyed the male figures in their life.
9968.statement: Students often think that women in Shakespeare's time always obeyed the male figures in their life.
9968.correction: There are many examples of women being disobedient and not following the rules of the male figures in their life.

2110.belief: Creative writing should be in present tense.
2110.statement: That creative writing should be in present tense.
2110.correction: Because diaries are records of events that have happened, they should be written in past tense.

5285.belief: Being an outsider is always a negative thing.
5285.statement: That being an outsider is always a negative thing.
5285.correction: Sometimes people are considered outsiders because they don't fit society's expectations of normal and that's not necessarily negative.

10091.belief: Symbols in literature mean the same to everyone.
10091.statement: That symbols in literature mean the same to everyone.
10091.correction: Our responses to symbolism depend on our experiences as well as exposure to certain concepts so we might all have very different responses.

5367.belief: Pathetic fallacy is only about using the weather to express emotions.
5367.statement: That pathetic fallacy is only about using the weather to express emotions.
5367.correction: Pathetic fallacy is a type of personification where emotions are given to a setting, an object or the weather.

834.belief: We can't do anything to help control our nerves.
834.statement: That we can't do anything to help control our nerves.
834.correction: While we can't stop the feeling of nervousness entirely, we can trick our body into relaxing more by smiling and using deep breathing.

9871.belief: George The Poet's attitude towards his city is wholly negative.
9871.statement: Students may think George The Poet's attitude towards his city is wholly negative.
9871.correction: George The Poet critiques certain aspects of London, particularly inequality and the way in which people often do not acknowledge the poverty in London.

9992.statement: Students may be used to starting any sensory language sentences with 'I can see, I can hear...'
9992.correction: Poetry allows us to innovate with traditional writing structures to help a rhythmic flow and sense of nostalgia; help students recognise the difference between 'I can see...' and 'Seeing...'

9772.statement: Students may misconceive what the phrase "my tongue" means initially.
9772.correction: Explain the figurative language involved in the phrase "my tongue" and the link to language.

5633.belief: The poem 'Island Man' only tells the story of someone that misses the Caribbean.
5633.statement: The poem 'Island Man' only tells the story of someone that misses the Caribbean.
5633.correction: The poem 'Island Man' can help to tell the story of any migrant who experiences nostalgia for their home country.

9747.statement: Students may not at first understand that they must use a parallel sentence structure when using correlative conjunctions e.g. Both 'Island Man' uses imagery as well as 'Search for My Tongue'.
9747.correction: Model a few sentences with correlative conjunctions to show that parallel structures are needed. e.g. Both 'Island Man' and 'Search for My Tongue' use imagery.

9985.statement: Students may be unfamiliar with the term 'region'.
9985.correction: Help students recognise and learn about their own region.

9761.statement: Students may not immediately understand the title if they have never come across 'colonialism' before.
9761.correction: Take some time unpicking why Clarke equates colonisation to stealing.

9785.statement: Students may not realise the importance of listening in discussions, as they may be thinking about what they have to say next.
9785.correction: Explain the importance of listening. Model a discussion with a pupil where you are not listening, ask them how it made them feel and ask the class how it affected the quality of the discussion.

9760.statement: Students may not immediately think they can relate to the poem, if their own home does not have distinct elements of their culture or heritage.
9760.correction: Explain how everyone can relate to the idea of having a filter on. Whilst Subramaniam takes off her filter and reveals her heritage at home, your students might reveal their true personality or hobbies through home.

9984.statement: Students may not understand the subtle difference between imagery and figurative language.
9984.correction: Whilst imagery can include figurative language and vice versa, imagery does not always have to be figurative.

8229.belief: The same punctuation rules apply in poetry and other types of writing (e.g. full stops are needed at the end of lines).
8229.statement: Pupils may think that the same punctuation rules apply in poetry and other types of writing (e.g. full stops are needed at the end of lines).
8229.correction: Poems are not bound to formal punctuation rules. Having flexibility allows the poet to shape their poem based on emotion rather than grammar rules.

5631.belief: A poem has to follow a similar rhythm the whole way through.
5631.statement: A poem has to follow a similar rhythm the whole way through.
5631.correction: By creating two different rhythms, we can juxtapose two places.

3659.belief: The most important thing in a poem is the words.
3659.statement: The most important thing in a poem is the words.
3659.correction: Structure is important, it can help tell your story. Not considering the structure of your poem is like an author not considering the beginning, middle and end of a novel.

4260.belief: As long as the content of a poem is good, the performance will automatically be good.
4260.statement: As long as the content of a poem is good, the performance will automatically be good.
4260.correction: Performance requires practise in a unique set of skills which are worth practising as a good performance can enhance the poem content.

645.belief: It is better to know everything about a character or text before reading.
645.statement: It is better to know everything about a character or text before reading.
645.correction: Making predictions can help us with our comprehension of complex texts and independent thinking.

5681.belief: The police force we have today is the one society has always had.
5681.statement: The police force we have today is the one society has always had.
5681.correction: Explain that the police force was a new concept to Victorians and thus civilians had a lot of anxiety around crime.

3931.correction: Explain that the point of a mystery story is for the detective to use clues to solve it and usually find a perpetrator.

5548.belief: Planning can often be seen as a waste of time.
5548.statement: Planning can often be seen as a waste of time.
5548.correction: You must take time to make notes and gather ideas so the analysis you write is strong.

5516.belief: Each piece of evidence can be looked at in isolation when thinking about the crime.
5516.statement: Each piece of evidence can be looked at in isolation when thinking about the crime.
5516.correction: Question your students' explanations to help them acknowledge where they have failed to consider certain pieces of evidence.

1981.belief: Connotation is the definition of a word.
1981.statement: Connotation is the definition of a word.
1981.correction: Connotation is a feeling that a word gives.

4703.belief: A modern reader and Victorian reader perceive the text and characters in the same way.
4703.statement: That a modern reader and Victorian reader perceive the text and characters in the same way.
4703.correction: Use Victorian context to explain the difference between our attitudes.

4266.belief: As long as I keep my headline and subheading short, they will be effective.
4266.statement: As long as I keep my headline and subheading short, they will be effective.
4266.correction: Headlines and subheadings must be crafted to fit the purpose of the article.

2307.belief: Details of a crime can be reported in any part of an article.
2307.statement: Details of a crime can be reported in any part of an article.
2307.correction: Explain to students that more and more information is revealed as an article develops.

4496.belief: It does not matter who you interview for your article.
4496.statement: It does not matter who you interview for your article.
4496.correction: You should choose your interviewee carefully depending on the effect you want to have.

10116.belief: The tail functions as a summary of the events.
10116.statement: The tail functions as a summary of the events.
10116.correction: Although a conclusion in any other form of writing would contain a summary, an article summary usually goes at the beginning.

8940.belief: Rhetorical devices can be used randomly throughout work with little thought.
8940.statement: Rhetorical devices can be used randomly throughout work with little thought.
8940.correction: Show that rhetorical devices have to be used for precise effect otherwise there is no point in using them.

1906.belief: Conan Doyle creates a scary atmosphere all the way through 'The Speckled Band'.
1906.statement: Conan Doyle creates a scary atmosphere all the way through 'The Speckled Band'.
1906.correction: If you look carefully, Conan Doyle carefully alters the atmosphere in order to build tension in the reader.

9759.statement: Students may not immediately piece together all of the pieces of evidence throughout the case.
9759.correction: Break the conclusion down for students with a visual depiction or flow diagram if necessary, explain that some clues were red herrings.

5539.belief: Planning is not necessary before writing.
5539.statement: Planning is not necessary before writing.
5539.correction: Planning is important in helping us structure our work and keep a clear focus.

4941.belief: A newspaper article can be written in the same style as a story retelling.
4941.statement: A newspaper article can be written in the same style as a story retelling.
4941.correction: Newspaper articles must have different elements to show they are an article - interview quotes and a concise way of writing things are key.

4504.correction: It is suspected that McCarthy's son is responsible for the murder of McCarthy, however Holmes still has a lot of investigating to do.

9718.statement: Students may be confused about Turner's fate at the end of the story.
9718.correction: Explain that no two Sherlock Holmes mysteries are the same. Two perpetrators can face different fates.

10857.correction: Conan Doyle manipulates his presentation of victims depending on how he wants the reader to view them.

9961.statement: Some students think that villains are one dimensional.

9258.belief: Sherlock Holmes mystery stories are almost identical.
9258.statement: Sherlock Holmes mystery stories are almost identical.
9258.correction: Whilst all Sherlock Holmes mystery stories are part of the detective fiction genre, the stories can differ a lot.

3847.belief: An introduction can be written without thoughtful planning.
3847.statement: An introduction can be written without thoughtful planning
3847.correction: To make an introduction worthwhile, and for it to effectively introduce an essay, it requires thoughtful planning

3183.belief: The front cover is just for 'show' and a way to identify a book.
3183.statement: The front cover is just for 'show' and a way to identify a book.
3183.correction: The images and font on a front cover can give you lots of clues about themes and genre.

9223.belief: Settings are only there to provide a backdrop for the story.
9223.statement: Settings are only there to provide a backdrop for the story.
9223.correction: Setting plays a crucial role in shaping the mood and atmosphere of a novel. It can also help us gain a deeper understanding of the characters and themes.

4277.belief: As long as I have used "like" or "as", I have created an effective simile.
4277.statement: As long as I have used "like" or "as", I have created an effective simile.
4277.correction: Consider this simile: 'Her voice was like a salad.' The comparison is unclear and doesn't enhance understanding.

2413.belief: Discussions are just 'chats' and aren't that important.
2413.statement: That discussions are just 'chats' and aren't that important.
2413.correction: Think about all of the times you may need to use your verbal skills e.g an interview or presentation. Being able to articulate yourself well verbally is an important skill to have.

4125.belief: Letters are only used in novels to drive the plot forward.
4125.statement: Letters are only used in novels to drive the plot forward.
4125.correction: Letters can also give a reader an insight into a character's thoughts and feelings, as well as background information. They can also be used as an effective way to create dramatic irony.

10221.belief: A theme is any idea or plot point in a text.
10221.statement: A theme is any idea or plot point in a text.
10221.correction: Themes are the most important ideas in a text. There may be multiple. The most important themes are the ones that are returned to over and over again, and explored in a number of different ways.

11142.belief: Writers will not use stories or characters that already exist. This is copying!
11142.statement: Writers will not use stories or characters that already exist. This is copying!
11142.correction: Storytelling is an ancient form. Many writers and artists are inspired by stories that have existed for thousands of years. This is because of their universal characters and timeless themes.

10180.belief: Tension is only about scary or dangerous situations.
10180.statement: Tension is only about scary or dangerous situations.
10180.correction: While scary or dangerous situations can create tension, tension can also arise from emotional conflicts, difficult decisions, or unresolved mysteries. It's about keeping readers eager to know what will happen next.

10876.belief: Villains are easily identifiable and will be always be introduced from the outset of a text.
10876.statement: Villains are easily identifiable and will be always be introduced from the outset of a text.
10876.correction: Consider the draugr's subtle and encroaching presence. Burge uses this slow reveal to create tension.

3696.belief: Including the theme of fate means that characters have no choice or control over their actions and are simply puppets of destiny.
3696.statement: Including the theme of fate means that characters have no choice or control over their actions and are simply puppets of destiny.
3696.correction: While fate in 'The Twisted Tree' suggests that certain events and abilities are predestined, characters still have the power to make choices that shape their journey.

4975.belief: The Norns are whimsical and conventionally beautiful.
4975.statement: The Norns are whimsical and conventionally beautiful.
4975.correction: Look at the descriptions of the Norns. Their beauty lies in their power and wisdom. They are "gnarled" and "wrinkled", which adds an air of authority to their presence. They are also described as "fierce".

1722.belief: The climax comes at the end of a story.
1722.statement: The climax comes at the end of a story.
1722.correction: The climax is actually the high point of tension and action in a story, not necessarily at the end. It usually occurs towards the end but is followed by the resolution where the remaining conflicts are settled.

8915.belief: The resolution of a story will leave no unanswered questions and all conflicts resolved.
8915.statement: The resolution of a story will leave no unanswered questions and all conflicts resolved.
8915.correction: Sometimes there can still be a few things left open or unresolved. This can make the story more interesting and leave readers thinking about what might happen next.

6174.belief: Writing a summary means including all details from the story.
6174.statement: Pupils might believe that writing a summary means including all details from the story.
6174.correction: Explain that a summary should only include the most important events and main ideas in a concise manner. Remind them that the goal is to capture the essence of the story, not every detail.

9949.belief: All stories fit perfectly into a traditional narrative arc with only one climax.
9949.statement: Students might think that all stories fit perfectly into a traditional narrative arc with only one climax.
9949.correction: While many stories follow a traditional narrative arc, some can have multiple climaxes or may not fit perfectly into the structure. The narrative arc is a helpful guide, but it's important to recognise that stories can vary and still be effective.

3348.belief: Gothic literature is only about horror and scary elements.
3348.statement: Gothic literature is only about horror and scary elements.
3348.correction: While Gothic literature often includes elements of horror, such as supernatural occurrences and eerie settings, it also explores complex themes like human psychology, societal anxieties and the supernatural as a metaphor for deeper fears or desires.

9886.belief: Making an inference is the same as guessing randomly without any evidence.
9886.statement: Students might think that making an inference is the same as guessing randomly without any evidence.
9886.correction: Inferences are not random guesses. They are logical conclusions drawn from clues or evidence presented in the text or context.

7779.belief: All draugr are depicted in Norse mythology and in 'The Twisted Tree' in the same way.
7779.statement: Pupils may think all draugr are depicted in Norse mythology and in 'The Twisted Tree' in the same way.
7779.correction: While draugr in Norse mythology generally share traits their specific appearances can vary between stories. Rachel Burge's portrayal in 'The Twisted Tree' offers her unique interpretation, reflecting the novel's narrative and atmosphere.

7780.belief: The draugr is simply a physical monster with no deeper significance or symbolism.
7780.statement: Pupils might think that the draugr is simply a physical monster with no deeper significance or symbolism.
7780.correction: While the draugr is indeed a fearsome physical entity, it also symbolises deeper themes such as death, decay and the persistence of fear. In Norse mythology, draugrs are more than just monsters; they embody the fears and anxieties of the living.

7883.belief: A headline alone is enough to convey the entire story of an article.
7883.statement: Pupils may think that a headline alone is enough to convey the entire story of an article.
7883.correction: Explain that while a headline grabs attention and hints at the article's content, it's the subheading and body text that provide the full details and context. Emphasise the importance of each element working together to inform the reader.

4942.belief: Newspaper articles must strictly adhere to factual reporting without any creative elements.
4942.statement: Newspaper articles must strictly adhere to factual reporting without any creative elements.
4942.correction: While newspaper articles are based on factual reporting, they often incorporate language devices like puns, alliteration and sensationalist language in headlines and sometimes throughout the article. These elements are used to engage readers.

8341.belief: The use of a formal tone and third person point of view is only necessary for professional journalism and not applicable to other forms of writing.
8341.statement: Pupils might think that the use of a formal tone and third person point of view is only necessary for professional journalism and not applicable to other forms of writing.
8341.correction: Explain that while formal tone and third person are essential in professional journalism, they are also important in many other types of writing, including more localised articles like this.

8304.belief: Symbols in the novel have only one clear meaning.
8304.statement: Pupils might think symbols in the novel have only one clear meaning.
8304.correction: Explain that symbols often have multiple meanings. For example, Martha's blindness can represent family secrets, vulnerability and hidden truths. Encourage looking for different interpretations.

6146.belief: Tension in a story is only created through dramatic events or actions.
6146.statement: Pupils might believe that tension in a story is only created through dramatic events or actions.
6146.correction: Tension can also be built through subtle elements like descriptive language, sensory details and the anticipation of what might happen next.

10232.belief: A thesis statement only needs to focus on one part of the book.
10232.statement: A thesis statement only needs to focus on one part of the book.
10232.correction: A thesis statement should address the overarching argument of your essay, which means it needs to consider the entire text.

8730.belief: All quotations need to be analysed in depth.
8730.statement: All quotations need to be analysed in depth.
8730.correction: Not all quotations need the same level of analysis. Main quotations are central to your argument and should be analysed to show how they support your thesis. Supporting quotations are used to reinforce the point made with the main quotations.

6055.belief: The conclusion should introduce new ideas or quotes.
6055.statement: Pupils may believe that the conclusion should introduce new ideas or quotes.
6055.correction: Explain that a conclusion should summarise the main points and restate the thesis in a new way, rather than introducing new evidence or arguments. Its purpose is to reinforce what has already been discussed, reinforcing the main arguments.

8347.belief: Using exclamatory sentences is appropriate in a newspaper article about Mormor's death to express strong emotions.
8347.statement: Pupils may think that using exclamatory sentences is appropriate in a newspaper article about Mormor's death to express strong emotions.
8347.correction: Explain that while exclamatory sentences express sudden or strong emotions, they are not appropriate for a factual newspaper article. Instead, emphasise using emotive language and other devices that convey the community's feelings respectfully.

6223.statement: Pupils might confuse compound and complex sentences, thinking that any sentence with more than one clause is a complex sentence.
6223.correction: A compound sentence has two main clauses that can each stand alone as separate sentences, joined by a coordinating conjunction. In contrast, a complex sentence has one main clause and at least one subordinate clause that cannot stand alone.

9137.belief: A script is just dialogue between characters and doesn't need any other elements.
9137.statement: A script is just dialogue between characters and doesn't need any other elements
9137.correction: While dialogue is a crucial part of a script, it's not the only component. A script also includes stage directions, which provide important instructions on how actors should move, behave, and speak.

7922.belief: Inferences are just guesses without any evidence.
7922.statement: Pupils might think that inferences are just guesses without any evidence.
