7922.correction: Inferences are not guesses; they are conclusions drawn from evidence in the text. For example, Burge describes the fog as "snaking" around Martha. We infer that it is dangerous and sinister because the word "snake" often implies danger and malice.

9589.belief: Stage directions are just suggestions and don't need to be followed exactly.
9589.statement: Stage directions are just suggestions and don't need to be followed exactly.
9589.correction: Stage directions are essential parts of the script that provide important guidance on how the scene should be performed. They help create the atmosphere, convey emotions and ensure the story is told as the writer intended.

6967.statement: Pupils may mistake dystopia and utopia as the words are similar
6967.correction: Explicitly explain the difference between the two and explain that they are antonyms

9990.statement: Students may use sentence fragments in their work
9990.correction: Showing exactly how sentence fragments obscure meaning and explaining why they should not be used

1885.belief: Compound sentences are better than simple sentences all of the time.
1885.statement: Compound sentences are better than simple sentences all of the time.
1885.correction: Make it explicit to students that sometimes simple sentences can be more suitable in their writing; long does not equal better.

9847.belief: Complex sentences are superior to other sentences.
9847.statement: Students may think that complex sentences are superior to other sentences.
9847.correction: Show the effect of all sentences working in harmony via a model.

8349.belief: Using any verb that is associated with people makes good quality personification.
8349.statement: Pupils think that using any verb that is associated with people makes good quality personification.
8349.correction: Provide pupils with a choices of verbs, including incongruous ones, to allow them to identify high quality personification.

4274.belief: As long as a similes compare something similar it is effective.
4274.statement: As long as a similes compare something similar it is effective.
4274.correction: Similes are much more powerful when used alongside vivid description. Work through example in learning cycle 1 to help unravel this.

2846.belief: Exclamatory sentences are the only sentences that express emotions.
2846.statement: Exclamatory sentences are the only sentences that express emotions
2846.correction: Interrogative sentences can also effectively show some emotions e.g. confusion, despair, by the character asking themselves questions

9779.statement: Students may overuse exclamation marks because they think it adds sophistication
9779.correction: Show pupils that exclamation marks are best used for dramatic effect

10735.correction: A semicolon always has to have an independent clause on either side of it.

7784.belief: Dystopian societies only involve dilapidated settings.
7784.statement: Pupils may think that dystopian societies only involve dilapidated settings.
7784.correction: Explain that there are two sides in a dystopia: those with power and control who live in luxury and ordinary citizens in run down areas.

2101.belief: You can create tone via 1-3 words.
2101.statement: You can create tone via 1-3 words.
2101.correction: Show that tone is established through consistent effort and crafting throughout the writing process - every word is picked precisely.

77.belief: Action is a key part of a description.
77.statement: Action is a key part of a description.
77.correction: Explain to pupils that the purpose of a description is to focus on certain aspects of a scene in order to set the tone and genre.

4855.belief: You do not need to check your work after writing it.
4855.statement: You do not need to check your work after writing it.
4855.correction: Show pupils the value of checking and editing their work - show the transformation from first draft to final draft.

6974.statement: Pupils might mistake a simile for metaphor and vice versa.
6974.correction: Go through simile and metaphor definitions and examples slowly and explicitly.

3024.belief: The first draft is the final draft.
3024.statement: That the first draft is the final draft.
3024.correction: The best writing is achieved through a cycle of initial creation, feedback and re-drafting.

9663.statement: Students add sophisticated punctuation as a tick box exercise.
9663.correction: The inclusion of sophisticated punctuation should always be driven first and foremost by effect. What effect will this punctuation achieve?

3393.belief: All the Greek myths have morals.
3393.statement: All the Greek myths have morals.
3393.correction: The Greek myths are not all moralistic. Indeed, the gods, mythological creatures and mortals often act in cruel, reactive, vengeful and immoral ways.

2611.belief: Ekphrastic poems are poems inspired by someone or something.
2611.statement: Ekphrastic poems are poems inspired by someone or something.
2611.correction: Ekphrastic poems are poems inspired by a piece of art, and they describe that piece of art in the poem.

499.belief: Auden is saying suffering is unimportant.
499.statement: Auden is saying suffering is unimportant.
499.correction: Auden presents extreme suffering, but he is exploring how, inevitably, when something terrible is happening, something ordinary is happening at the same time too.

11016.belief: Williams didn't use any methods in his poem because he is just describing a painting.
11016.statement: Williams didn't use any methods in his poem because he is just describing a painting.
11016.correction: Every word in a poem is carefully selected. Williams could have made any number of choices about what he depicted in terms of focus, structure, tone and language. We can explore these methods, and add layers of meaning to the painting.

10580.belief: The use of adjectives is a simple technique, so there isn't much point analysing a writer's use of them, or planning for them in your own writing.
10580.statement: The use of adjectives is a simple technique, so there isn't much point analysing a writer's use of them, or planning for them in your own writing.
10580.correction: Adjectives are a wonderful way to express tone, nuanced meaning and atmosphere. As such, they can be rich for analysis, and have a powerful effect on your own descriptive writing.

849.belief: You can't talk about two different texts in the same paragraph.
849.statement: You can't talk about two different texts in the same paragraph.
849.correction: It can be tricky to talk about two texts in one paragraph, but it often makes for a stronger comparison. A good way to start is to consider one aspect of the texts you wish to compare, and then draw out the differences in your analysis.

4006.belief: The Lady of Shalott chooses to take her own life on the way to Camelot.
4006.statement: The Lady of Shalott chooses to take her own life on the way to Camelot.
4006.correction: The Lady of Shalott realises that, because she got up from her loom, she is now cursed. Knowing she will die from this curse, she gets into the boat to sail to Camelot. She realises she will not make it there alive.

9409.belief: If you are in solitude, you feel lonely.
9409.statement: If you are in solitude, you feel lonely.
9409.correction: Solitude can be a pleasant state, one that lots of people seek out. It is different from feeling lonely or isolated.

839.belief: You can't include quotations when exploring enjambment.
839.statement: You can't include quotations when exploring enjambment.
839.correction: If analysing enjambment, you must include a specific example. Just as you would include a quotation to explore a simile (for example) so must you include a quotation to explore enjambment.

11140.belief: Writers can use any object to symbolise any idea.
11140.statement: Writers can use any object to symbolise any idea.
11140.correction: Writers can get their messages across via inventive and innovative methods. However, there are some key symbols in literature which have a generally accepted meaning. For example, a rose to symbolise love, or a pearl to symbolise perfection.

10578.belief: You should use an adjective to describe every noun.
10578.statement: You should use an adjective to describe every noun.
10578.correction: Adjectives can help add interest and atmosphere to your writing. But not every noun needs an adjective. This can become overwhelming for the reader.

10305.belief: A third person omniscient narrator must develop each character in the same amount of detail.
10305.statement: A third person omniscient narrator must develop each character in the same amount of detail.
10305.correction: Whilst a third person omniscient narrator can develop many characters, they don't need the same amount of space, detail and time in a written piece. You can still have a central character, and minor characters who are more or less important.

5107.belief: Once you have used an image or idea in a piece of writing, you can't reuse it in the same piece.
5107.statement: Once you have used an image or idea in a piece of writing, you can't reuse it in the same piece.
5107.correction: Sometimes repeating an idea or image throughout a piece can help give it a sense of structure. You might change certain details, but you can repeat them.

10721.belief: Using onomatopoeia is the only way to create a sense of sound in a piece of writing.
10721.statement: Using onomatopoeia is the only way to create a sense of sound in a piece of writing.
10721.correction: Onomatopoeia can be a helpful tool to rely on in some pieces of writing. However, alliteration, plosives and sibilance are often more sophisticated and more subtle. They also allow for a greater range of sounds to be generated.

4405.belief: A Mami Wata is always presented as a mermaid who saves the souls of enslaved people.
4405.statement: A Mami Wata is always presented as a mermaid who saves the souls of enslaved people.
4405.correction: Mami Wata is a water spirit and has a rich tradition in West, Central and Southern Africa. Bowen has used the deity in her novel and presented her as a mermaid with a specific task, but the goddess is presented in different ways in other art.

10181.belief: The term complex sentence is a synonym for a long sentence.
10181.statement: The term complex sentence is a synonym for a long sentence.
10181.correction: A complex sentence is a technical term. It refers to a sentence that has a main clause and a subordinate clause. Sentences can be long but if they don't have a subordinate clause, they are not a complex sentence.

3045.belief: Flashback is the only way to include information about a character's past.
3045.statement: Flashback is the only way to include information about a character's past.
3045.correction: Flashback is a powerful method and one which lots of writers rely on. However, there are many other ways to include details about a character's past. For example, explanation from a character or dialogue between characters.

4598.belief: Middle English is the same as Old English. Both are general terms, and mean the same thing.
4598.statement: Middle English is the same as Old English. Both are general terms, and mean the same thing.
4598.correction: Middle English was spoken from about 1100-1500. Old English was spoken before 1100. Both are technical terms and have a specific meaning.

3686.belief: You have to include each aspect of characterisation in the same paragraph, and always in the same order.
3686.statement: You have to include each aspect of characterisation in the same paragraph, and always in the same order.
3686.correction: Chaucer has a particular way of introducing and describing his characters. However, this is one way to do it, amongst many. You will see lots of different writers use the same methods of characterisation, but in different orders and structures.

312.belief: When annotating, you should highlight, underline and circle interesting things. You don't need to write anything down as you will remember what you thought.
312.statement: When annotating, you should highlight, underline and circle interesting things. You don't need to write anything down as you will remember what you thought.
312.correction: Symbols, highlights and underlinings are all useful, but only if accompanied by short written notes which remind you what it was you found interesting. Otherwise your symbols become meaningless.

313.belief: Annotating means highlighting everything you think is important in a text.
313.statement: Annotating means highlighting everything you think is important in a text.
313.correction: Annotating is a skill that requires time and thought. Using symbols and short notes makes your annotations helpful and understandable, even if you come back to them at a much later date.

10466.belief: We have two different presentations of Achilles. One of them must be right, and one must be wrong.
10466.statement: We have two different presentations of Achilles. One of them must be right, and one must be wrong.
10466.correction: What Miller and Barker do with their novels is show how important perspective is. For Patroclus, Achilles is awe inspiring and innocent. For Briseis, he is quite the opposite. Their perspectives are based on their relationship with him.

3036.belief: 'The Fisherman the and Jinni' is a framing story because there is a story within it.
3036.statement: 'The Fisherman the and Jinni' is a framing story because there is a story within it.
3036.correction: The story of King Yunan and his sage is a story within a story. In 'One Thousand and One Nights', the frame story is only that of Shahrazad and Shahrayar. This frame story punctuates all the tales, with dialogue between husband and wife throughout.

3065.belief: The folktales have no connection to the frame story.
3065.statement: The folktales have no connection to the frame story.
3065.correction: The folktales are being told by Shahrazad. The fact that she is trying to save her life by telling the stories is important. But more than this, you can also make connections between the ideas, plot and characters in the folktales to the frame story.

3039.belief: The five part narrative structure is the only way to structure a story.
3039.statement: The five part narrative structure is the only way to structure a story.
3039.correction: There are lots of ways to create a story that is structured. This is one example. The most important thing to remember is that whatever your structure, it should be considered and carefully planned.

9163.belief: Each section of the five part narrative structure equals one paragraph in your writing.
9163.statement: Each section of the five part narrative structure equals one paragraph in your writing.
9163.correction: The five part narrative structure is a helpful way to help plan plot and character. However, some sections might be longer than others. Some might require multiple paragraphs, others just one.

847.belief: You can't repeat any ideas in creative writing. Once you have used them once, you must create new ideas in every successive paragraph.
847.statement: You can't repeat any ideas in creative writing. Once you have used them once, you must create new ideas in every successive paragraph.
847.correction: Repetition of certain ideas or images can give your writing a sense of structure. This is particularly true in your final paragraph where repeating ideas from your first paragraph can alert your reader to the idea that you are about to finish.

5875.belief: Proofreading and rewriting are the same thing.
5875.statement: Proofreading and rewriting are the same thing.
5875.correction: Proofreading is the final stage of the writing process. It is about checking for small errors - often grammatical. Rewriting is a larger task which requires you to think about the effects you want to create.

4339.belief: The magical potion is removed from everyone's eyes at the end of the play.
4339.statement: The magical potion is removed from everyone's eyes at the end of the play.
4339.correction: Demetrius still has the magical potion on his eyes. This is why he is in love with Helena.

5574.belief: If a play is a comedy, it won't have any moments of sadness in it.
5574.statement: If a play is a comedy, it won't have any moments of sadness in it.
5574.correction: When thinking about genre, we consider the overall tone, plot and features of a play. However, many comedies have moments of sadness, just as many tragedies have moments of humour.

10340.belief: Titania seems to have some power, but Hermia has none.
10340.statement: Titania seems to have some power, but Hermia has none.
10340.correction: Hermia defies her father by saying that she will marry Lysander, and refusing to marry Demetrius. She is also willing to leave her father, and the place she was born rather than obey her father.

951.belief: The characters in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' are Elizabethan.
951.statement: The characters in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' are Elizabethan.
951.correction: The play's first audiences were Elizabethan, and Shakespeare explores Elizabethan attitudes and ideas in the play. But the play is set in Athens many centuries before the Elizabethan period.

836.belief: You can't compare one scene to another. You must focus on one at a time.
836.statement: You can't compare one scene to another. You must focus on one at a time.
836.correction: A play is not a sequence of unconnected scenes and characters. They all work together to present and explore particular ideas. You should compare characters and scenes in order to understand a play, its characters and ideas more deeply.

260.belief: Analysis means zooming in to individual words and explaining what they mean.
260.statement: Analysis means zooming in to individual words and explaining what they mean.
260.correction: Exploring quotations is more than just looking at individual words and offering paraphrase or synonym. Your exploration of the quotation should develop your ideas about the question, and look at dramatic methods (more than just individual words).

5138.belief: There is one interpretation of Puck (either malevolent or mischievous) and you have to work out which one is correct.
5138.statement: There is one interpretation of Puck (either malevolent or mischievous) and you have to work out which one is correct.
5138.correction: A play, and its characters, can be interpreted in many different ways. Different performances will draw out particular interpretations.

5039.belief: Oberon's commands, status and dominance in the dialogue mean he can only be interpreted as powerful.
5039.statement: Oberon's commands, status and dominance in the dialogue mean he can only be interpreted as powerful.
5039.correction: There is much to suggest Oberon's power in this scene, but dialogue can be interpreted in many ways, and performance can affect how we perceive a character. There is no single reading of the play.

5035.belief: Oberon asks Puck to turn Bottom's head into that of a donkey.
5035.statement: Oberon asks Puck to turn Bottom's head into that of a donkey.
5035.correction: Puck follows Oberon's orders, but in his own time, he gets up to his own mischief. He decides to transform Bottom and Oberon does not set out for Titania to fall in love with this particular character.

2013.belief: Context should be included in one sentence at the end of each analytical paragraph.
2013.statement: Context should be included in one sentence at the end of each analytical paragraph.
2013.correction: You can include contextual ideas where relevant - this could be at the start, middle or multiple times in a paragraph. Contextual ideas will often help you develop your analysis of a particular quotation or character.

5038.belief: Oberon and Puck deliberately try and create disorder between Hermia, Lysander, Helena and Demetrius.
5038.statement: Oberon and Puck deliberately try and create disorder between Hermia, Lysander, Helena and Demetrius.
5038.correction: Oberon orders Puck to put the magical potion on Demetrius so that he falls in love with Helena. Puck makes a genuine mistake by putting it on Lysander.

5037.belief: Oberon knows Titania will fall in love with Bottom.
5037.statement: Oberon knows Titania will fall in love with Bottom.
5037.correction: Oberon hopes Titania will fall in love with something "vile" but he doesn't know about Bottom, or his transformation, until Puck tells him the joke he has played.

3874.belief: It isn't important that Puck's mistake is genuine.
3874.statement: It isn't important that Puck's mistake is genuine.
3874.correction: Without understanding what happens, and why, in Act 2, Scene 2, we won't have an accurate understanding of Shakespeare's characterisation of Puck which deepens and develops throughout the play.

5911.correction: Puck's disrespect is targeted at particular characters. He is shown as respectful to Oberon, for example, and other high status characters.

5036.belief: Oberon finds the disorder between the Athenian nobles funny.
5036.statement: Oberon finds the disorder between the Athenian nobles funny.
5036.correction: As soon as Oberon realises Puck's mistake, he swiftly tries to correct it.

5912.belief: Puck tries to create more chaos after realising his mistake.
5912.statement: Puck tries to create more chaos after realising his mistake.
5912.correction: Puck is consistently shown to follow Oberon's orders in relation to the Athenian nobles, and to try and do so correctly. However, he does find it very funny, even though he didn't deliberately create the situation.

10339.belief: Titania, Lysander and Demetrius have the antidote applied to them.
10339.statement: Titania, Lysander and Demetrius have the antidote applied to them.
10339.correction: So that the play can end in happy marriages between all four Athenian nobles, only Lysander has the antidote applied to him. Demetrius is still under the influence of the magical potion.

10720.belief: Using one quotation per paragraph is enough.
10720.statement: Using one quotation per paragraph is enough.
10720.correction: Using multiple quotations per paragraph can be effective if you select quotations which link. Select quotations from across the text.

9280.belief: It is not significant that Puck performs the epilogue. It could have been any of the characters.
9280.statement: It is not significant that Puck performs the epilogue. It could have been any of the characters.
9280.correction: There are many different ideas to explore in terms of why Puck performs this epilogue. It could speak to his centrality to the plot, his infamous reputation amongst the play's first Elizabethan audiences, and the way we should interpret key themes.

245.belief: You should only analyse one quotation per paragraph.
245.statement: You should only analyse one quotation per paragraph.
245.correction: Analysing multiple quotations, and exploring the connections between them, makes for the most powerful analysis.

2783.belief: You should only ever consider one Shakespearean play at a time. Comparing plays and characters is irrelevant and confusing.
2783.statement: You should only ever consider one Shakespearean play at a time. Comparing plays and characters is irrelevant and confusing.
2783.correction: Comparing characters can be an excellent way to deepen your understanding of Shakespeare as a writer, and to understand the significance of how a particular character has been created.

5317.belief: Paragraphs can only focus on one character at a time.
5317.statement: Paragraphs can only focus on one character at a time.
5317.correction: Comparing characters can be a useful way to deepen your understanding and analysis.

11145.belief: If you are writing about a character, you should just write down everything you know about them.
11145.statement: If you are writing about a character, you should just write down everything you know about them.
11145.correction: When writing about a character, you should consider how you interpret them and why. You should explain this main idea in your thesis.

3850.belief: Introductions are the same as thesis statements.
3850.statement: Introductions are the same as thesis statements.
3850.correction: An introduction includes a thesis statement. However, an introduction should include a more general statement about the text, as well as a more general statement about the given character or theme as well as the thesis.

8725.belief: Every quotation in a main body paragraph should be analysed.
8725.statement: Every quotation in a main body paragraph should be analysed.
8725.correction: Some quotations should be analysed, but others you can simply embed into sentences.

1914.correction: Conclusions are about summing up your overall argument (your thesis) rather than continuing to develop it via analysis of new quotations.

247.belief: You must analyse every quotation at word level.
247.statement: You must analyse every quotation at word level.
247.correction: Sometimes exploring individual words can be helpful, but more often than not it makes for shallow analysis which is not helpful in answering the question. Look at 'bigger' methods than single words.

9032.belief: There are no rules in debating. It is just another way to argue or have an argument and does not need preparation.
9032.statement: There are no rules in debating. It is just another way to argue or have an argument and does not need preparation.
9032.correction: Formal debating is an important part of society and allows important issues to be discussed in a constructuve way. It takes consideration and preparation to be involved in an effective debate.

2199.belief: In a debate you can only argue a stance you truly believe in.
2199.statement: In a debate you can only argue a stance you truly believe in.
2199.correction: Part of the skill of debating is being able to create, justify and convincingly present an argument that might not reflect your own personal viewpoint.

9271.belief: You always have to show both sides of the argument in a debate or discussion.
9271.statement: You always have to show both sides of the argument in a debate or discussion.
9271.correction: In a debate, it is much more skilfull to present a single line of argument.

4879.belief: I do not need to plan for a debate.
4879.statement: I do not need to plan for a debate.
4879.correction: To participate effectively in debate you will need to have clear arguments and rebuttals, that are backed up with evidence. Planning will ensure you can do this confidently.

9945.belief: Of speeches as being a form of protest, but poems or songs.
9945.statement: Students think of speeches as being a form of protest, but poems or songs.
9945.correction: Emphasise the wide range of text types used in the lesson.

9895.belief: They need to be balanced in their writing and discuss both sides of a debate.
9895.statement: Students often think they need to be balanced in their writing and discuss both sides of a debate.
9895.correction: Teach the difference between opinion writing and argument writing.

9728.statement: Students often don't value their own knowledge or experiences when aiming to persuade.
9728.correction: Encourage students to use examples that they are familiar with.

4878.belief: You need to be personally affected by something to make a speech about it.
4878.statement: That you need to be personally affected by something to make a speech about it.
4878.correction: Draw attention to Hillary Clinton as an advocate.

9893.belief: A motif is a symbol used once or think it is deployed in the same way as a semantic field.
9893.statement: Students can think a motif is a symbol used once or think it is deployed in the same way as a semantic field.
9893.correction: Remind them of the etymology - there has to be movement and change of the motif. A semantic field does not have to be symbolic.

2565.belief: It is easy to confuse motifs with extended metaphors.
2565.statement: It is easy to confuse motifs with extended metaphors.
2565.correction: A motif uses recurring elements that can employ a range of techniques. An extended metaphor is a sustained comparison across a text.

9862.belief: To evaluate something is to say whether or not you like it.
9862.statement: Students often think that to evaluate something is to say whether or not you like it.
9862.correction: Keep reminding them of the criteria. Does a text measure up to a standard being set?

9938.belief: Serious topics need serious text types such as articles or speeches.
9938.statement: Students often think that serious topics need serious text types such as articles or speeches.
9938.correction: Encourage students to consider why a writer might choose to use a poem to write about a serious topic and take a stand.

2917.belief: Fairy tales are written solely for children.
2917.statement: Fairy tales are written solely for children.
2917.correction: Fairy tales are primarily stories about transformation and therefore this form appeals to many writers, especially those who are interested in social issues.

9844.belief: There is a very clear distinction between poetry and music lyrics.
9844.statement: Students may think that there is a very clear distinction between poetry and music lyrics.
9844.correction: Encourage students to consider what the poetry and song lyrics have in common. For example the use of verses and refrains, as well as the use of figurative language, often crosses over.

2970.belief: Figurative language, like metaphors, is not used in presentations.
2970.statement: Figurative language, like metaphors, is not used in presentations.
2970.correction: Stress how much stronger presentations can be when it allows the audience to make associations with objects and items they are familiar with.

9828.belief: They have to be balanced when they deliver persuasive presentations.
9828.statement: Students often think they have to be balanced when they deliver persuasive presentations.
9828.correction: Be clear about taking a stand and picking a side. A presentation which is clear in its stance has much more impact.

4558.belief: Memorising a presentation, or having a script, makes for a more confident delivery.
4558.statement: Memorising a presentation, or having a script, makes for a more confident delivery.
4558.correction: An effective presentation will have an element of spontaneity and naturalism about it. Relying on a script, or repeating a speech word for word, can lead to a robotic delivery and a less convincing presentation.

2002.belief: Content alone is enough for an effective formal presentation.
2002.statement: Content alone is enough for an effective formal presentation.
2002.correction: Consider the most engaging speakers and how they use tone, gestures and eye contact. Delivering a presentation is so much more than just the words on a page.

4138.belief: 'Life Doesn't Frighten Me' is saying that life isn't scary.
4138.statement: 'Life Doesn't Frighten Me' is saying that life isn't scary.
4138.correction: The poem lists many scary and frightening things. It presents some of the world's dangers. The speaker, however, is not frightened of life despite these dangers.

274.belief: Angelou's poem is unstructured - the stanzas are uneven and she talks about lots of different things.
274.statement: Angelou's poem is unstructured - the stanzas are uneven and she talks about lots of different things.
274.correction: Every piece of writing has a structure - even a shopping list. Structure is about the how a text is put together - at its most simple, beginning, middle and end. But we can also look for other structural features. In this case, stanzas and a refrain.

5654.belief: Poems are meant to be read in your head.
5654.statement: Poems are meant to be read in your head.
5654.correction: When poets write poems, they play close attention to their sounds and rhythm. As such, it's often important and desirable to hear poems aloud.

2971.belief: Figurative language and metaphors are synonyms.
2971.statement: Figurative language and metaphors are synonyms.
2971.correction: All metaphors are examples of figurative language. But not all figurative language is a metaphor. For example, personification, hyperbole and simile are also examples of figurative language.

5477.belief: Personal opinions about texts are not valid. Only analysis is valid.
5477.statement: Personal opinions about texts are not valid. Only analysis is valid.
5477.correction: Being a student of English can often feel like this. But expressing your opinions about your feelings towards a text - those you read in and outside the classroom - is very important and just as much a part of the subject of English as analysis.

5462.belief: Performing poetry is just about reading it aloud.
5462.statement: Performing poetry is just about reading it aloud.
5462.correction: Watching people perform poetry is very popular. The most engaging performers carefully consider how they will say the poem, and how they will engage with their audiences.

793.belief: The caged bird is presented as completely powerless.
793.statement: The caged bird is presented as completely powerless.
793.correction: Although the bird in the cage is confined, he still has power, through his song which speaks to his unbroken spirit. We are meant to draw a parallel to the strength of the Black community.

5476.belief: Personal opinions in English don't matter. Only analysis is valid.
5476.statement: Personal opinions in English don't matter. Only analysis is valid.
5476.correction: Being a student of English can often feel like this. But expressing your opinions about your feelings towards a text - those you read in and outside the classroom - is very important and just as much a part of the subject of English as analysis.

2973.belief: Figurative language is a synonym for a metaphor or simile.
2973.statement: Figurative language is a synonym for a metaphor or simile.
2973.correction: Metaphor and simile are both specific examples of figurative language. Figurative language is a broader term. Allusion, personification and hyperbole are other common examples of figurative language.

273.belief: Angelou copied Dunbar. Copying is not allowed.
273.statement: Angelou copied Dunbar. Copying is not allowed.
273.correction: Many writers learn from, and are inspired by, others. Angelou's poem is very different to Dunbar's - her personal style and voice come through - but the central metaphor 'speaks' from one poem to another, developing a relationship between them.

1852.belief: Comparing a poem's beginning and end doesn't count as analysis. It's too simple to be interesting.
1852.statement: Comparing a poem's beginning and end doesn't count as analysis. It's too simple to be interesting.
1852.correction: At its most basic (and often most powerful), a text's structure is its beginning, middle and end. Commenting on the journey - emotional or physical - that a writer has taken us on is a great way to start exploring structure.

236.belief: Every American president has a poem read at their inauguration.
236.statement: Every American president has a poem read at their inauguration.
236.correction: Presidents have choice over some elements of their inauguration. President Clinton was only the second president to have a poem read at his ceremony, and he specifically asked for Angelou to write and perform it.

9527.belief: The speaker in 'On Aging' doesn't think aging affects you.
9527.statement: The speaker in 'On Aging' doesn't think aging affects you.
9527.correction: The speaker lists some of the things that happen to you physically when you get older - she faces the reality. However, what she does want to change are people's reactions and perceptions of what these changes mean.

9270.belief: You shouldn't talk about poems as a group. This will make your comments too general.
9270.statement: You shouldn't talk about poems as a group. This will make your comments too general.
9270.correction: You can make clear comments about a poet's work as a whole, as long as these comments are supported by specific examples from specific poems.

9339.belief: Single paragraph outlines take too long to plan. You should just start writing.
9339.statement: Single paragraph outlines take too long to plan. You should just start writing.
9339.correction: Single paragraph outlines give you time to think and prepare. Spending time on these means that you will be able to write your paragraph efficiently knowing that it has a clear focus with well-selected supporting detail.

842.belief: You can't plan a poem. Poems are inspired, and just flow from the heart.
842.statement: You can't plan a poem. Poems are inspired, and just flow from the heart.
842.correction: Poems, just like paragraphs, can be planned. You can consider ideas and methods. Indeed, because poems are often shorter than other texts, planning each idea and method is even more important - no word can be wasted.

843.belief: You can't plan a stanza of a poem. It's not like a paragraph or an essay.
843.statement: You can't plan a stanza of a poem. It's not like a paragraph or an essay.
843.correction: Stanzas are like paragraphs. They need structure and focus. Spending time planning their methods, vocabulary and ideas make writing the stanza easier.

5632.belief: A poem with a good rhythm always rhymes.
5632.statement: A poem with a good rhythm always rhymes.
5632.correction: Rhythm is about the flow, beat and sound of a poem. Rhyme can sometimes develop rhythm, but it is not necessary.

1857.belief: Comparisons are either clear similarities or clear differences.
1857.statement: Comparisons are either clear similarities or clear differences.
1857.correction: Use examples from slides to demonstrate how comparisons are often more complex than ideas being completely similar or completely different.

3592.belief: Identifying language devices is the most important skill when analysing author's language choices.
3592.statement: Identifying language devices is the most important skill when analysing author's language choices.
3592.correction: When looking at the question, ask pupils whether 'Guthrie uses a simile' would be an appropriate response to the question. If not, why not?

11117.belief: The working class are the social class most likely to commit crime.
11117.statement: The working class are the social class most likely to commit crime.
11117.correction: What types of crime are more likely to be committed by the wealthy? Why might they be less likely to be punished?

3107.belief: "You" is the only form of direct address when addressing a reader/audience.
3107.statement: "You" is the only form of direct address when addressing a reader/audience.
3107.correction: When teaching the over reliance on direct address, rapidly fire questions to one pupil, addressing them as 'you'. Ask them how this feels.

10355.belief: Topic sentences are only used in essay writing.
10355.statement: Topic sentences are only used in essay writing.
10355.correction: Remind pupils that topic sentences are signposts for readers, indicating to them the direction our writing will be travelling in.

7287.statement: Pupils start a speech by directly addressing the audience and explaining the purpose of the speech.
7287.correction: Ask pupils if the best method of getting your own way is by stating what you want straight away.

1700.belief: Clear and confident delivery of speeches requires a consistent pace of delivery throughout.
1700.statement: Clear and confident delivery of speeches requires a consistent pace of delivery throughout.
1700.correction: Model the delivery of a sentence which starts at pace, but slows down to draw attention to particular vocabulary choices.

9930.belief: Scientific advancements have always been celebrated.
9930.statement: Students often think that scientific advancements have always been celebrated.
9930.correction: In reality, scientists faced a lot of backlash for their ideas, mostly because many of them contradicted the teachings of the Bible.

9869.belief: Frankenstein is the name of the creature.
9869.statement: Students think that Frankenstein is the name of the creature.
9869.correction: Frankenstein is the name of the scientist who created the hideous creature that students are often familiar with.

5962.statement: Pupils do not appreciate the extent of Frankenstein's immorality.
5962.correction: In pursuit of knowledge, Frankenstein broke natural and political laws. He robbed graves and tortured live animals to achieve his ambition.

9850.belief: The Creature did something to terrify/hurt Victor.
9850.statement: Students often think that the Creature did something to terrify/hurt Victor.
9850.correction: Victor takes an instant dislike to the Creature because of its ugliness. Victor shuns the Creature immediately, purely because of its looks.

6689.statement: Pupils forget that the description of the Creature is written from Frankenstein's perspective.
6689.correction: Shelley describes the Creature so horribly through the eyes of Frankenstein to show his disgust with his creation.

9818.statement: Students tend to think of humans as being good and monsters as being evil.
9818.correction: In this novel, the line between good and evil is blurred. Shelley forces us to question who the real monster is in the novel.

9665.statement: Students do not appreciate the Creature's eloquence and the fact that he has educated himself.
9665.correction: The Creature is a persuasive and eloquent character who manages to convince Victor to begin making him a mate.

9940.belief: Shelley was opposed to scientific advancement.
9940.statement: Students think that Shelley was opposed to scientific advancement.
9940.correction: Shelley was not opposed to scientific advancement; she was opposed to unethical and limitless scientific practices.

9899.belief: They only need to plan one single paragraph outline.
9899.statement: Students might think that they only need to plan one single paragraph outline.
9899.correction: Students will need to plan one paragraph outline per section of their response.

9800.statement: Students often simply 'method spot' in analytical responses.
9800.correction: The writer's intention should form part of students' analysis of the text, as they should be outlining why the writer has used the method.

9780.statement: Students panic about unseen activities and think that there is a 'right' or 'wrong' answer.
9780.correction: The text is unseen - students are not supposed to be experts on it. They just need to read the text and give their opinions about it - any well-evidenced opinion is the 'right' answer.

9790.statement: Students might not recognise this as a Gothic setting, as it is not overtly frightening or eerie.
9790.correction: Brontë's use of contrasting colours, isolation and cold make this a Gothic setting. Gothic descriptions do not have to be terrifying at all times.

7877.belief: Gothic settings have to be utterly terrifying to count as Gothic.
7877.statement: Pupils think that Gothic settings have to be utterly terrifying to count as Gothic.
7877.correction: Gothic settings are not about frightening the reader as much as possible. They are about making the reader feel unsettled and creating an atmosphere of mystery and dark intrigue.

9826.belief: Atmosphere is created purely through the description of a physical setting.
9826.statement: Students think that atmosphere is created purely through the description of a physical setting.
9826.correction: Atmosphere can also be created through characters interacting with one another, as we see in Chapter 11 of 'Jane Eyre'.

9770.statement: Students often make the mistake of using a new word they have just learned inaccurately, in an attempt to show off their knowledge.
9770.correction: The point of learning new vocabulary is to give students options and choices so that they can select the most specific and useful word in their writing. Sometimes, the most specific word choice isn't the new vocabulary.

9795.statement: Students do not recognise the value in using semantic fields - they think that semantic fields are just a method that they can spot in other writers' texts.
9795.correction: Using semantic fields can help us to include figurative language, such as extended metaphors. They are means of including other methods - they are not necessarily a stand-alone method.

8519.statement: Pupils do not understand that they have to think carefully about their use of figurative language and plan it before they begin writing.
8519.correction: Students need to consider carefully what kind of atmosphere they are trying to create. When comparing their setting to something else, the 'something else' needs to fit with the atmosphere they are aiming to create.

9969.belief: If they write a horror story that is full of blood and gore, that this makes it Gothic.
9969.statement: Students think that if they write a horror story that is full of blood and gore, that this makes it Gothic.
9969.correction: Gothic literature is about unsettling and mystifying the reader - not traumatising them with gory descriptions and extreme violence. There can be more fear in what is not revealed, than what is revealed.

7189.statement: Pupils often reveal things early-on in descriptions by saying things like 'it was a painting' and then proceeding to describe it.
7189.correction: It can be much more effective to describe your narrator's view before revealing what the view actually is. This way, the reader is kept in a state of anticipation, as they try to work out what the view is.

2271.belief: In descriptive writing, students often just describe what their protagonist can see. They often neglect the other senses.
2271.statement: In descriptive writing, students often just describe what their protagonist can see. They often neglect the other senses.
2271.correction: To create the most vivid description possible, students should focus their description on the five sense, subtly moving between exploring how the scene feels, smells, looks, tastes and sounds.

9909.belief: Once they have written their first draft, the piece is finished.
9909.statement: Students often think that once they have written their first draft, the piece is finished.
9909.correction: Writing is a process that involves several drafts of the same piece. Each time, editing and rewriting the draft makes the piece of writing better.

9793.statement: Students might not recognise that there is a possibility that the sound of the old man's heart beating, may be the sound of the narrator's own heart beating.
9793.correction: Some may interpret the sound of the old man's heart beating as the sound of the narrator's own heart beating, with anticipation and excitement at the prospect of the imminent murder.

9879.belief: Irony is a term only used in comedy.
9879.statement: Students might think that irony is a term only used in comedy.
9879.correction: There is a dark comedy to this story, created through the use of irony, whereby the narrator insists that he is not 'mad' but then proceeds to murder and dismember an old man simply because he hates one of the old man's eyes.

9982.statement: Students often do not understand the depth of meaning that symbolism can provide.
9982.correction: Symbols communicate hidden or deeper meanings to the reader, so that they can better understand the characters or themes of the text.

9891.statement: Students often think of methods exclusively as 'similes/metaphors' etc.
9891.correction: The writer's method is anything they do consciously. This could be choosing one, single word over another.

9865.belief: The first version of their work is the finished piece.
9865.statement: Students think that the first version of their work is the finished piece.
9865.correction: Redrafting work improves its quality, depth and coherence. Students should be encouraged to appreciate, and embrace the value of redrafting their work.

9955.belief: Tone and voice are the same thing.
9955.statement: Students often think that tone and voice are the same thing.
9955.correction: Voice is the identity of the writer and the beliefs they convey, whereas tone is the way in which these beliefs are conveyed.

9989.statement: Students often do not use descriptions in functional writing frequently enough.
9989.correction: Descriptive language massively enhances functional writing. Anecdotes are a brilliant example of how descriptive writing can be used to connect to the reader/audience.

9796.statement: Students often rush the ending of their work - particularly if they are writing in timed conditions.
9796.correction: The ending is arguably the most important part of the piece of writing. Students need to leave their reader with a clear message that is memorable. The ending ties together the threads of the argument and reinforces the writer's viewpoint.

9727.statement: Students often don't think to include rhetorical devices within their topic sentences.
9727.correction: Just because the topic sentences introduces the main idea for the paragraph, that does not mean the topic sentence can't be really creative and engaging. It's crucial that it is engaging to motivate the reader to learn more about the topic.

9970.belief: They have to write from their own perspective - that the 'voice' in the article has to be their own.
9970.statement: Students often think that they have to write from their own perspective - that the 'voice' in the article has to be their own.
9970.correction: Students can create a voice. For example, they could write the article from the perspective of a teacher or a parent. This is still voice.

9960.belief: Using lots of the pronoun 'you' is an effective use of direct address. They tend to do this a lot in rhetorical questions.
9960.statement: Students think that using lots of the pronoun 'you' is an effective use of direct address. They tend to do this a lot in rhetorical questions.
9960.correction: Using 'you' too many times can create an accusatory tone that can actually make the reader defensive. Sometimes, it can be better to approach direct address more subtly, by speaking to an imagined reader or addressing the readers collectively.

3347.belief: Gothic only applies to external settings like buildings and the weather.
3347.statement: Gothic only applies to external settings like buildings and the weather.
3347.correction: The Gothic is about psychological states as much as setting.

9776.statement: Students may misuse the varying forms of the word "symbolism."
9776.correction: Explicitly teach them how the various forms are used in sentences.

9746.statement: Students may find the idea of house as a metaphor for the self challenging.
9746.correction: Draw their attention to their own ideas around houses.

5474.belief: The persona is the same as the writer.
5474.statement: That the persona is the same as the writer.
5474.correction: Emphasise the difference. Draw attention to the different personas in 'The Haunted Palace' and 'The Raven'. Same writer, different personas.

9975.statement: Students thinking they need to find big differences in the poems.
9975.correction: It's often better to choose similarities and then explain and explore the subtle differences.

9980.statement: Students might try to read the poem rather than recite.
9980.correction: Encourage students to learn as much of the poem as possible.

2676.statement: That the English language developed quickly.
2676.correction: The English that we speak today was shaped across many hundreds of years by lots of significant events in our history.

5065.belief: Old English was created exclusively by the Anglo-Saxons.
5065.statement: That Old English was created exclusively by the Anglo-Saxons.
5065.correction: The Anglo-Saxons' Germanic languages contributed to Old English but languages already spoken in Britain – and Latin – also played a part.

2357.belief: Different translations of the Lord's Prayer over time have been purely literal.
2357.statement: That different translations of the Lord's Prayer over time have been purely literal.
2357.correction: When new translations are made, writers change both the language and the content to suit modern audiences.

5828.belief: The process of amelioration and pejoration mean a word completely changes its meaning.
5828.statement: That the process of amelioration and pejoration mean a word completely changes its meaning.
5828.correction: Pejoration and amelioration refer to a word becoming more negative/positive and this does not mean the word completely changes its meaning.

11058.belief: 'word blending' is a type of compound.
11058.statement: That 'word blending' is a type of compound.
11058.correction: 'Word blending' combines only part of other words whereas word compounds combines the entirety of two existing words to form a new one.

9678.statement: Students should avoid short or one-word sentences in favour of longer, complex sentences.
9678.correction: If used correctly, shorter sentences can be great for amending pace and giving emphasis to particular parts of a speech.

4278.belief: As long as they are using language devices in their speeches, this is enough.
4278.statement: That as long as they are using language devices in their speeches, this is enough.
4278.correction: There is great variety in quality in the execution of language devices. The best devices are creative, original and well-matched to purpose.

9722.belief: Students should constantly be changing the pitch of their voice when speaking.
9722.statement: That students should constantly be changing the pitch of their voice when speaking.
9722.correction: Pitch is an effective tool when delivering speeches. It should be used to make a speech more engaging and shouldn't be used arbitrarily.

8222.belief: When pupils think about the role of rules in society, they tend to focus on the role of more punitive rules and argue that rules are restrictive.
8222.statement: When pupils think about the role of rules in society, they tend to focus on the role of more punitive rules and argue that rules are restrictive.
8222.correction: Try to get pupils to understand the necessity for rules and laws - particularly those that ban harming others. Get students to imagine what life would be like if harming others was not prohibited.

7932.belief: The island in the novel is like a tropical paradise.
7932.statement: Pupils often think the island in the novel is like a tropical paradise.
7932.correction: Draw their attention to the suggestion of danger in the language used.

6839.statement: Pupils often judge Piggy by the critical standards employed by the other boys.
6839.correction: Pick out examples of how sensible and intelligent Piggy is and how his judgement is usually sound.

8217.belief: The rift in the novel is only between Ralph and Jack.
8217.statement: Pupils may think that the rift in the novel is only between Ralph and Jack.
8217.correction: Draw attention to how the boys are increasingly living separately: Piggy is on his own, the "littluns" are a group by themselves and Simon sneaks away to be alone.

9875.belief: Golding's reference to a world order in "ruins" refers to the damaged sandcastles and their ruined life on the island.
9875.statement: Students might think that Golding's reference to a world order in "ruins" refers to the damaged sandcastles and their ruined life on the island.
9875.correction: Remind students of Golding's wartime experiences and the events of WWII. Golding is referring to the world the boys left behind as well as the world on the island.

9924.belief: Ralph doesn't blow the conch to summon the boys back because he is afraid of Jack.
9924.statement: Students may think that Ralph doesn't blow the conch to summon the boys back because he is afraid of Jack.
9924.correction: Ralph is not afraid of Jack. He is afraid that if he blows the conch and the boys don't return, he will have lost his authority.

9983.statement: Students may not understand that Sam and Eric have not actually seen the parachutist.
9983.correction: Unpick the description given by Sam and Eric. Were we (the reader) actually shown the different aspects of the beast?

7094.statement: Pupils may be puzzled by Ralph's seemingly sudden descent into the violence and savagery that seems to have captured the other boys.
7094.correction: Point out how Jack's more aggressive behaviour appeals to the boys.

9716.statement: Students may be confused about what is actually happening in the encounter between the beast and Simon.
9716.correction: Remind them that Simon has a tendency to lose consciousness. They need to be able to interpret this encounter on multiple levels.

7936.belief: Only Jack's hunters are involved in the killing of Simon.
7936.statement: Pupils sometimes think that only Jack's hunters are involved in the killing of Simon.
7936.correction: Draw attention to the one sentence where Golding says that Ralph and Piggy want to be part of the group.

9835.belief: The boys all feel the same about the killing of Simon.
9835.statement: Students may think the boys all feel the same about the killing of Simon.
9835.correction: Focus on words used: Some talk about "murder," some call the killing an "accident" or pretend that they left "early".

9915.belief: Piggy's death is an accident, similar in kind to Simon's, an example of boys getting carried away.
9915.statement: Students may think that Piggy's death is an accident, similar in kind to Simon's, an example of boys getting carried away.
9915.correction: Draw pupils' attention to the fact that Roger is compared to a hangman. A hangman kills intentionally.

9798.statement: Students may see the rescue as wholly positive.
9798.correction: Draw your pupils' attention to the lack of understanding of their ordeal. Also, to the fact rescue comes on a warship and the officer is carrying a revolver.

9819.statement: Students have a tendency to view Ralph as a morally-virtuous character who does no wrong.
9819.correction: Ralph does behave immorally and wickedly in the text - he is mean to Piggy about his asthma and he participates in the murder of Simon. What separates Ralph from the others is the remorse he shows for his actions and how he learns from them.

7934.belief: The island turned Jack into the cruel and bloodthirsty leader he is by the end of the novel.
7934.statement: Pupils often think that the island turned Jack into the cruel and bloodthirsty leader he is by the end of the novel.
7934.correction: From the very beginning, Jack was characterised as unpleasant and egomaniacal. He treats the choir terribly in the first chapter. Jack arguably always had the traits of a dictatorial leader. The island has exacerbated these traits, not created them.

7056.statement: Pupils often overlook Simon's significance in this novel.
7056.correction: Simon is a very important character because he shows us that, in a world of evil, we can still act in a compassionate and civilised manner. Through Simon, Golding reminds us that our behaviour is a choice.

6433.statement: Pupils often fail to recognise Ralph's role in the ostracism of Piggy.
6433.correction: Ralph is the first person to ostracise Piggy, by banning him from accompanying the boys on their expedition. He also calls Piggy by the name he begged Ralph not to use - Piggy. Once Jack senses Piggy's vulnerability within the group, he exploits it.

7933.belief: The island is presented as idyllic in the first chapter.
7933.statement: Pupils think that the island is presented as idyllic in the first chapter.
7933.correction: Whilst there are aspects of the description that present the island as idyllic, Golding's descriptions are characterised by a sense of threat in more ominous undertones. He achieves this through his use of dark and light and through his use of verbs.

4318.belief: Lots of students do not realise that this novel was actually inspired by an earlier, 19th century novel called 'Coral Island' by Ballantyne.
4318.statement: Lots of students do not realise that this novel was actually inspired by an earlier, 19th century novel called 'Coral Island' by Ballantyne.
4318.correction: Golding uses the established genre and subverts its conventions to create a horrifying exploration of what evil truly is and where it comes from.

9951.belief: Symbols in a text have to be physical objects that represent ideas.
9951.statement: Students think that symbols in a text have to be physical objects that represent ideas.
9951.correction: Symbolism is the use of images, words or nouns to represent abstract ideas or qualities - symbols do not have to be physical objects that can be picked up and held.

9874.belief: Golding sits on the 'nature' side of the nature/nurture debate.
9874.statement: Students think that Golding sits on the 'nature' side of the nature/nurture debate.
9874.correction: Golding does not provide us with a concrete answer- he suggests that we all have the capacity (or the impulses) to behave sinfully, but it takes the right circumstances for brutality to emerge.

9978.statement: Students might try to draw parallels between Jack and the snake from the Garden of Eden.
9978.correction: Arguably, the temptation is not Jack himself, but the savagery and evil that resides within him. It is the "beast" within him that tempts him to evil.

9842.belief: Characters are not methods. They tend to think of methods as just 'similes' or 'metaphors'.
9842.statement: Students often think that characters are not methods. They tend to think of methods as just 'similes' or 'metaphors'.
9842.correction: Any choice that the writer makes consciously is a method. This includes their use of characterisation. Anything the character says or does is a method.

9864.belief: The first attempt at their response is the finished version.
9864.statement: Students often think that the first attempt at their response is the finished version.
9864.correction: Redrafting your work has many benefits and the second attempt is always superior. Taking time to reflect on your work and identify areas for improvements allows you to recognise any lack of clarity in your explanations.

4140.belief: Life was simply bad 'then' and 'good' now.
4140.statement: That life was simply bad 'then' and 'good' now.
4140.correction: Exploring the similarities between the past and now, can help draw out the nuances of societal expectations and stereotypical representations.

3505.belief: Historically, societal expectations were focused on women.
3505.statement: That historically, societal expectations were focused on women.
3505.correction: Both men and women were subject to societal expectations. However, men had much more freedom and power and it's important to acknowledge this difference.

510.belief: Autobiographies are not considered literary or forms of literature.
510.statement: Autobiographies are not considered literary or forms of literature.
510.correction: Just like other forms of writing, writers of autobiographies will use literary devices to convey emotions and document events in detail.

9405.belief: Only soldiers on the front line had direct experiences of conflict.
9405.statement: Only soldiers on the front line had direct experiences of conflict.
9405.correction: Who does war impact? Besides being a soldier, what other roles do people have in war?

4257.belief: As long as I can back up my answer, I can put forward any interpretation of the text.
4257.statement: As long as I can back up my answer, I can put forward any interpretation of the text.
4257.correction: Using tentative language can lead to a more exploratory approach, rather than presenting 'right' or 'wrong' interpretations.

5308.belief: Pankhurst and the suffragettes were peaceful protesters.
5308.statement: Pankhurst and the suffragettes were peaceful protesters.
5308.correction: How does Pankhurst's speech convey some of the radical tactics or attitudes employed by the suffragettes? Pankhurst and her followers pushed boundaries and challenged societal norms to fight for women's rights.

4254.belief: As long as I am comparing the key points of two sources that is enough.
4254.statement: As long as I am comparing the key points of two sources that is enough.
4254.correction: Using both comparative and correlative conjunctions will ensure there is nuance in your comparisons. They will aslo help keep your comparisons succinct.

10673.belief: When used, rhetorical devices have only one possible effect or outcome.
10673.statement: When used, rhetorical devices have only one possible effect or outcome.
10673.correction: Writers can craft rhetorical devices to create different tones and match their purpose, audience and form. For example, direct address can be used to sound confrontational or it can create an intimate and personal tone.

5226.belief: Opinions are just what you think and don't need to be informed by anything.
5226.statement: Opinions are just what you think and don't need to be informed by anything.
5226.correction: Opinions should be informed by available information or evidence. For example: prior knowledge, contextual information and the writer's language choices, can all help to create informed opinions.

5479.belief: The only perspective presented in a text is the writer's.
5479.statement: The only perspective presented in a text is the writer's.
5479.correction: Texts can also include viewpoints of characters, experts or sources the writer references. In this article we also hear the subject's perspective through the use of quotations.

835.belief: You can't compare different text types to each other. For example, an article to a memoir.
835.statement: You can't compare different text types to each other. For example, an article to a memoir.
835.correction: By comparing different forms, we can often come to understand why a writer chose a particular text type more deeply - what this particular text type allowed them to do or convey to the reader.

9179.belief: You should select one quotation from each text in a comparative paragraph.
9179.statement: You should select one quotation from each text in a comparative paragraph.
9179.correction: Like in a powerful analytical paragraph, selecting multiple quotations from each text will help strengthen your argument. Selecting these quotations in the planning stage is key.

3503.belief: Historical texts only portray stereotypical representations of women.
3503.statement: Historical texts only portray stereotypical representations of women.
3503.correction: Even though societal expectations and stereotypes exist, this does not mean that all people conform to these standards - even in the past!

2838.belief: Evidence, or quotations, need to be long when used in an analytical paragraph or response.
2838.statement: Evidence, or quotations, need to be long when used in an analytical paragraph or response.
2838.correction: If you select the right words, single words can provide an opportunity for rich analysis. Layering your comments means you can say a lot about a little!

5537.belief: Planning isn't a useful step in the writing process and it takes too long.
5537.statement: Planning isn't a useful step in the writing process and it takes too long.
5537.correction: How might planning help to organise our thoughts into a coherent response? How can planning improve the efficiency of the writing process?

11161.belief: When writing about serious issues, the main tone of your writing should be angry and confrontational.
11161.statement: When writing about serious issues, the main tone of your writing should be angry and confrontational.
11161.correction: Think about what engages you. An audience is far more likely to be engaged if they feel like they have a rapport with the speaker.

5482.belief: A persuasive speech needs to be angry and aggressive.
5482.statement: A persuasive speech needs to be angry and aggressive.
5482.correction: What is Watson's tone? How does she motivate and persuade her audience without being confrontational? You don't want to alienate any audience members.

11157.belief: When writing persuasively you should use as many rhetorical devices as possible.
11157.statement: When writing persuasively you should use as many rhetorical devices as possible.
11157.correction: Whilst using rhetorical devices is a great way to engage your audience, they need to be used sparingly and crafted carefully to ensure they don't lose their impact.

5483.belief: In persuasive writing, I just need to include a range of rhetorical devices and sophisticated vocabulary.
5483.statement: In persuasive writing, I just need to include a range of rhetorical devices and sophisticated vocabulary.
5483.correction: Whilst it is important to use rhetorical devices and choose interesting language, you must also consider the structure of your writing. This ensures that your argument has a clear progression and your message doesn't get lost.

2477.belief: I don't have time to write an effective closing, I just need to get my work finished!
2477.statement: I don't have time to write an effective closing, I just need to get my work finished!
2477.correction: The ending is arguably the most important part of the piece of writing. You need to leave your audience with a clear message that is memorable. Writing effective closings will get quicker the more you practice using specific strategies.

4624.belief: Mind mapping is the only way to plan a piece of writing.
4624.statement: Mind mapping is the only way to plan a piece of writing.
4624.correction: Mind mapping is a good place to start, but isn't always useful for considering structure. Using single paragraph outlines is an effective way to ensure a cohesive stricture and a clearly developed line of argument.

8938.belief: Rewriting and improving responses is a waste of time.
8938.statement: Rewriting and improving responses is a waste of time.
8938.correction: How does the process of revising and rewriting develop vocabulary use? How does rewriting support the writing of future responses?

2003.belief: Content alone is enough for an effective speech.
2003.statement: Content alone is enough for an effective speech.
2003.correction: Consider the most engaging speakers and how they use tone, gestures and eye contact. Giving a speech is so much more than just the words on a page.

4559.belief: Memorising the speech, or having a script, makes for a more confident delivery.
4559.statement: That memorising the speech, or having a script, makes for a more confident delivery.
4559.correction: An effective speech will have an element of spontaneity and naturalism about it. Relying on a script, or repeating a speech word for word, can lead to a robotic delivery and a less convincing speech.

4402.belief: Malevolent characters are always obviously and outwardly evil characters.
4402.statement: Malevolent characters are always obviously and outwardly evil characters.
4402.correction: Ask pupils whether they can think of any characters from literature where their malevolence is implied or not explicitly stated at first. These characters are often dangerously deceptive.

7055.statement: Pupils will sometimes overload the physical description of their character and list each individual detail, often using cliches.
7055.correction: Describing every part of a character’s appearance in detail can overwhelm the reader. It's better to provide purposeful descriptions that integrate physical appearance with personality to create an engaging and convincing character.

8127.belief: A physical description of a character is enough to help the reader understand what the character's personality is like.
8127.statement: Pupils may think that a physical description of a character is enough to help the reader understand what the character's personality is like.
8127.correction: Though physical description is really useful, considering verb and adverb choices in particular allows the reader to really imagine a character. For example, how they walk, talk and behave around others are all telling of their character.

4275.belief: As long as similes or metaphors follow the correct rules they will be effective.
4275.statement: As long as similes or metaphors follow the correct rules they will be effective.
4275.correction: Many comparisons in similes and metaphors are clichéd and this often takes away from a description and makes it unimaginative. The challenge is to try be original in your thought!

8346.belief: Using contrast and juxtaposition in character descriptions means simply listing opposing traits without showing how they interact or affect each other.
8346.statement: Pupils might think that using contrast and juxtaposition in character descriptions means simply listing opposing traits without showing how they interact or affect each other.
8346.correction: It's important to show how the contrasting traits of characters impact each other. For example, instead of just stating that one character is kind and the other is cruel, describe a scene where their actions and behaviors directly conflict.

3653.belief: The most important part of dialogue is what is inside the speech marks.
3653.statement: The most important part of dialogue is what is inside the speech marks.
3653.correction: What is said through dialogue is really important, but it's also crucial to consider how that dialogue is to be said. Careful selection of verbs and adverbs give the reader a crucial insight into how dialogue should be read.

7763.belief: Descriptions of setting only serve as background and do not contribute to character development or tone of a piece of writing.
7763.statement: Pupils might think that descriptions of setting only serve as background and do not contribute to character development or tone of a piece of writing.
7763.correction: Settings are integral to storytelling as they can reflect and enhance a character's emotions, personality, and the overall tone of the scene. For example, a gloomy, rainy setting can mirror a character's sadness or create a foreboding atmosphere.

7776.belief: It doesn't always matter where paragraphs go as long as the text is broken up in places.
7776.statement: Some pupils might think it doesn't always matter where paragraphs go as long as the text is broken up in places.
7776.correction: Effective paragraphing is important to the reader's experience of the text. It helps them to follow what they're reading more easily and well crafted paragraphs allow the writer to reveal information in a way that suits their writing best.

8131.belief: Planning isn't a helpful or worthwhile exercise.
8131.statement: Some pupils think that planning isn't a helpful or worthwhile exercise.
8131.correction: Planning allows us to carefully consider our ideas before writing and allows us to work out what ideas work best for the task we've been given. Planning often results in a final stronger piece of work so is very worthwhile!

6389.statement: Pupils often don't see the value in editing work and think once the first draft is finished, the work on it is done.
6389.correction: Writing is a process that involves multiple stages. Revising and editing are crucial steps to refine your work, enhance clarity, and improve overall quality. Even professional writers revise their drafts several times before publishing.

3873.belief: It isn't important to consider the ethics of writing about war. It is a topic just like any other.
3873.statement: It isn't important to consider the ethics of writing about war. It is a topic just like any other.
3873.correction: There are important questions to be asked when considering writing about any harrowing experience, particularly war.

10428.belief: Trench warfare was fighting characterised by intense and constant action.
10428.statement: Trench warfare was fighting characterised by intense and constant action.
10428.correction: Trench warfare was characterised by intense periods of action, but also long periods of inaction which could be demoralising, boring and harrowing.

338.belief: Anyone who breathed in gas died immediately.
338.statement: Anyone who breathed in gas died immediately.
338.correction: Gas attacks killed about three percent of people immediately, but there were long term physical and psychological effects for those who experienced gas attacks.

840.belief: You can't link quotations from across a text in a short story.
840.statement: You can't link quotations from across a text in a short story.
840.correction: Being able to link quotations from any text together is a key skill in English. It helps make your analysis thoughtful and convincing.

4228.belief: Those living in Britain during World War One faced no threat or privation other than their loved ones being far away.
4228.statement: Those living in Britain during World War One faced no threat or privation other than their loved ones being far away.
4228.correction: World War One was what is known as 'total war' meaning that those in Britain felt its impact in their day to day life.

846.belief: You can't refer to other writers or texts in your analysis.
846.statement: You can't refer to other writers or texts in your analysis.
846.correction: Often, you will be asked to write about a text, and that text should certainly be your focus. However, you can refer to other writers or texts if they help develop your analysis and understanding. This is called literary context.

1817.belief: There are no common symbols across literature.
1817.statement: There are no common symbols across literature.
1817.correction: There are many common symbols across literature which writers use knowing that many of their readers will know what they mean. For example, a crown to symbolise power. A rose to symbolise love. Birds to symbolise freedom.

10646.belief: You can only use single paragraph outlines to plan analytical writing.
10646.statement: You can only use single paragraph outlines to plan analytical writing.
10646.correction: We structure so much of our writing using paragraphs. All paragraphs, whether creative or analytical or something else, require a clear and carefully planned structure.

1777.belief: Commas and full stops are interchangeable.
1777.statement: Commas and full stops are interchangeable.
1777.correction: Full stops divide independent clauses and create a longer pause than a comma. Full stops divide ideas and create clear writing. Commas divide subordinate clauses and lists. They create a shorter pause.

4747.belief: Mr. Woodifield intentionally tries to upset the boss.
4747.statement: Mr. Woodifield intentionally tries to upset the boss.
4747.correction: Mr. Woodifield seems unaware that he has upset the boss, and his cruelty in mentioning his son's grave in Belgium is thoughtless rather than deliberately cruel.

945.belief: Every character is a foil to another because all characters are different.
945.statement: Every character is a foil to another because all characters are different.
945.correction: Whilst characters, like humans, are unique, not every character serves as a foil. Strangely, character foils often have similarities in terms of who they are, and what has happened to them, but their reactions to these things are different.

246.correction: There are some quotations that you will want to analyse in depth, and consider their methods and the range of ways they might be interpreted. However, there will also be quotations that link to your topic sentence, but don't need to be analysed.

5139.belief: There is one interpretation of a text and it is your job as a student of English to find the correct interpretation.
