9822.statement: Students do not think that they can analyse the poem's title.
9822.correction: In analytical responses, students can absolutely analyse the poem's title! This can be a great way to start a response or comparison.

9882.belief: Larkin must have had a hostile relationship with his family because of this poem and some of his other poems.
9882.statement: Students often think that Larkin must have had a hostile relationship with his family because of this poem and some of his other poems.
9882.correction: Larkin didn't have a hostile relationship with his parents - he was just a cynical man who held quite bleak views. This doesn't mean he hated his parents - he just recognised that people are products of their own parents.

9995.statement: Students often want to be told the 'right' answer in English and think there is a right answer for every question.
9995.correction: There are no 'right' answers in this lesson - this lesson asks students to consider different possibilities and interpretations and to make up their own minds about the poem.

9910.belief: There is only 'one right interpretation' of a poem.
9910.statement: Students often think that there is only 'one right interpretation' of a poem.
9910.correction: Students are shown in this lesson that poetry can be read in several different ways and that any interpretation is valid. Students should be encouraged to explore multiple interpretations when discussing poetry.

9731.statement: Students may fail to recognise that arguably, this poem is a series of stories instead of one 'big' story.
9731.correction: Dove arguably tells several small stories which all contribute to our understanding of the depth of love between her and her husband - Fred.

8264.belief: The speaker does not love their partner very much.
8264.statement: Pupils think that the speaker does not love their partner very much.
8264.correction: The speaker does love their partner - very much. The speaker, unlike other lovers, refuses to make promises that they aren't 100% sure they can't keep - they arguably find promising 'forever' unrealistic.

8156.belief: The poet does not support the idea of love.
8156.statement: Pupils might think that the poet does not support the idea of love.
8156.correction: In the poem, the speaker is expressing their love for their partner. The speaker does support love, and acknowledges the benefits it can bring - they just also acknowledge the great harm it can cause.

10917.belief: All war poems from the anthology are equally comparable.
10917.statement: All war poems from the anthology are equally comparable.
10917.correction: Some war poems are more suitable for comparison, depending on which question you are asked. You should make your decision based on which ideas and themes you want to discuss.

9857.belief: They can only discuss the similarities OR the differences between poems.
9857.statement: Students think that they can only discuss the similarities OR the differences between poems.
9857.correction: Though they should approach the comparison by identifying key or significant similarities or difference, within that, they can also explore the subtle variations between poems too.

9988.statement: Students often use context as a 'bolt-on'.
9988.correction: Context is a valuable additional source of evidence for your argument. Context should be relevant, specific and support your argument. It should be 'peppered' throughout your essay and not 'bolted-on' at the end.

9846.belief: They can only compare two poems from the same thematic cluster within the anthology.
9846.statement: Students might think that they can only compare two poems from the same thematic cluster within the anthology.
9846.correction: Students can compare any pair of poems as long as the poems have some similarities.

9901.belief: They need to 'zoom in' on every word when analysing a quotation.
9901.statement: Students often think that they need to 'zoom in' on every word when analysing a quotation.
9901.correction: Often, it can be useful to discuss the 'bigger' method that the poet is using e.g. their use of personification. By thinking about bigger methods, the students may be more focused on the themes of the poem and the poet's intentions.

11172.belief: WW1 poets portrayed dying for their country as glorious.
11172.statement: WW1 poets portrayed dying for their country as glorious.
11172.correction: While some WW1 poets did portray it as glorious, poets such as Wilfred Owen depicted the horrors and futility of the war.

10947.belief: The way a poet uses punctuation in a poem is not useful to analyse.
10947.statement: The way a poet uses punctuation in a poem is not useful to analyse.
10947.correction: Creating pauses within poetic lines using punctuation, such as caesuras, can create ideas of separation or disjointedness.

1838.belief: A comparative response should only focus on the differences between two poems.
1838.statement: A comparative response should only focus on the differences between two poems.
1838.correction: An effective comparative response considers the similarities between the poems as well as nuanced differences within those similarities.

9403.belief: Soldiers were always aware of what they were signing up for.
9403.statement: Soldiers were always aware of what they were signing up for.
9403.correction: Many men and boys who signed up to fight for the British Empire were unaware of the realities of war and what it would mean for them.

10944.belief: The only way to interpret a regular rhyme scheme is to suggest that it brings a sense of calmness to the poem.
10944.statement: The only way to interpret a regular rhyme scheme is to suggest that it brings a sense of calmness to the poem.
10944.correction: As well as a sense of calm, a regular rhyme scheme can also create ideas of control and predictability.

1841.belief: A comparative topic sentence should only focus on the differences between poems.
1841.statement: A comparative topic sentence should only focus on the differences between poems.
1841.correction: A comparative topic sentence should either state the similarities or differences between the poems in relation to the central focus of the paragraph.

5639.belief: This poem is primarily about familial conflict.
5639.statement: This poem is primarily about familial conflict.
5639.correction: Although the speaker and Kate are family relations, the conflict between them is focused on their shared love interest and so their family connection is inconsequential.

9531.belief: The speaker feels as though her cousin Kate has ruined her life completely.
9531.statement: The speaker feels as though her cousin Kate has ruined her life completely.
9531.correction: While the speaker does feel that Kate has stolen the life she deserved/desired, she also feels that she can have the 'last laugh' since she has given birth to the nobleman's son.

4320.belief: Love poems always contain ideas of warmth and happiness.
4320.statement: Love poems always contain ideas of warmth and happiness.
4320.correction: Love is not always warm or happy - love poems often reflect the uncertainty, worry, and pain that love can bring people.

10706.belief: Using an irregular structure always creates a sense of freedom.
10706.statement: Using an irregular structure always creates a sense of freedom.
10706.correction: While it can create a sense of freedom, an irregular structure can also create ideas of unpredictability and uncertainty.

9394.belief: Society's attitudes towards female pleasure have completely changed since the 1800s.
9394.statement: Society's attitudes towards female pleasure have completely changed since the 1800s.
9394.correction: While society's attitudes towards female pleasure are less extreme than in the 1800s, arguably there is still a sense of shame attached to female pleasure in modern society.

687.belief: Blake is opposed to all education.
687.statement: Blake is opposed to all education.
687.correction: Blake critiques oppressive institutions, not education itself, reflecting Romanticism's focus on freedom and natural growth.

9121.belief: 'The Schoolboy’s' simple language and regular structure suggest that it is a straightforward poem about childhood rather than a deeper critique of institutional control.
9121.statement: 'The Schoolboy’s' simple language and regular structure suggest that it is a straightforward poem about childhood rather than a deeper critique of institutional control.
9121.correction: While the language and structure may seem simple, Blake uses them deliberately to reflect the monotony and rigidity of school life.

5622.belief: The poem is just about the childhood memories of summer and picking fruit.
5622.statement: The poem is just about the childhood memories of summer and picking fruit.
5622.correction: Heaney uses the extended metaphor of blackberry picking to explore nostalgia and the fleeting nature of youth and time.

697.belief: The "Bluebeard" allusion represents only danger and violence in childhood.
697.statement: The "Bluebeard" allusion represents only danger and violence in childhood.
697.correction: The allusion reflects both the danger and the intense, unrestrained joy of childhood, where pleasure feels almost forbidden.

10234.belief: The thesis statement is just a summary of the poems.
10234.statement: The thesis statement is just a summary of the poems.
10234.correction: An effective comparative thesis will highlight a key comparison and difference between the texts, showing how they deepen an understanding of the key themes and ideas.

5629.belief: This poem is entirely autobiographical, written about Clarke's experiences of motherhood.
5629.statement: This poem is entirely autobiographical, written about Clarke's experiences of motherhood.
5629.correction: This poem was written just after the birth of Clarke's fist daughter so does reflect on her experiences of motherhood but the later scenes of a older child playing out are necessarily fictional.

4211.belief: Lines 9-16 of the poem use abstract imagery to convey the moment of the birth in the hospital room.
4211.statement: Lines 9-16 of the poem use abstract imagery to convey the moment of the birth in the hospital room.
4211.correction: While this is one way of interpreting these lines, others have argued the abstract images could reflect society's unfair expectations of mothers and the nature of the developing maternal relationship.

5628.belief: This poem doesn’t seem like a typical love poem because it doesn’t present love as happy or ideal. Most love poetry tends to focus on idealised romantic love.
5628.statement: This poem doesn’t seem like a typical love poem because it doesn’t present love as happy or ideal. Most love poetry tends to focus on idealised romantic love.
5628.correction: Ewing shows love as fragile but meaningful. By exploring romantic, familial, and self-love, she challenges idealised love poetry and redefines what love can look like—real, complex, and powerful.

10348.belief: The tone of ‘Origin Story’ is simply nostalgic or romantic.
10348.statement: The tone of ‘Origin Story’ is simply nostalgic or romantic.
10348.correction: Although there are nostalgic and tender elements in the poem, the overall tone is more assertive and self-possessed. This confident tone reflects a deeper purpose: reclaiming identity, celebrating heritage, and asserting authorship over her story.

5658.belief: Both poems use a first-person persepctive and therefore express similar attitudes towards love and identity.
5658.statement: Both poems use a first-person persepctive and therefore express similar attitudes towards love and identity.
5658.correction: While both use first-person perspective, ‘Catrin’ shows intense, ongoing maternal love, and ‘Origin Story’ reflects on a past, fragile romantic love. The attitudes differ because one is direct and personal, the other reflective and shaped by memory.

4265.belief: As long as I include quotations from both poems and mention some similarities or differences, I’m doing a good comparative analysis.
4265.statement: As long as I include quotations from both poems and mention some similarities or differences, I’m doing a good comparative analysis.
4265.correction: Without analysis, the response does not explain how or why the poets present their ideas, or what effects those choices have. This limits the depth and quality of the comparison.

2598.belief: The most effective comparisons only come from poems with the most obvious similarities.
2598.statement: The most effective comparisons only come from poems with the most obvious similarities.
2598.correction: Insightful comparisons can often emerge from contrasting poems. Exploring differences can uncover complexity and nuance, enriching analysis beyond what similarity alone can achieve.

5551.belief: Planning takes too much time and isn’t worth it when writing an essay.
5551.statement: Planning takes too much time and isn’t worth it when writing an essay.
5551.correction: Planning saves time overall. It helps you organise your ideas, stay focused, and write more clearly and effectively, making your essay stronger and easier to complete.

5088.belief: Once I’ve written my essay, I don’t need to think about it again.
5088.statement: Once I’ve written my essay, I don’t need to think about it again.
5088.correction: When you have the opportunity to rewrite or redraft your work, you should take it! It helps you deepen your thinking, develop your ideas more clearly, and express yourself with greater precision. Writing is a process, not just a product.

2590.belief: Education is only ever a positive power.
2590.statement: Education is only ever a positive power.
2590.correction: Consider Pinnock's words about her parents' generation and why and how education can be used as a tool of oppression.

2223.correction: Del does see the value in formal education, but was turned away from it through a lack of support and understanding.

757.correction: Brod expresses that he loved and respected England until his naturalisation process which destabilised his sense of self and opened his eyes to some of the injustices he faces, in his present and his past.

10881.belief: Viv irrevocably rejects the formal education system.
10881.statement: Viv irrevocably rejects the formal education system.
10881.correction: Viv questions what she is learning and why, but stays within formal education, perhaps because of her chosen university course which may reflect her experiences and identity in a way that her schooling hasn't.

5521.correction: Pinnock sees the very real power of formal education, but opens our eyes to how that power has been used for ill, and how it could be used for good.

2012.belief: Context should be the final sentence of each analytical paragraph.
2012.statement: Context should be the final sentence of each analytical paragraph.
2012.correction: Context should be woven in to paragraphs where relevant; context should help develop and enrich your ideas.

5530.belief: A plan isn't a useful revision tool.
5530.statement: A plan isn't a useful revision tool.
5530.correction: Creating a plan, and revisiting it, is an excellent way to revise. It can be quicker than writing a full essay, but still requires you to think about a particular essay question and your argument in response to it.

5800.belief: Priestley suggests that all gender roles have been successfully challenged by the end of the play.
5800.statement: Priestley suggests that all gender roles have been successfully challenged by the end of the play.
5800.correction: A more nuanced view is that argaubly Priestley shows both progress and resistance, suggesting that while some characters challenge gender roles, societal change is slow and not fully realised.

4748.belief: Mrs Birling is a woman and therefore she automatically shares the same struggles as Eva Smith.
4748.statement: Mrs Birling is a woman and therefore she automatically shares the same struggles as Eva Smith.
4748.correction: While both are women, Mrs Birling's high class gives her power to uphold societal norms, whereas Eva, from a lower class, is oppressed by them.

9254.belief: Sheila’s transformation at the end of the play is entirely optimistic, showing that she has completely embraced responsibility and will lead a future free from societal inequality.
9254.statement: Sheila’s transformation at the end of the play is entirely optimistic, showing that she has completely embraced responsibility and will lead a future free from societal inequality.
9254.correction: While Sheila's growth is significant, her awareness is limited and she’s still part of the system she criticises. Priestley uses her character to show potential for change, but also highlights the ongoing challenges of inequality.

4397.belief: The male characters fully embody societal expectations of masculinity.
4397.statement: The male characters fully embody societal expectations of masculinity.
4397.correction: Both Gerald and Eric's remorse reveal internal conflict, showing the struggles and complexities inherent in societal expectations.

2770.belief: Eva Smith doesn’t have dialogue and therefore she can’t be analysed in depth.
2770.statement: Eva Smith doesn’t have dialogue and therefore she can’t be analysed in depth.
2770.correction: Eva’s lack of dialogue actually makes her more powerful to analyse. Her silence and absence force the audience to focus on how others speak about her.

5534.belief: Planning an essay just means listing points I want to cover and then writing a draft straight away.
5534.statement: Planning an essay just means listing points I want to cover and then writing a draft straight away.
5534.correction: Whilst this can work, clearly understanding your argument, structuring your ideas, and deciding what evidence or quotations to use before you start writing can be much more efficient and effective.

1701.belief: There are clear distinctions between good leaders and bad leaders in 'Animal Farm'.
1701.statement: That there are clear distinctions between good leaders and bad leaders in 'Animal Farm'.
1701.correction: Although 'Animal Farm' is simply written, its messages are complex. What is Orwell wanting to reveal about leadership in general?

716.belief: Boxer is only presented as naïve and gullible.
716.statement: That Boxer is only presented as naïve and gullible.
716.correction: Why does Napoleon set the dogs on Boxer? There are moments when Boxer begins to challenge what he is being told by the pigs.

2459.belief: I don't need to bother with a conclusion.
2459.statement: I don't need to bother with a conclusion.
2459.correction: Who will be reading your response? Imagine them reading your final sentence, how do you want them to feel?

11150.belief: Writing essays is not like creative writing, it doesn't matter how you write things so much.
11150.statement: Writing essays is not like creative writing, it doesn't matter how you write things so much.
11150.correction: Not writing clearly and accurately can mean excellent ideas can be lost once written down.

290.belief: 'Animal Farm' is a simple story about leadership and power.
290.statement: That 'Animal Farm' is a simple story about leadership and power.
290.correction: Stylistically it is simple, but why does Orwell do this? What does he hope to achieve by making his novella accessible?

5254.statement: That Orwell presents "good" leaders and "bad" leaders.
5254.correction: Think about the impact of Mr. Jones and the pigs on the animals' lives. Is it easy to distinguish which one is better or worse?

4873.belief: You need to learn lots of quotes to write a successful essay.
4873.statement: You need to learn lots of quotes to write a successful essay.
4873.correction: Picking a few 'hard working', analytically rich quotes is a better strategy. It's what you do with them that counts.

2796.belief: Everyone considers 'Romeo and Juliet' to be about love.
2796.statement: That everyone considers 'Romeo and Juliet' to be about love.
2796.correction: Some critics consider 'Romeo and Juliet' to be primarily about violence and society instead.

629.belief: Benvolio is a peaceful character in 'Romeo and Juliet'.
629.statement: Benvolio is a peaceful character in 'Romeo and Juliet'.
629.correction: While Benvolio calls for peace, he engages in violence when he thinks it is necessary.

4303.belief: Lord Capulet and Tybalt share the same views on all the Montagues.
4303.statement: Lord Capulet and Tybalt share the same views on all the Montagues.
4303.correction: While Lord Capulet wishes to join the fight in Act 1, Scene 1, he encourages Tybalt to leave Romeo alone at the Caplulet ball.

4565.belief: Men were supposed to be the 'bigger man' and act rationally in the face of a challenge to their honour.
4565.statement: That men were supposed to be the 'bigger man' and act rationally in the face of a challenge to their honour.
4565.correction: In Elizabethan England, men were expected to defend their honour.

4302.belief: Lord Capulet only considers Juliet to have dishonoured herself through her refusal of the marriage to Paris.
4302.statement: Lord Capulet only considers Juliet to have dishonoured herself through her refusal of the marriage to Paris.
4302.correction: Arguably, Lord Capulet also thinks he and the Capulet family are also dishonoured by Juliet's refusal.

4398.belief: The male characters in Shakespeare's 'Romeo and Juliet' are always keen to fight.
4398.statement: That the male characters in Shakespeare's 'Romeo and Juliet' are always keen to fight.
4398.correction: In Act 5, Scene 3, Romeo and Paris both seem reluctant to fight.

8727.belief: Any quotation from the text adds weight to your argument.
8727.statement: Any quotation from the text adds weight to your argument.
8727.correction: For a quotation to be effective, it has to be relevant to the point you are making.

5148.belief: There is only one plot point that fits to each part of Freytag's structure.
5148.statement: There is only one plot point that fits to each part of Freytag's structure.
5148.correction: When discussing climax, ask pupils if any other events in the play could be considered the climax.

7983.belief: Macbeth has all of the characteristics of a tragic hero.
7983.statement: Pupils think Macbeth has all of the characteristics of a tragic hero.
7983.correction: Use learning cycle 2 to draw out a debate about whether Macbeth actually learnt a lesson, highlighting where pupils may not agree.

6092.belief: Lady Macbeth is solely responsible for the downfall of her husband.
6092.statement: Pupils believe Lady Macbeth is solely responsible for the downfall of her husband.
6092.correction: When discussing Macbeth's intrigue in the prophecies, challenge pupils to question whether Lady Macbeth is responsible at this point.

9682.statement: Students become over-reliant on the quotation: "Is this a dagger which I see before me?"
9682.correction: Draw attention to other quotations which both illustrate Macbeth can see a dagger, but also demonstrate the flaws in his character.

10235.belief: Thesis statements have to be very general.
10235.statement: Thesis statements have to be very general.
10235.correction: Thesis statements can be specific, but they should offer opportunity to consider different interpretations.

502.belief: All audiences will feel the same about Macbeth's death.
502.statement: All audiences will feel the same about Macbeth's death.
502.correction: Remind pupils that the joy of literature is exploring different responses to the same text. Use LC1 to identify these differences.

10233.belief: A thesis statement is just a rewording of the essay question.
10233.statement: A thesis statement is just a rewording of the essay question.
10233.correction: The essay question is useful in formulating a thesis, however try using key question vocabulary and using it to form your own argument.

9903.belief: The novel is Gothic in the typical sense.
9903.statement: Students may think that the novel is Gothic in the typical sense.
9903.correction: Be clear about subversion and how it works in the novella. Although Stevenson uses some Gothic elements they are not always used in the typical way for the genre.

9902.belief: The novel is entirely about secrets.
9902.statement: Students think the novel is entirely about secrets.
9902.correction: Remind them how often Hyde is observed committing crimes.

9867.belief: The fog is purely designed to create an eerie Gothic atmosphere.
9867.statement: Students think that the fog is purely designed to create an eerie Gothic atmosphere.
9867.correction: Be clear about the symbolic nature of fog. The fact that it can allow for partial visibility.

2503.belief: The dream is only caused by Utterson being in a state of distress.
2503.statement: That the dream is only caused by Utterson being in a state of distress.
2503.correction: Unpick the details of the dream to show the parallels with the plot.

9939.belief: Setting is used solely to create atmosphere.
9939.statement: Students sometimes think that setting is used solely to create atmosphere.
9939.correction: Encourage students to see Stevenson's use of setting as figurative as well as literal.

9614.belief: Stevenson presents good and evil as complete opposites.
9614.statement: That Stevenson presents good and evil as complete opposites.
9614.correction: Remind students how easily Hyde and Jekyll blur into one.

2486.belief: Dr. Jekyll enjoys the experience of being Mr. Hyde.
2486.statement: That Dr. Jekyll enjoys the experience of being Mr. Hyde.
2486.correction: Encourage students to notice the different ways that Dr. Jekyll has declined.

9725.statement: Students often don't realise that Dickens' deliberately capitalised on a popular genre.
9725.correction: Dickens wanted the novella to become a bestseller, as this would give his message the best chance of reaching as many people as possible.

9932.statement: Students might think that Scrooge is evil.
9932.correction: Scrooge is not evil - he is immoral. A distinction between the two needs to be clarified.

7854.belief: There are only four ghosts in the novella.
7854.statement: Pupils think there are only four ghosts in the novella.
7854.correction: Pupils forget about the numerous ghosts that Scrooge sees when he looks out of the window at the end of Stave 1.

9872.belief: The Ghost of Christmas Present is actually holding Plenty's horn.
9872.statement: Students often think that the Ghost of Christmas Present is actually holding Plenty's horn.
9872.correction: Dickens carefully clarifies that the torch is "in a shape not unlike Plenty's horn", showing that the torch is not actually Plenty's horn.

9937.belief: Scrooge's visit with the Ghost of Christmas Present is limited to Christmas Day.
9937.statement: Students think that Scrooge's visit with the Ghost of Christmas Present is limited to Christmas Day.
9937.correction: Scrooge's time with the spirit goes beyond Christmas Day - to the Twelfth Day of Christmas, showing how time is manipulated in the novella.

9979.statement: Students try to include as much knowledge as possible in their responses.
9979.correction: Encourage students to be selective in their choice of ideas and to explain their choices.

9922.belief: They should present lots of different ideas in an essay.
9922.statement: Students think they should present lots of different ideas in an essay.
9922.correction: Whilst you should present lots of different knowledge, the knowledge should all form part of the same idea or argument.

9927.belief: All 'Romantic' poems should be compared, all 'war' poems must be compared, all 'nature' poems must be compared.
9927.statement: Students may think that all 'Romantic' poems should be compared, all 'war' poems must be compared, all 'nature' poems must be compared.
9927.correction: The nuances of the question are the most important factor when deciding which poems to compare.

632.belief: The best analysis identifies similarities and differences between poems in the anthology.
632.statement: The best analysis identifies similarities and differences between poems in the anthology.
632.correction: The best analysis will look for nuanced variations between similarities (e.g. 'Both 'Bayonet Charge' and 'Remains' explore the impact of war on individuals. However, Remains focuses more on war's aftermath and the psychological effect it can have.')

9821.belief: Agard went to school in Britain and that is the reason for his Eurocentric education.
9821.statement: Students may think that Agard went to school in Britain and that is the reason for his Eurocentric education.
9821.correction: Agard was schooled in Guyana whilst it was a British colony, this is the reason for his Eurocentric education. Learning about the colonisation of Guyana can help students to understand Agard's indignation.

9758.statement: Students may have not heard of the folk tales and nursery rhymes in the poem so may not be able to identify them as such.
9758.correction: The use of nursery rhymes and folk tale was a deliberate stylistic choice, perhaps Agard is indignant about the trivial nature of some of his education.

7044.statement: Pupils may notice the theme of oppression in ‘The Émigrée’ due to the mention of war, but not notice this in 'Checking Out Me History'.
7044.correction: 'Checking Out Me History' explores how Agard presents colonisation and its effects as oppressive.

9336.belief: There is a single, clear interpretation of 'Tissue'.
9336.statement: There is a single, clear interpretation of 'Tissue'.
9336.correction: There are varied interpretations of the poem and - as long as they are supported by evidence - they are valid. Students may focus on the comparison of power to paper or on the similar fragility between paper and human life.

5640.belief: The poem has a regular, repetitive structure of nine, unrhyming quatrains.
5640.statement: The poem has a regular, repetitive structure of nine, unrhyming quatrains.
5640.correction: Although most of the poem is written in this way, there is a sudden and sharp break to this form with the final stanza being a single line. You may wish to discuss this with your class (learning cycle 2 discusses the significance of this break).

9675.belief: Writing about how the poet wants the reader to feel is enough when writing about intent.
9675.statement: Students may assume that writing about how the poet wants the reader to feel is enough when writing about intent.
9675.correction: To add sophistication and criticality to writing, evaluative verbs can be very effective when discussing the writer's intent.

9762.statement: Students may immediately want to compare 'Tissue' with ‘The Émigrée’ due to the immediate connection with light and displacement.
9762.correction: If we look more closely at 'Tissue', we can find solid links between poems about the ephemerality of human power.

4798.belief: 'My Last Duchess' and 'Checking Out Me History' are written over 100 years apart, thus won't make for the most effective comparison.
4798.statement: 'My Last Duchess' and 'Checking Out Me History' are written over 100 years apart, thus won't make for the most effective comparison.
4798.correction: When looking at poems to compare, look closely at similarities between big ideas and you can find nuanced links between poems that are written in different socio-political contexts.

3583.belief: The idea of "paradise" is the same for everyone.
3583.statement: That the idea of "paradise" is the same for everyone.
3583.correction: We all have our own concept of what "paradise" looks like and what it might mean in terms of our memories and connections to the world.

2270.belief: Descriptions of colours are only there to provide a visual aid.
2270.statement: That descriptions of colours are only there to provide a visual aid.
2270.correction: Colour symbolism is deeply important to the meaning of the poem as well.

5637.belief: A poem has only one meaning.
5637.statement: That a poem has only one meaning.
5637.correction: A poem can have many different meanings woven together because we are all made up of different ideas and our views on the world are rarely singular.

5659.belief: If a poet doesn't conform to a poetic form then they are rejecting it.
5659.statement: If a poet doesn't conform to a poetic form then they are rejecting it.
5659.correction: By not using a particular poetic form, or subverting a poetic form, a poet may be critiquing a certain expectation or making a certain comment on society.

9282.statement: That silence is a negative thing.
9282.correction: Silence can also be peaceful, enriching and calming.

686.belief: "black" and "white" imagery always relates to ideas of absence and emptiness.
686.statement: That "black" and "white" imagery always relates to ideas of absence and emptiness.
686.correction: While "black" and "white" imagery can signal a sense of absence and emptiness, we could also interpret them as showing strength and purity.

10473.belief: When two poets use the same technique then they have the same intended outcome.
10473.statement: When two poets use the same technique then they have the same intended outcome.
10473.correction: Poetic techniques can be interpreted in a number of different ways, so you can't assume that if a second poet uses the same technique as a first then it will have the same meaning.

9308.belief: Since you normally only compare two poems, it's not useful to make connections across the whole anthology.
9308.statement: Since you normally only compare two poems, it's not useful to make connections across the whole anthology.
9308.correction: Making connections across the whole anthology allows you to see the threads that connect the poems which will extend your comparative responses.

8819.belief: Referencing any contextual information about the poets is useful.
8819.statement: That referencing any contextual information about the poets is useful.
8819.correction: Contextual information needs to enhance your argument and understanding of the poem for it to be meaningful.

5533.belief: Planning is not an effective use of time.
5533.statement: That planning is not an effective use of time.
5533.correction: Planning helps to to write a developed, detailed and cohesive response.

3879.belief: There isn't a purpose to analytical writing.
3879.statement: That there isn't a purpose to analytical writing.
3879.correction: The purpose of analytical writing is to convince the reader of your ideas about the text(s).

5072.belief: Once an answer is completed you don't need to return to it.
5072.statement: That once an answer is completed you don't need to return to it.
5072.correction: It's useful to think of your first response to a question as your first draft and then go back to it and rewrite and edit where necessary.

9314.belief: Singh's wife is presented exclusively as a sweet and gentle character.
9314.statement: Singh's wife is presented exclusively as a sweet and gentle character.
9314.correction: Although Singh does speak softly of his wife, she also has a fierce streak. This is shown when her eyes are described as like 'guns' and through the description of her arguments with Singh's parents.

5627.correction: Although the poem doesn't follow a conventional and predictable rhyme scheme, it does have some irregular and half rhymes (e.g. "chapatti" and "chutney"). This structure imitates the playful and joyous content of the poem.

2926.belief: The farmer is simply trying to care for his wife, his actions are well-intentioned and innocent.
2926.statement: The farmer is simply trying to care for his wife, his actions are well-intentioned and innocent.
2926.correction: The farmer's attempts to care for his wife may initially seem genuine, but the poem suggests a deeper complexity to their relationship. The bride's evident distress and desire to escape challenge the notion of the farmer's benevolence.

257.belief: Analysis should focus on the bride.
257.statement: Analysis should focus on the bride.
257.correction: Although there is lots to say about the bride - and her treatment in the relationship - the farmer also presents a rich source of analysis through his often contradictory actions throughout the poem (explored in the written task in Learning Cycle 2).

9532.belief: The speaker kills Porphyria out of love, and his actions can be seen as a romantic gesture.
9532.statement: The speaker kills Porphyria out of love, and his actions can be seen as a romantic gesture.
9532.correction: The speaker's actions aren't a romantic gesture but a sign of his disturbed mind. His love is possessive and obsessive, shown by his desire to control Porphyria. The calm tone he uses to describe the murder show his detachment from reality.

5710.belief: Porphyria is entirely passive and without agency.
5710.statement: Porphyria is entirely passive and without agency.
5710.correction: Porphyria displays agency by actively seeking out the speaker and initiating intimacy. Her actions challenge societal norms, reflecting her independence and desire, despite her eventual victimisation.

5655.belief: All of these poems present relationships which are dysfunctional in some way.
5655.statement: All of these poems present relationships which are dysfunctional in some way.
5655.correction: Although 'Porphyria's Lover' and 'The Farmer's Bride' appear to show abusive, controlling relationships, the relationship in 'Singh Song!' is presented as a much more conventionally loving one.

1840.belief: Comparative responses are just a list of similarities and differences.
1840.statement: Comparative responses are just a list of similarities and differences.
1840.correction: While identifying similarities and differences is essential, your comparative response should also articulate a clear argument that ties these observations together.

9928.belief: Romantic poems are only about love and beauty.
9928.statement: Students might think Romantic poems are only about love and beauty.
9928.correction: Romantic poems also explore deep emotions, the sublime in nature, individualism and sometimes darker themes like sorrow and longing, reflecting the complexity of human experience.

3972.belief: Knowing that the Brownings were married to each other is an important piece of contextual information.
3972.statement: Knowing that the Brownings were married to each other is an important piece of contextual information.
3972.correction: Although it is relevant to know they were married, it is in linking their own unconventional marriage to the subversive presentation of love and relationships in their poems that the best contextual points can be found.

10859.belief: All Victorian poets held the same views and attitudes towards societal issues.
10859.statement: All Victorian poets held the same views and attitudes towards societal issues.
10859.correction: Victorian poets had diverse views. Some challenged norms, others reinforced them. Consider each poem's own unique perspective.

9849.belief: Context should be mentioned separately at the end of their paragraphs, rather than integrated throughout their analysis.
9849.statement: Students may think context should be mentioned separately at the end of their paragraphs, rather than integrated throughout their analysis.
9849.correction: Context should be woven into your analysis to enrich your interpretation e.g. 'Nagra's depiction of family duties versus personal desires draws from his British-Indian experience, showcasing challenges faced by second-generation immigrants.'

10342.belief: Titles shouldn't form a part of your analysis.
10342.statement: That titles shouldn't form a part of your analysis.
10342.correction: The title forms our first impression of the poem and therefore is a rich area for analysis.

9654.correction: Structural choices are consciously made by the poet in order to influence the meaning of the poem.

10119.belief: You should take imagery at face value.
10119.statement: That you should take imagery at face value.
10119.correction: Imagery in poetry is often metaphorical and symbolises a deeper meaning.

9535.belief: The speaker of the poem is the poet.
9535.statement: That the speaker of the poem is the poet.
9535.correction: A poet may talk about their own experiences through the speaker, or they may be exploring another aspect of the human psyche and experience through the speaker.

1985.belief: You should consider the bigger picture of a text rather than minute detail.
1985.statement: That you should consider the bigger picture of a text rather than minute detail.
1985.correction: Zooming in on individual words is a powerful analytical tool that allows you to see patterns in meaning.

9291.statement: That similes and metaphors are interchangeable.
9291.correction: Similes and metaphors are conceptually different since, in a simile, one thing does not become another while in a metaphor they do become each other.

9180.belief: You should select quotations by spotting methods within a poem.
9180.statement: That you should select quotations by spotting methods within a poem.
9180.correction: While analysing methods is an important part of understanding a text, selecting quotations should focus on which word(s) create an evocative impression.

1856.belief: Comparison involves spotting the differences between poems.
1856.statement: That comparison involves spotting the differences between poems.
1856.correction: Arguably, the best comparisons are where there is an exploration of subtle differences within similarities.

11194.belief: Your feelings about a poem are irrelevant.
11194.statement: That your feelings about a poem are irrelevant.
11194.correction: How you respond to a poem forms the basis of your argument about a poem - it helps you to understand how a poet has created meaning.

5125.belief: There is one correct way of organising your thoughts for a plan.
5125.statement: That there is one correct way of organising your thoughts for a plan.
5125.correction: Creating a plan is designed to help you see what your argument is - there is no definitive way of how you should organise your thoughts.

255.belief: Analysing a text is an individual exercise.
255.statement: Analysing a text is an individual exercise.
255.correction: Having discussions around a text can help us build on our ideas and reconsider different ways of interpreting the text.

10347.belief: The tone and mood of the poem are the same thing.
10347.statement: That the tone and mood of the poem are the same thing.
10347.correction: Tone refers to the attitude of the writer towards the subject matter while mood refers to the effect the writing has on the reader.

9274.belief: Sibilance only creates a sinister atmosphere.
9274.statement: That sibilance only creates a sinister atmosphere.
9274.correction: Sibilance can also create a soothing atmosphere.

1992.belief: Considering which poem you have a stronger emotional reaction to is not worthwhile.
1992.statement: That considering which poem you have a stronger emotional reaction to is not worthwhile.
1992.correction: Comparing your personal responses to poems can help you to see how the poet has managed to create meaning and mood through their writing.

3582.belief: The idea of life being temporary must always be a sad notion.
3582.statement: That the idea of life being temporary must always be a sad notion.
3582.correction: The idea of life being temporary might inspire us to live life to the fullest.

1846.belief: Comparing language is the best way to compare poems.
1846.statement: That comparing language is the best way to compare poems.
1846.correction: As well as comparing the language, you can also compare the use of form, structure and voice in poems.

5478.belief: Personal responses involve making guesses about the writer's context and state of mind.
5478.statement: That personal responses involve making guesses about the writer's context and state of mind.
5478.correction: Personal responses consider how and why a poem might create a certain emotion in the reader or what they say about society in general.

4285.belief: You should only look for differences between poems in a comparative response.
4285.statement: That you should only look for differences between poems in a comparative response.
4285.correction: A comparative response involves analysing and exploring the similarities and differences in how two poems present an idea or concept.

10743.belief: Using tentative language makes your argument seem less convincing.
10743.statement: That using tentative language makes your argument seem less convincing.
10743.correction: Using tentative language acknowledges that we are exploring poets' intentions and that there are many valid interpretations of a text.

248.belief: You can only analyse what techniques a poet chooses to use.
248.statement: That you can only analyse what techniques a poet chooses to use.
248.correction: Sometimes it's very powerful to analyse why a poet may have chosen not to use a technique in contrast to one who did choose to use it.

4086.belief: 'Leave Taking' is either universal, or about specific experiences and characters.
4086.statement: 'Leave Taking' is either universal, or about specific experiences and characters.
4086.correction: Like with many texts, we must hold both the idea of Leave Taking's universal themes with the specific experiences of its characters.

5672.belief: There is no point talking about the minor characters in a play - they are not important.
5672.statement: There is no point talking about the minor characters in a play - they are not important.
5672.correction: Each character, no matter how seemingly insignificant, is crafted by the writer and placed in the text for a specific purpose. It is your job to consider what their purpose is.

4085.belief: 'Leave Taking' is a commentary on the experiences of all women.
4085.statement: 'Leave Taking' is a commentary on the experiences of all women.
4085.correction: Pinnock presents the unique stories of her created characters. The centrality of women suggests she is making some sort of social comment, but she is not generalising about every single woman's experience of the world.

838.belief: You can't explore the dramatic function of off stage characters.
838.statement: You can't explore the dramatic function of off stage characters.
838.correction: Off stage characters can help develop a world beyond the stage itself, grounding the play in its own reality.

10880.belief: Viv, Del and Enid are not British citizens.
10880.statement: Viv, Del and Enid are not British citizens.
10880.correction: All three women are British citizens. Enid relocated from one part of the Commonwealth to another. During this post war period, this ensured legal status in Britain. Viv and Del were born in Britain.

2011.belief: Context can't be used in a thesis statement. It must be saved for main body paragraphs.
2011.statement: Context can't be used in a thesis statement. It must be saved for main body paragraphs.
2011.correction: Including context in a thesis statement is a powerful way to start an essay. It shows you understand the writer's intentions with their work.

3586.belief: Ideas for one essay question can't be used in any other essay on the same text.
3586.statement: Ideas for one essay question can't be used in any other essay on the same text.
3586.correction: By the end of exploring and writing about a text, you will realise that there are certain ideas and references which you can rely on over and over.

11139.belief: Writers always create entirely original characters, and using similar character types or archetypes makes a story unoriginal.
11139.statement: Writers always create entirely original characters, and using similar character types or archetypes makes a story unoriginal.
11139.correction: Archetypes explore universal themes, evolving with context. Writers reshape them, making characters unique while keeping familiar depth.

3809.belief: The Inspector is a ghost and his supernatural qualitites should be interpreted literally.
3809.statement: The Inspector is a ghost and his supernatural qualitites should be interpreted literally.
3809.correction: Whilst this is one interpretation, it must be considered alongside the symbolic value of the Inspector’s supernatural elements and Priestley’s purpose.

5576.belief: The play is definitely a religious allegory, and all interpretations align with this view.
5576.statement: The play is definitely a religious allegory, and all interpretations align with this view.
5576.correction: While the religious allegory is a valid interpretation, it’s important to consider it as one lens. Focussing on one interpretation may limit a deeper analysis of the text’s complexity.

3985.belief: Labeling literary features like "metaphor" or "imagery" is enough to demonstrate analysis.
3985.statement: Labeling literary features like "metaphor" or "imagery" is enough to demonstrate analysis.
3985.correction: Feature spotting is not analysis. You need to explain how the writer's choices create different meanings and link to the writer's intention and wider themes.

674.belief: The Birlings are not guilty of any crimes in 'An Inspector Calls' because they do not face legal consequences.
674.statement: The Birlings are not guilty of any crimes in 'An Inspector Calls' because they do not face legal consequences.
674.correction: While the Birlings do not face legal prosecution, Priestley uses their moral failings to argue that crime is not only a legal matter.

3937.belief: Justice is exclusively linked to legal punishment.
3937.statement: Justice is exclusively linked to legal punishment.
3937.correction: In 'An Inspector Calls', Priestley challenges the idea that justice is solely legal. He presents moral and psychological punishment, showing that guilt and self-reflection drive real change, not just legal consequences.

8937.belief: Rewording or summarising the main points of a question will lead to a developed response.
8937.statement: Rewording or summarising the main points of a question will lead to a developed response.
8937.correction: A nuanced response goes beyond rewording the question. It requires you to engage deeply with the text, offering detailed analysis and considering multiple layers of meaning.

9382.correction: Does Snowball enjoy the "milk and apples" too? What is he awarded after the Battle of the Cowshed and how does this position Snowball?

9381.belief: Snowball isn't to blame for the failed revolution.
9381.statement: Snowball isn't to blame for the failed revolution.
9381.correction: How many examples can you find where Snowball supports hierarchical ideas that go against the ideals of equality?

953.belief: The characters are referred to as real people. For example "Old Major describes himself as...".
953.statement: The characters are referred to as real people. For example "Old Major describes himself as..."
953.correction: Think about the purpose of the characters and why Orwell has constructed them the way he has.

11020.belief: The windmill is only presented as a negative.
11020.statement: The windmill is only presented as a negative.
11020.correction: Explore Snowball's initial plans. How does he view the role of the windmill? Orwell is showing how industry and progress can be exploited.

4709.belief: Mollie is the only character interested in sugar as a luxury.
4709.statement: Mollie is the only character interested in sugar as a luxury.
4709.correction: Napoleon orders sugar for his table and his consumption alone. What does this tell us about the hypocrisy of the pigs?

10236.belief: Thesis statements and topic sentences are the same.
10236.statement: That thesis statements and topic sentences are the same.
10236.correction: Differentiate; the thesis statement is a comment on the text as a whole, and a topic sentence has a focus on a specific part of the text.

6426.statement: Pupils often fail to consider the symbolic importance of Duncan and, in particular, Malcolm in the play.
6426.correction: Ask pupils what the moral message of the play would be if Malcolm did not end the play as king.

6755.statement: Pupils often get mixed up between a noun appositive and a relative clause.
6755.correction: The relative pronoun 'who' could lead to pupils trying to add too much extra detail about a character, a noun appositive encourages brevity.

549.belief: Banquo's main purpose in the play is to act as a foil, highlighting Macbeth's treachery.
549.statement: Banquo's main purpose in the play is to act as a foil, highlighting Macbeth's treachery.
549.correction: Explore the purpose of Fleance, by asking pupils how they think events would have unfolded if Fleance had been killed too.

5986.belief: Macbeth and his wife have never had children.
5986.statement: Pupils assume Macbeth and his wife have never had children.
5986.correction: Remind pupils about Lady Macbeth's "I have given suck" (1.7). Explore the idea that the Macbeths may have had a child die in infancy.

6091.belief: Lady Macbeth holds most of the responsibility for Macbeth's actions.
6091.statement: Pupils believe Lady Macbeth holds most of the responsibility for Macbeth's actions.
6091.correction: When considering the witches' role, ask pupils which ideas can be used to counter the significance of Lady Macbeth's role in his downfall?

4333.belief: Macduff acts as a foil to Macbeth solely because he is noble and courageous.
4333.statement: Macduff acts as a foil to Macbeth solely because he is noble and courageous.
4333.correction: Ask pupils if Macbeth had dealt with his grief/devastation like Macduff would there have been different outcomes?

6068.belief: All exam questions need unique ideas and responses.
6068.statement: Pupils believe that all exam questions need unique ideas and responses.
6068.correction: When looking at the question in the first learning cycle, ask pupils if they can use ideas/arguments from previous 'Macbeth' essays.

11041.belief: Women were completely powerless in patriarchal societies.
11041.statement: Women were completely powerless in patriarchal societies.
11041.correction: While women's lives were restricted, they were not completely powerless.

11050.belief: Women always took a passive role in relationships in the Elizabethan era.
11050.statement: That women always took a passive role in relationships in the Elizabethan era.
11050.correction: Arguably, Juliet takes an active role in her relationship with Romeo.

3103.belief: Forgiveness is always a personal choice.
3103.statement: That forgiveness is always a personal choice.
3103.correction: Sometimes people feel societal pressure to forgive someone.

5320.belief: Paris is an unimportant plot device in 'Romeo and Juliet'.
5320.statement: That Paris is an unimportant plot device in 'Romeo and Juliet'.
5320.correction: Paris' interactions with Lord Capulet and Juliet arguably reveal contemporary stereotypes of relationships between men and women.

8944.belief: The rhythm of a character's speech is unimportant.
8944.statement: That the rhythm of a character's speech is unimportant.
8944.correction: Exploring the rhythm of a character's speech can reveal their emotional state.

2792.belief: Everyone believes we all have control over our life and decisions.
2792.statement: That everyone believes we all have control over our life and decisions.
2792.correction: If you believe in fate, then you believe that our life is predetermined and our decisions ultimately don't matter.

3287.belief: We can get a definitive idea of the writer's intentions from the text.
3287.statement: We can get a definitive idea of the writer's intentions from the text.
3287.correction: We can never truly know what the writer's intentions were but we can tentatively explore ideas.

9625.belief: All stories can be unambiguously plotted on a Freytag's Pyramid. It is clear which element is which.
9625.statement: All stories can be unambiguously plotted on a Freytag's Pyramid. It is clear which element is which.
9625.correction: Complex stories, like Jekyll and Hyde, are open to interpretation as to how each element can be plotted on the pyramid.

9615.belief: Stevenson just replicates or reiterates common gothic conventions.
9615.statement: Stevenson just replicates or reiterates common gothic conventions.
9615.correction: Many common gothic conventions are used but subverted too (the setting of Regent's Park subverts gothic settings).

2009.belief: Context is a bolt-on and can just be added onto the end of a paragraph.
2009.statement: Context is a bolt-on and can just be added onto the end of a paragraph.
2009.correction: Context should be a considered and interwoven part of any essay.

4745.belief: Mr. Utterson is an example of a respectable, Victorian gentleman.
4745.statement: Mr. Utterson is an example of a respectable, Victorian gentleman.
4745.correction: The reality is more complex. Utterson seems more concerned with protecting the reputation of Jekyll than pursuing any real justice.

4746.belief: Mr. Utterson is judgemental of all immoral behaviour.
4746.statement: Mr. Utterson is judgemental of all immoral behaviour.
4746.correction: Mr. Utterson seems incredibly judgemental of the Victorian poor and their behaviour but he is willing to turn a 'blind eye' to his friends.

10988.belief: Whether Dr. Lanyon being a foil for Dr. Jekyll is a straightforward answer.
10988.statement: Whether Dr. Lanyon being a foil for Dr. Jekyll is a straightforward answer.
10988.correction: Whether Lanyon is a foil for Jekyll is debatable. They have clear differences (e.g. scientific views) but similarities too (curiosity).

9841.belief: All the characters are hypocritical because they are all keeping secrets.
9841.statement: Students often think all the characters are hypocritical because they are all keeping secrets.
9841.correction: Keep drawing their attention back to the keywords and their definitions.

9911.belief: A parable is just a story with a moral/didactic message.
9911.statement: Students think that a parable is just a story with a moral/didactic message.
9911.correction: The word 'parable' relates specifically to the stories told by Jesus in the Gospels. A story with a moral/didactic message is an allegory.

9888.belief: Marley's message is only about Christianity and not aimed at everyone.
9888.statement: Students think that Marley's message is only about Christianity and not aimed at everyone.
9888.correction: Marley's Ghost's message is one of morality. When he alludes to biblical parables, he does it to draw attention to their moral lessons.

9931.belief: Scrooge is a Christ-figure in the novella.
9931.statement: Students think that Scrooge is a Christ-figure in the novella.
9931.correction: Whilst some parallels are arguably evident between Scrooge and Christ, the idea that Tiny Tim is a Christ-figure is probably more viable.

7147.statement: Pupils do not recognise the significance of Dickens' description of Scrooge's fireplace.
7147.correction: The description contains a multitude of allusions that enhance our understanding of the characters Marley's Ghost and Scrooge.

9856.statement: Students often think that different ideas equal different arguments.
9856.correction: Show students our Oak pupils' suggestions. Their suggestions are not different arguments, but different ideas which can form an argument.

9934.belief: Scrooge raising Bob's wage is an act of charity or generosity.
9934.statement: Some students might think that Scrooge raising Bob's wage is an act of charity or generosity.
9934.correction: Scrooge never paid Bob fairly to begin with. He is therefore not doing him a favour by raising his wage, but simply doing the decent thing.

9726.statement: Students often don't realise that they need to carefully consider what the question is asking them.
9726.correction: Before students can plan anything, they need to consider what the question is actually asking them to do. Rephrasing the question can help.

1647.belief: When choosing a topic, you should not choose something personal to focus on.
1647.statement: When choosing a topic, you should not choose something personal to focus on.
1647.correction: Choosing something meaningful and personal can help you to find and develop your authentic voice. It's all about ensuring you talk about the topic in enough detail and complexity, regardless of what you choose.

8050.belief: They need to write out their whole presention before they deliver it.
8050.statement: Pupils sometimes think they need to write out their whole presention before they deliver it.
8050.correction: It can be much more effective to verbally plan and practice presentations without writing it in full. Approaching the tasks verbally can increase pupil confidence in articulating ideas out loud.

6116.belief: They are the only person to feel nervous or scared about public speaking.
6116.statement: Some pupils believe that they are the only person to feel nervous or scared about public speaking.
6116.correction: Most people feel nervous before speaking, even the most experienced public speakers. It's all about understanding what nerves are and how you can manage them.

2601.belief: I can effectively practise my presentation in my head.
2601.statement: I can effectively practise my presentation in my head.
2601.correction: Although it is good to think about your presentation, you will need to practise delivering it out loud. This will give you a much better idea of timing and pace.

8989.belief: The role of an audience member isn't particularly important.
8989.statement: The role of an audience member isn't particularly important.
8989.correction: Emphasise the power of a supportive and respectful audience. Being an encouraging audience member can help peers succeed.

704.belief: Books are irrelevant to them and their lives.
704.statement: Books are irrelevant to them and their lives.
704.correction: Books are one way of sharing stories - stories have always been part of human history as they are a way of forming connections and understanding the world around us.

9702.belief: West Egg and East Egg are actual geographical locations.
9702.statement: Students might believe that West Egg and East Egg are actual geographical locations.
9702.correction: While West Egg and East Egg are based on real places on Long Island, they are fictional locations created by Fitzgerald to symbolise different social classes and the contrasts between new and old wealth.

5224.belief: All opinions in response to written texts are equal.
5224.statement: All opinions in response to written texts are equal.
5224.correction: The best personal responses to texts will evaluate the writer's craft in eliciting that opinion.

2654.belief: The ending of a text isn't as important as the story itself.
2654.statement: That the ending of a text isn't as important as the story itself.
2654.correction: The ending of a text defines the story - it offers resolution or poses questions and can impact the way we see characters and the way we interpret the overall meaning of a story.

3890.belief: It's best to give the reader all of the backstory at the start of a novel so that they understand the context of the events.
3890.statement: It's best to give the reader all of the backstory at the start of a novel so that they understand the context of the events.
3890.correction: By feeding information to the audience slowly, it arguably builds discomfort in the reader and creates an unsettling environment.

9600.belief: Starting with a vivid description of the character's pain is a great way to hook a reader.
9600.statement: Starting with a vivid description of the character's pain is a great way to hook a reader.
9600.correction: While beginning with a vivid description of pain can add an element of shock, it often doesn't leave the reader anywhere to go emotionally. It might be more effective to leave vivid descriptions of pain for the climax of a text.

8806.belief: A recurring image happens by accident - especially if it's an everyday object then it's likely to be meaningless.
8806.statement: That a recurring image happens by accident - especially if it's an everyday object then it's likely to be meaningless.
8806.correction: Images are often symbols for deeper meaning in literature - especially everyday, domestic objects and then can represent ideas about the central theme of a text.

9268.belief: You shouldn't edit and rewrite your writing as you are doing it.
9268.statement: That you shouldn't edit and rewrite your writing as you are doing it.
9268.correction: Often it's very effective to rewrite your work as you go so that you can continually craft an effective idea and ensure you are creating a cohesive piece.

2333.belief: Dialogue is a superfluous part of a text and can't be analysed in the same way as other structural or language features.
2333.statement: That dialogue is a superfluous part of a text and can't be analysed in the same way as other structural or language features.
2333.correction: We can analyse dialogue by considering how it's structured, how the conversation is divided up, the use of punctuation and through the use of body language.

3654.belief: The only important part of writing a dialogue is thinking about which words the characters are going to use.
3654.statement: That the only important part of writing a dialogue is thinking about which words the characters are going to use.
3654.correction: When writing dialogue, you want to consider how you can show emotion through descriptions of facial expressions, body language, and your use of punctuation and structure.

1986.belief: We should only consider the image that a simile offers us.
1986.statement: That we should only consider the image that a simile offers us.
1986.correction: While the image may be particularly evocative, it's also useful to analyse the connotations of the comparative image as that can reveal layers to what the writer is trying to portray to the reader.

3895.belief: It's impossible to create imaginative similes.
3895.statement: That it's impossible to create imaginative similes.
3895.correction: While your mind will often go to common similes at first, you can consider how you can use synonyms/antonyms, sensory details, and extra detail in order to create imaginative similes.

11133.belief: You can write the opening of a story without knowing the ending.
11133.statement: You can write the opening of a story without knowing the ending.
11133.correction: An effective opening builds up the atmosphere in order to lead the reader to the ending; therefore, you have to know what the ending is in order to create a cohesive atmosphere in the opening.

11098.belief: The words exchanged between characters are the most effective way to convey the relationship between them.
11098.statement: The words exchanged between characters are the most effective way to convey the relationship between them.
11098.correction: Often, the most effective dialogue comes from considering body language and the balance of the lines.

2409.belief: Discourse around teenagers in the 1950s and 60s would be entirely different to discourse around teenagers nowadays.
2409.statement: Discourse around teenagers in the 1950s and 60s would be entirely different to discourse around teenagers nowadays.
2409.correction: There are some strong similarities between the media portrayal of teenagers from decades ago and now e.g. their ability to shape trends.

9953.belief: A text has a sole purpose e.g. only to persuade or only to argue.
9953.statement: Students sometimes think that a text has a sole purpose e.g. only to persuade or only to argue.
9953.correction: Draw their attention to the tone of Mark Twain's speech - he's quite humorous.

9855.belief: Differences need to be large when comparing texts.
9855.statement: Students often think that differences need to be large when comparing texts.
9855.correction: Encourage them to look for subtle differences.

9662.statement: Students may be more accustomed to writing informative articles. In Learning Cycle 2, they may want to explain how love has changed over time rather than give their opinion on it.
9662.correction: Students can create a more engaging article, which is more vibrant with a clear sense of voice, by including their opinion on a topic.

9993.statement: Students might be used to writing their memories as a stream of consciousness, without stopping to consider craft.
9993.correction: Writing memories as a stream of consciousness is a good place to start. However, once one thinks about publishing work, editing and conscious crafting is necessary.

7849.belief: Foreshadowing can only be used for upcoming events of a negative nature.
7849.statement: Pupils may think foreshadowing can only be used for upcoming events of a negative nature.
7849.correction: If pupils want to hint at positive memory to come, foreshadowing can also be used.

9695.belief: Open letters have to be written to those in powerful positions.
9695.statement: Students may believe that open letters have to be written to those in powerful positions.
9695.correction: There are open letters on a wide range of topics and niches. All that an open letter requires is a strong feeling about something.

9929.belief: Sassoon's style of open letter is the only way to write an open letter.
9929.statement: Students may think that Sassoon's style of open letter is the only way to write an open letter.
9929.correction: Open letters can have a range of purposes. Those that will never be read by the recipient or where the writer doesn't expect to create change (e.g. open letter to Mondays) will typically involve more humour.

3868.belief: Irony is the same thing as a coincidence.
3868.statement: That irony is the same thing as a coincidence.
3868.correction: Irony is a contrast between expectations and reality whereas coincidence involves a great deal of luck, or chance.

9913.belief: That some people are just naturally funny and that being funny can't be taught.
9913.statement: Students sometimes think that that some people are just naturally funny and that being funny can't be taught.
9913.correction: Explain that humour is a skill that can be developed and practised by using words and phrases deliberately.

9884.belief: Lee's account is true of all North Koreans.
9884.statement: Students may think that Lee's account is true of all North Koreans.
9884.correction: Draw attention to the fact the book is a memoir. It is personal and about what she recalls and what she felt. The context helps us appreciate her own experience.

9952.belief: They have to tell a story chronologically.
9952.statement: Students often think that they have to tell a story chronologically.
9952.correction: Encourage them to consider how many books and films start with an exciting event and then go back to explain the exposition of the story.

9941.belief: They should show or tell the key details of a story immediately.
9941.statement: Students often think that they should show or tell the key details of a story immediately.
9941.correction: Encourage them to think about mysteries and thrillers which keep the identify of the villain secret.

9834.belief: This book describes what life is like for the majority of people who live in Malawi.
9834.statement: Students may think that this book describes what life is like for the majority of people who live in Malawi.
9834.correction: Draw attention to the fact that the book is an autobiography and, therefore, is about the writer's own experiences.

9885.belief: Linguistic devices should be used as often as possible.
9885.statement: Students often think that linguistic devices should be used as often as possible.
9885.correction: Encourage them to use linguistic devices judiciously. Overuse can be as as much of a problem as underuse.

2859.belief: Any expert view adds credibility to your argument.
2859.statement: That any expert view adds credibility to your argument.
2859.correction: Ideally, a quotation from an expert should be recent and the expert should have knowledge that is relevant to the topic.

373.belief: An argument is a disagreement and something which is confrontational.
373.statement: An argument is a disagreement and something which is confrontational.
373.correction: In an article, an argument is a reason or set of reasons given in support of an idea, action or theory that you give the reader in order to convince them that your idea is correct.

3695.belief: Including any statistics is enough to make your argument more convincing.
3695.statement: Including any statistics is enough to make your argument more convincing.
3695.correction: In order to be convincing, statistics have to be credible.

9661.statement: Students may not be accustomed to forming an opinion on a narrator, typically seeing them as a neutral figure in a story.
9661.correction: First person narrators are often protagonists of their stories and they can retell the events in any way they want to. This allows us to be critical of a narrator.

10449.belief: We can always trust the narrator in a story to tell us the truth about events and people.
10449.statement: That we can always trust the narrator in a story to tell us the truth about events and people.
10449.correction: Writers will sometimes create unreliable or untrustworthy narrators.

4818.belief: A narrative written in the first person perspective conveys the writer's voice.
4818.statement: A narrative written in the first person perspective conveys the writer's voice.
4818.correction: A narrative written in the first person perspective does not necessarily reflect the writer's voice but a construct.

7108.statement: Pupils may not realise that they can choose a unique narrative perspective for their creative writing as they may not have come across that many narrative perspectives other than human.
7108.correction: Tell pupils that writers have written from the perspective of animals, objects, abstract ideas etc. Give examples. 'Black Beauty' is written from a horse's perspective. 'The Book Thief' is narrated by Death.

8613.statement: Pupils may be used to encountering a detached third person narrator thus expecting most narrators to be trustworthy and reliable.
8613.correction: When a writer chooses to write a story from a characters' perspective, we have to consider that each character is fallible or unreliable. Thus, we have to re-filter (through our own consciousness) the information we get from a first person narrator.

7148.statement: Pupils may not recognise how terms of endearment can be patronising.
7148.correction: Terms of endearment are traditionally used as a sign of affection but they can be used to subdue, belittle or appease someone (depending on the context).

3964.belief: We have to know everything about a narrator and their world in order for a story to make sense.
3964.statement: We have to know everything about a narrator and their world in order for a story to make sense.
3964.correction: Through slow crafting of a voice, we can let our reader work out the true nature of our narrator, world and characters as they read.

4887.belief: You just need to say that your character isn't human to create an artifical voice.
4887.statement: That you just need to say that your character isn't human to create an artifical voice.
4887.correction: To create an artificial voice, you want to consider how your character would describe themselves, their surroundings, and their interactions in a way that shows they are not human.

2533.belief: Dystopian voices have to fit the archetype (e.g. rebellious, overly critical) in order to be compelling.
2533.statement: Dystopian voices have to fit the archetype (e.g. rebellious, overly critical) in order to be compelling.
2533.correction: Ishiguro subtly crafts his voices to allow the reader to reflect on their own world.

10647.belief: You can never use slang, colloquialisms and idioms in narrative writing.
10647.statement: You can never use slang, colloquialisms and idioms in narrative writing.
10647.correction: If slang, colloquialism and idioms are part of your narrative voice, it is okay to use them but you have to ensure your use of them comes across as deliberate, consistent and that you have secure grammar and control over the piece of work.

4820.belief: All narratives have to follow the traditional story arc and have a chronological order for them to make sense.
4820.statement: All narratives have to follow the traditional story arc and have a chronological order for them to make sense.
4820.correction: Short stories often have to manipulate the traditional story structure to be engaging from the very beginning.

5601.belief: Plot is the most important part of a narrative.
5601.statement: Plot is the most important part of a narrative.
5601.correction: Voice is equally important to plot when writing a narrative. Ask students: if there was a resolution to the story but no distinct voice, how would the story change? Would it be effective, enjoyable?

9956.belief: Travel writing needs to be about far away places.
9956.statement: Students may think that travel writing needs to be about far away places.
9956.correction: Draw their attention to the social messages implied in the titles 'Down and Out in Paris and London' and 'Travels with Charley: In Search of America'.

1990.belief: When considering description, students often focus on the external effect.
1990.statement: When considering description, students often focus on the external effect.
1990.correction: Ask how things might look different depending on your personality or circumstances? Offer examples e.g. how a town might be described differently by someone who enjoys living there and someone who dislikes living there.

9972.belief: All writing should begin at the beginning and move through the middle to the end.
9972.statement: Students may think that all writing should begin at the beginning and move through the middle to the end.
9972.correction: Encourage them to think about how stories, especially films, often start with an exciting scene.

9827.belief: Attitudes are often strong and one dimensional.
9827.statement: Students think that attitudes are often strong and one dimensional.
9827.correction: Encourage them to think about how it is possible for a book or a film to be both frightening and enjoyable.

9898.belief: They need to include as much as possible in their argument and support their ideas with overly long quotations.
9898.statement: Students sometimes think they need to include as much as possible in their argument and support their ideas with overly long quotations.
9898.correction: Encourage students to select short and precise quotations to keep their writing concise.

9721.statement: Students often consider that sophisticated writing always involves using complex and challenging vocabulary.
9721.correction: Draw attention to the way very simple words are used to create complex effects.

9707.statement: Students may confuse analogies with other comparative based figures of speech such as simile and metaphor.
9707.correction: Encourage students to think of students as an extended example and the core purpose is explanation not the evocation of associations and related imagery.

9897.belief: They need exciting experiences to write in a compelling manner.
9897.statement: Students often think that they need exciting experiences to write in a compelling manner.
9897.correction: Stress how the quality of writing is more important than the topic being written about.
