8171.belief: They should present a balanced view in opinion-based writing.
8171.statement: Pupils often think that they should present a balanced view in opinion-based writing.
8171.correction: It is much more convincing and persuasive to only present one side of the argument.

6432.statement: Pupils often fail to realise that they don't have to write from their own perspective.
6432.correction: Inform pupils that it can be incredibly powerful to write from another, imagined perspective.

9738.statement: Students may feel that their viewpoint needs to be established in the very first line or so.
9738.correction: Viewpoint can be alluded to in the first few lines and firmly established at the end of the first paragraph or section.

9700.belief: The topic sentence has to be a straight-forward statement of opinion.
9700.statement: Students believe that the topic sentence has to be a straight-forward statement of opinion.
9700.correction: The topic sentence, like any other part of their writing, can be written creatively, forcing the reader to infer the writer's opinion.

9693.statement: Students often believe that longer sentences are more sophisticated.
9693.correction: Great writing needs to be concise. Students should be aiming for precision, rather than sophistication.

9896.belief: They need to describe everything in a setting.
9896.statement: Students think that they need to describe everything in a setting.
9896.correction: Ask students to 'bounce' around a scene, only describing the most influential and important aspects of it.

9880.belief: The more items within a scene they can describe, the better the description.
9880.statement: Students think that the more items within a scene they can describe, the better the description.
9880.correction: Ask them to consider how they can create atmosphere by limiting their focus to 3-4 focal points in the setting and using figurative language

9852.belief: Describing something's overall appearance makes a good description.
9852.statement: Students often think that describing something's overall appearance makes a good description.
9852.correction: Description is about making your reader imagine what you are imagining. You have to give really specific details about a person or setting.

9959.belief: Using figurative language to describe emotions means using similes and metaphors.
9959.statement: Students think using figurative language to describe emotions means using similes and metaphors.
9959.correction: Students should use figurative language more subtly, in verbs and adjectives to create extended metaphors.

9900.belief: They need to write an 'exciting' story which includes lots of action.
9900.statement: Students think that they need to write an 'exciting' story which includes lots of action.
9900.correction: A genuinely engaging story allows the reader to empathise with the character(s) and experience the same emotions as them, at the same time.

947.belief: Characters either conform to or subvert stereotypes within texts.
947.statement: That characters either conform to or subvert stereotypes within texts.
947.correction: We might see Romeo and Juliet as both conforming to and subverting societal expectations of gender at different moments in 'Romeo and Juliet' - characters are typically multifaceted rather than one note.

5319.belief: Parents have always taken their children's wishes into account.
5319.statement: That parents have always taken their children's wishes into account.
5319.correction: In Elizabethan England, children were expected to act in a way that would benefit their family through work or marriage.

3837.belief: We can only interpret Friar Lawrence as a mentor figure to Romeo.
3837.statement: That we can only interpret Friar Lawrence as a mentor figure to Romeo.
3837.correction: Though Friar Lawrence offers Romeo advice, we might also see his portrayal in a more negative light.

108.belief: Adding in an alternative interpretation weakens your argument.
108.statement: Adding in an alternative interpretation weakens your argument.
108.correction: As long as your alternative interpretation supports your overall argument then it will strengthen your argument.

3752.belief: Individuality has always been associated with being unique and making your own decisions.
3752.statement: Individuality has always been associated with being unique and making your own decisions.
3752.correction: In the sixteenth century, individuals were seen as existing as part of a network of social and family structures.

3753.belief: Individuality is always celebrated in literature.
3753.statement: Individuality is always celebrated in literature.
3753.correction: Arguably, Shakespeare could be seen as demonstrating the consequences of individuality through 'Romeo and Juliet'.

10692.belief: Using counter-arguments throughout your essay makes it a stronger argument.
10692.statement: Using counter-arguments throughout your essay makes it a stronger argument.
10692.correction: You should have one clear, critical response to the question that informs your whole essay.

7133.statement: Pupils may only recognise the destructive force of ambition in the play.
7133.correction: It is also possible to consider the destructive force of guilt as central to the play.

3419.belief: Guilt is only observable in Macbeth and Lady Macbeth after the murder of King Duncan.
3419.statement: Guilt is only observable in Macbeth and Lady Macbeth after the murder of King Duncan.
3419.correction: We can look at early scenes in the play through the lens of guilt since Shakespeare has a clear motive for centering the play on guilt.

4148.belief: Light is only referenced and significant in Macbeth's 'Stars, hide your fires' soliloquy taken from Act 1, Scene 4.
4148.statement: Light is only referenced and significant in Macbeth's 'Stars, hide your fires' soliloquy taken from Act 1, Scene 4.
4148.correction: If we look closely at what could be considered 'minor' scenes in the play, we can begin to build a clear and nuanced idea of the motif of light throughout.

9781.statement: Students may have only perceived the hallucinations in the play as summoned by the witches.
9781.correction: We can read the same elements of the play through many different lenses. All interpretations are valid.

9737.statement: Students may be familiar with the function of sleep, but less aware of the symbolism and connotations.
9737.correction: Whilst sleep is vital for healing and serves a restorative function, it also symbolises innocence and vulnerability.

694.belief: Blood only symbolises violence and bloodshed.
694.statement: Blood only symbolises violence and bloodshed.
694.correction: Blood comes to symbolise psychological turmoil and guilt as the play progresses.

9848.belief: Concluding sentences are a repetition of topic sentences.
9848.statement: Students may think that concluding sentences are a repetition of topic sentences.
9848.correction: Concluding sentences focus on the writer's intentions and link to but do not repeat topic sentences.

5801.belief: Priestley wrote 'An Inspector Calls' solely to change the views of his audience.
5801.statement: Priestley wrote 'An Inspector Calls' solely to change the views of his audience.
5801.correction: While it may seem that Priestley wrote 'An Inspector Calls' solely to change the views of his audience, it could also be argued that a 1945 audience would lean towards socialist ideals and therefore his play aimed to solidify these views.

4839.belief: Naturalism and expressionism are too different and cannot be used together in the same play.
4839.statement: Naturalism and expressionism are too different and cannot be used together in the same play.
4839.correction: Arguably, Priestley blends both styles. Naturalism makes the setting realistic, while expressionism distorts reality to highlight emotional and symbolic themes, strengthening his political message.

5575.belief: The play is definitely Brechtian or purely social realism.
5575.statement: The play is definitely Brechtian or purely social realism.
5575.correction: The ideas behind Brechtian theatre and social realism were part of the cultural landscape when Priestley was writing. Instead of fitting it into one category, it’s better to consider how Priestley may have been influenced by these forms.

10210.belief: Texts can only be compared to others from the same time period or literary movement.
10210.statement: Texts can only be compared to others from the same time period or literary movement.
10210.correction: In reality, comparing texts across different periods or movements can enrich understanding, as themes, ideas, and literary techniques often transcend time.

3810.belief: The Inspector can only be interpreted as representing absolute truth, as he always speaks with authority and moral certainty.
3810.statement: The Inspector can only be interpreted as representing absolute truth, as he always speaks with authority and moral certainty.
3810.correction: The Inspector may not represent absolute truth. He selectively reveals information and uses moral rhetoric, which could suggest he's guiding the audience toward a particular interpretation of events.

9616.belief: You must stick to a single interpretation or approach throughout your essay to make a strong argument.
9616.statement: You must stick to a single interpretation or approach throughout your essay to make a strong argument.
9616.correction: Whilst you should have an overarching argument, embracing nuance by exploring multiple interpretations deepens your analysis. This approach strengthens your argument by showing the text’s complexity and layers.

1910.belief: The concept of truth is something that cannot be changed.
1910.statement: The concept of truth is something that cannot be changed.
1910.correction: Our perception of what it true can be altered by those around us.

4018.belief: Language cannot alter how you see someone else.
4018.statement: Language cannot alter how you see someone else.
4018.correction: Alienating and divisive language can be used to create the perception that someone is an outsider and separate from our social group.

3838.belief: The only interpretation of Orwell's 'Animal Farm' is that the pigs' desire for power leads to the animals' oppression.
3838.statement: The only interpretation of Orwell's 'Animal Farm' is that the pigs' desire for power leads to the animals' oppression.
3838.correction: We might also interpret the animals as being complicit in allowing their oppression to happen.

293.belief: The animals in 'Animal Farm' are unintelligent and therefore cannot grasp complex language.
293.statement: The animals in 'Animal Farm' are unintelligent and therefore cannot grasp complex language.
293.correction: Conversely, we might suggest that the pigs' simplification of the animals' language suppresses their ability to use language to express themselves.

4817.belief: The narrative voice of 'Animal Farm' reports the truth to the reader.
4817.statement: The narrative voice of 'Animal Farm' reports the truth to the reader.
4817.correction: Arguably, the narrative voice withholds information about the pig's oppressive behaviour.

4019.correction: The language that we use to present facts can alter people's perception of the facts and therefore, in essence, change the facts.

6137.belief: The stage directions are written by whoever is putting on a production of the play.
6137.statement: Pupils may believe that the stage directions are written by whoever is putting on a production of the play.
6137.correction: Although there is some interpretation of how an actor peforms a scene, the stage directions will have been written by the playwright as part of the script.

5987.belief: Mai’s bedsit is only a negative symbol of her failure to integrate into British society.
5987.statement: Pupils may assume Mai’s bedsit is only a negative symbol of her failure to integrate into British society.
5987.correction: Highlight that while the bedsit represents her struggles, it also serves as a place of support and stability for other characters, symbolising her resilience and strength.

6064.belief: Enid's flat is a straightforward symbol of her success and assimilation into British culture, ignoring its role as a site of personal and cultural conflict.
6064.statement: Pupils may believe that Enid's flat is a straightforward symbol of her success and assimilation into British culture, ignoring its role as a site of personal and cultural conflict.
6064.correction: Remind pupils that while the flat does represent Enid's material success it is also the site of many of the play's conflicts.

7693.belief: All characters view Jamaica as an idealised homeland.
7693.statement: Pupils may think that all characters view Jamaica as an idealised homeland.
7693.correction: Explain that while Brod and Mai idealise Jamaica, Enid's more cynical view highlights the hardships she faced there, creating tension between characters' perspectives.

8314.belief: Temporal ellipsis is used solely because the playwright wants to avoid showing certain events on stage due to logistical constraints or a desire to avoid graphic scenes.
8314.statement: Pupils may think that temporal ellipsis is used solely because the playwright wants to avoid showing certain events on stage due to logistical constraints or a desire to avoid graphic scenes.
8314.correction: While practical concerns can influence a playwright’s decision, temporal ellipsis is primarily a deliberate artistic choice to emphasise emotional or psychological consequences over the event itself.

8334.belief: A turning point in a play only involves a major event, such as a character's death, without recognising the emotional or relational changes that accompany it.
8334.statement: Pupils might think that a turning point in a play only involves a major event, such as a character's death, without recognising the emotional or relational changes that accompany it.
8334.correction: It’s important to clarify that a turning point not only indicates a significant event but also involves the emotional and relational dynamics of the characters e.g. the emotional aftermath of Mooma's death as well as the event itself.

6976.statement: Pupils might mistakenly believe that generational conflict only refers to disagreements between parents and children, overlooking the broader societal influences that shape the conflict.
6976.correction: Generational conflict in 'Leave Taking' isn't just about family disagreements; it is also influenced by the different social, cultural, and historical experiences that shape each generation’s view of identity and belonging.

3770.belief: The Industrial Revolution was a wholly positive change for society because machines created jobs and allowed for foriegn travel.
3770.statement: The Industrial Revolution was a wholly positive change for society because machines created jobs and allowed for foriegn travel.
3770.correction: While there were many advantages to the Industrial Revolution, there were also many disadvantages such as pollution, worsening of working conditions and a widening of the class divide.

3875.belief: There isn't much point analysing setting to learn about theh characters or themes of text; it just provides the scenery for the action to take place in.
3875.statement: There isn't much point analysing setting to learn about theh characters or themes of text; it just provides the scenery for the action to take place in.
3875.correction: Often writers use setting to subtly foreshadow events or symbolise important paralells to characters. Analysing settings is a useful way to learn more about characters and key themes.

10861.belief: Most Victorians were religious people which meant that they behaved in a way that was morally good.
10861.statement: Most Victorians were religious people which meant that they behaved in a way that was morally good.
10861.correction: While most Victorians were religious and followed stict moral codes, they did so only in public. Behind clsosed doors, immoral and debaucherous behaviour was common.

3631.belief: Immoral behaviour was something only the lower classes engaged in.
3631.statement: Immoral behaviour was something only the lower classes engaged in.
3631.correction: Immoral behaviour was something that crossed class boundaries but it manifested differently; for the lower classes, vice was survival-based with many turning to crime to survive whereas the wealthy engaged in debauchery and illicit affairs.

4319.belief: There were lots of treatments available to Victorians to help them recover from psychological conditions.
4319.statement: There were lots of treatments available to Victorians to help them recover from psychological conditions.
4319.correction: While there were lots treatments available, many showed serious misunderstandings about human psychology. They were ineffecive, some were inhumane and many left patients with long-term psychological damage.

9126.belief: All scientific developments during the Industrial Revolution were positive in terms of their impact on society.
9126.statement: All scientific developments during the Industrial Revolution were positive in terms of their impact on society.
9126.correction: While the Industrial Revolution was considered to be the 'golden age' of scientific development and innovation, much of the pioneering research was conducted under unethical conditions.

265.belief: Analytical paragraphs should lead by identifying how a writer uses language, form and/or structure.
265.statement: Analytical paragraphs should lead by identifying how a writer uses language, form and/or structure.
265.correction: The best analytical writing begins by exploring how key ideas or attitudes in a poem link to the question focus, supported by analysis of how the writer uses language, form and/or structure to convey these ideas or attitudes.

3766.belief: The Industrial Revolution brought great prosperity to the Britain; factories helped to provide wealth equality because it provided jobs to help poor people out of poverty.
3766.statement: The Industrial Revolution brought great prosperity to the Britain; factories helped to provide wealth equality because it provided jobs to help poor people out of poverty.
3766.correction: The Industrial Revolution did bring great prosperity but unfortunately the wealth was not shared across all social classes. Industrial wealth improved the lives of business owners but poor people suffered due to low wages and overcrowding.

5434.belief: People who work hard enough can escape poverty.
5434.statement: People who work hard enough can escape poverty.
5434.correction: This was a common belief in Victorian times when people in poverty faced much social stigma. Unfortunately, poverty was not easy to escape; many poor people were uneducated, had no access to healthcare and lived in cramped conditions.

10954.belief: Wealth alone guaranteed a high social status in Victorian society.
10954.statement: Wealth alone guaranteed a high social status in Victorian society.
10954.correction: While wealth was important to securing high social status, reputation was extremely important to wealthy Victorians. Arranged marriages and inheritance were key levers to ensure a good family reputation.

2334.belief: Dickens aims to shame his wealthy readers into showing compassion by demonstrating that poor people cannot enjoy Christmas because of the poverty they are forced to live in.
2334.statement: Dickens aims to shame his wealthy readers into showing compassion by demonstrating that poor people cannot enjoy Christmas because of the poverty they are forced to live in.
2334.correction: While Dickens does use the novella to encourage his readers to show compassion, his depictions of poor people do show them enjoying Christmas. In fact, we could argue poorer characters seem happier because they are able to enjoy simple pleasures.

10956.belief: Wealthy Victorians did feel bad about those living in poverty but had no power to do anything about it.
10956.statement: Wealthy Victorians did feel bad about those living in poverty but had no power to do anything about it.
10956.correction: Many wealthy Victorians felt little sympathy for the poor, believing instead that people in poverty were lazy or morally inferior.

11113.belief: Workhouses were a positive form of social reform; instead of being sent to prison, poor people were offered the chance to work off any debts they had.
11113.statement: Workhouses were a positive form of social reform; instead of being sent to prison, poor people were offered the chance to work off any debts they had.
11113.correction: Workhouses were an alternative to debtor's prison but they were not positive places; inmates were separated from their families, lived in squalid conditions and forced to do hard labour for 10-12 hours a day.

5702.belief: Poppies is a poem about a mother whose son died during WWI.
5702.statement: Poppies is a poem about a mother whose son died during WWI.
5702.correction: Although Poppies are a symbol of remembrance for those who died in WWI, Weir uses her poem to draw attention to the many conflicts that have occurred throughout history. It isn't clear which conflict the son is heading off to fight in.

4281.belief: We no longer experience gender inequality in today's society.
4281.statement: We no longer experience gender inequality in today's society.
4281.correction: Although today's society is much more progressive than Victorian society, there are still areas where gender inequality is experienced, although it is usually much more subtle and institutionalised.

2597.belief: Effective comparative analysis leads by comparing the poets' use of literary methods.
2597.statement: Effective comparative analysis leads by comparing the poets' use of literary methods.
2597.correction: The most effective comparative analysis writing should lead by comparing key ideas of attitudes in both poems.

2017.belief: Context is required in every paragraph of a comparative analytical response.
2017.statement: Context is required in every paragraph of a comparative analytical response.
2017.correction: Context is important to include in your response but it isn't necessary in every paragraph. In order to avoid 'bolt-on' context, it should only be used when it is relevant to the point you're making in that paragraph.

2448.belief: It doesn't matter which two poems you choose to compare as all of them can be compared with each other.
2448.statement: It doesn't matter which two poems you choose to compare as all of them can be compared with each other.
2448.correction: In theory, you can compare any two poems from the anthology however it's important to remember that some have more connections than others. You should aim to select two poems with a range of connections to avoid tenuous links.

264.belief: Analytical paragraphs should lead by comparing how the writers use language, form and/or structure.
264.statement: Analytical paragraphs should lead by comparing how the writers use language, form and/or structure.
264.correction: The best comparative analytical writing begins by exploring connections between the key ideas or attitudes in a poem, supported by analysis of how writers use language, form and/or structure to convey these ideas or attitudes.

9528.belief: The speaker calls himself "unfinished" because he didn't participate in the initiation ceremony.
9528.statement: The speaker calls himself "unfinished" because he didn't participate in the initiation ceremony.
9528.correction: The line says that his tribe would consider him unfinished, but doesn't explain how the speaker himself feels.

9530.belief: The speaker feels as though he doesn't belong in either 'home' (Zambia or the UK).
9530.statement: The speaker feels as though he doesn't belong in either 'home' (Zambia or the UK).
9530.correction: The speaker seems to identify more with his African culture, reflecting on how his identity is "unfinished" which implies it isn't lost completely.

3980.belief: 'Kumukanda' can only be compared to other anthology poems about cultural identity (e.g. 'Jamaican British' and 'The Émigrée'.
3980.statement: 'Kumukanda' can only be compared to other anthology poems about cultural identity (e.g. 'Jamaican British' and 'The Émigrée'.
3980.correction: Although poems centred around cultural identity and inner conflict are most obvious choices to compare, you could compare 'Kumukanda' with another poem that focuses on grief and loss (for example 'I Remember, I Remember').

2331.correction: Although Wales features in the title of this poem, Dharker moved to Scotland just before her first birthday. She references Glasgow (where she grew up) in the second stanza of the poem.

5664.belief: The poetic voice in the poem is definitely Imtiaz Dharker.
5664.statement: The poetic voice in the poem is definitely Imtiaz Dharker.
5664.correction: While Dharker uses some of her life experiences as references in the poem (Glasgow, 1960s and 1970s), there are also many examples which may not relate to her life. Arguably she is trying to seem relatable to all readers.

9537.belief: The speaker of the poem wants everyone to be more tolerant and united.
9537.statement: The speaker of the poem wants everyone to be more tolerant and united.
9537.correction: Although the speaker does claim to want this, he does also confess that he finds it challenging at times, especially when it comes to his personal relationship with "you".

5623.belief: This poem has a clear message about togetherness and division.
5623.statement: This poem has a clear message about togetherness and division.
5623.correction: This poem is an abstract exploration of the different ways divisions and togetherness affect our relationships with each other (both personal relationships and our relationships in society).

10310.belief: All three poems explore conflict and belonging related to cultural identity because all three poets have an intercultural identity.
10310.statement: All three poems explore conflict and belonging related to cultural identity because all three poets have an intercultural identity.
10310.correction: All three poets have an intercultural identity and this is reflected in many of their poems. However here, only 'Kumukanda' explores these ideas directly. Dharker focuses on identity and growing up; Kunial explores belonging in a more abstract way.

9792.statement: Students may not recognise that this poem is a metaphor for human mortality and the approach of death.
9792.correction: Keats wrote this poem after he had been diagnosed with tuberculosis. Perhaps this poem was his way of accepting his own approaching death.

9816.statement: Students tend to confuse tone and mood. They are not the same thing.
9816.correction: Tone is the way in which the poet expresses their feelings towards the subject matter. Mood is the atmosphere that is created by the tone. Tone creates mood.

9918.belief: This poem is just about Wordsworth's time ice-skating as a child.
9918.statement: Students often think that this poem is just about Wordsworth's time ice-skating as a child.
9918.correction: The poem also portrays the sheer power and beauty of nature. It is as much about nature as it is Wordsworth's childhood.

9831.belief: Because Wordsworth loved nature, he couldn't be frightened of it.
9831.statement: Students think that because Wordsworth loved nature, he couldn't be frightened of it.
9831.correction: Wordsworth respected and loved nature - he understood the sheer size and power of nature versus his own existence. His own insignificance in the face of such astonishing and breath-taking views arguably made him feel slightly fearful.

9004.belief: Romantic poems are about the beauty of nature.
9004.statement: That Romantic poems are about the beauty of nature.
9004.correction: While Romantic poets often wrote admiringly about nature, they are primarily concerned with their interaction with nature.

5644.belief: This poem is about a speaker who is mourning the loss of summer.
5644.statement: This poem is about a speaker who is mourning the loss of summer.
5644.correction: The poem can also be read as a metaphor for the passing of time. Whilst there are moments which feel mournful in the poem, there is a sense of hope and encouragement.

8950.belief: Rhythm and rhyme are used to make the text sound poetic.
8950.statement: Rhythm and rhyme are used to make the text sound poetic.
8950.correction: Pupils should always link the poet's use of rhythm and rhyme back to their intentions. How does this help explore some of the messages the poet is trying to convey?

9870.belief: The frogs are literally attacking the speaker.
9870.statement: Students think that the frogs are literally attacking the speaker.
9870.correction: The description in the poem of the frogs as an army is the speaker's perception of the frogs - it is how he imagines them to be behaving.

251.belief: When analysing this poem, students might not use terminology as well as they could.
251.statement: When analysing this poem, students might not use terminology as well as they could.
251.correction: Heaney uses a lot of onomatopoeia in his descriptions within this poem, as well as semantic fields and figurative language.

9787.statement: Students might not realise that they can talk about how the theme of nature is used in a poem, as well as how it is presented.
9787.correction: Keats and Dickinson both use the theme of nature as a vehicle to explore human emotion. Here, the theme of nature is used almost as a method in the poems.

9677.statement: Students often avoid analysing structure because they sometimes struggle to understand what it actually is and means.
9677.correction: The structure of a text is just how the poem has been put together - what comes where and why. Using the words 'establishes' 'builds on' and 'ends' will encourage students to talk about structure more confidently.

9824.belief: They will only be asked to answer one poetry question.
9824.statement: Students might think that they will only be asked to answer one poetry question.
9824.correction: The examination requires students to answer 2 questions: the first one is an analysis of a single poem; the second one is a comparison question.

9908.belief: Once they have written a response, it is the finished product.
9908.statement: Students often think that once they have written a response, it is the finished product.
9908.correction: The first draft is simply a first attempt - improvements can always be made and the second draft is always stronger.

399.belief: Art is always meant to be beautiful.
399.statement: Art is always meant to be beautiful.
399.correction: Art can be a means of sparking discussion, representing political views, or addressing problems in society.

2991.belief: The final word of a poem is an unimportant detail.
2991.statement: The final word of a poem is an unimportant detail.
2991.correction: The final word of the poem offers us the lasting impression of the poem's message.

10126.belief: Taking a photograph of someone's suffering is an effective way of showing their suffering to others.
10126.statement: Taking a photograph of someone's suffering is an effective way of showing their suffering to others.
10126.correction: Arguably, both Duffy and Ghose reveal the futility of using art as a means of showing their suffering to others.

10505.belief: Typically, literature presents the idea of a simple life as dull and monotonous.
10505.statement: Typically, literature presents the idea of a simple life as dull and monotonous.
10505.correction: Literary movements such as the Romantics presented an idealised view of a simple, rural existence.

3605.belief: You should ignore any parts of the poem that don't fit with your overall interpretation.
3605.statement: You should ignore any parts of the poem that don't fit with your overall interpretation.
3605.correction: To create a nuanced argument, you want to think about why the poet may have chosen not to present a cohesive whole to the poem.

830.belief: You cannot be both respected and feared.
830.statement: You cannot be both respected and feared.
830.correction: The Romantic sublime was the concept that we should feel awe towards nature - a mixture of both fear and respect.

5171.belief: There is only one valid interpretation of a method.
5171.statement: There is only one valid interpretation of a method.
5171.correction: There might be several different ways of interpreting a method.

11144.belief: You have to be writing in the C18th to use Romantic conventions in your writing.
11144.statement: You have to be writing in the C18th to use Romantic conventions in your writing.
11144.correction: While Romanticism was a predominant movement in the C18th and C19th, more modern poets can also adhere to Romantic conventions and present a Romantic view of the world.

10990.belief: While comparing poems, you should only look for similarities between them.
10990.statement: While comparing poems, you should only look for similarities between them.
10990.correction: To create an effective comparison, you want to find nuanced differences within overall similarities.
